   

To August, Elise, Hillary, Rosie, and Stella

 

# [PREFACE TO THE  
REVISED EDITION](#contents.xhtml#pre1)

Why update this book after only two years? Some numbers help answer this question. Close to 70% of the text in this “revised edition” is new. A quarter of these changes come from wholly new chapters. One example is [Chapter 12](#chapter12.xhtml), which focuses on artificial intelligence. In the first edition, AI flowed through the book—and it still does. But the extraordinary and unexpected advances of 2022 and 2023 warranted a dedicated discussion of computer vision, machine learning, and generative transformer models, in addition to the many ways in which they are accelerating and enriching the development of the Metaverse.

[Chapters 10](#chapter10.xhtml) and [11](#chapter11.xhtml), which cover mixed-reality hardware and blockchains, were in the original book, but have been entirely replaced. These fields are in their seventh and second decades respectively, but also saw remarkable evolutions in the span of only 24 months. Apple’s Vision Pro is not only the highest-profile “head-mounted display” since the early prototypes of the 1950s, but Apple’s most significant product launch since 2007’s iPhone. The company is also believed to have spent more than twice as long and 10–15 times as much developing this headset as it did on the iPhone, too, or roughly eight years and $20–$30 billion in total. Facebook has spent more than $60 billion on its suite of mixed-reality devices since 2014 and spent much of 2023 unveiling prototypes of devices that might appear later this decade—some of which more closely resemble the eyes of a dragonfly than a camera, but which help us understand the enormous sums spent on research and development and the role of hundreds of millions of years of evolution in charting humanity’s digital future.

In November 2021, the combined market cap of all publicly traded cryptocurrencies peaked at roughly $3 trillion. In April 2022, the field experienced its largest-ever decline—falling from $2.25 trillion to $825 billion in just ten weeks. That same year, Ethereum seamlessly completed its “merge,” which is one of the blockchain community’s most impressive and important achievements, only to then engage in a “royalties war” that may have upended the technology’s core value propositions. With over $80 billion raised by blockchain start-ups since 2012—only 20% of which was invested prior to 2020—each passing month provides substantially more evidence of blockchain’s feats and failures, as well as its challenges and potential, and the debates in between. By March 2024, nearly two years after crypto’s historic crash, its combined market cap had crept back to $2.6 trillion.

Not all Metaverse technologies were radically altered over the past 24 months, but each one progressed. In 2023, Google unveiled a new quantum computer that was 241 million times more powerful than its 2019 edition. Nvidia, a 30-year-old company that was originally focused on designing graphics processing units for video gaming, has become one of the world’s most important companies due to the aforementioned advances in AI, and its GPUs among the tech world’s most valuable resources. Nvidia’s founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, has predicted the economy of the Metaverse will one day exceed that of the physical world. In 2023, SpaceX’s Starlink launched its 5,650th satellite, with its internet constellation constituting close to two-thirds of all active satellites orbiting the earth. By 2024, Facebook is expected to own or de facto control close to 13% of the global submarine internet backbone, with a particular concentration in the African and Asian-Pacific continents. The leaps in computing and networking ([Chapters 5](#chapter5.xhtml) and [6](#chapter6.xhtml)) change the balance of power in the Metaverse, its likely business model, and global potential.

Interoperability ([Chapter 8](#chapter8.xhtml)), one of the most fraught and unpredictable aspects of the Metaverse’s development, also surged in 2022 and 2023. Epic Games unveiled Verse, which it envisioned as the “programming language of the Metaverse,” alongside its expanded *Fortnite* ecosystem, including *LEGO Fortnite*, *Rocket Racing*, and *Fortnite Festival*, which led to all-time highs in users, player hours, and revenues for the more than six-year-old title. Two months later, the Walt Disney Company announced a $1.5 billion dollar investment into Epic Games to produce a “new, persistent, and interoperable universe” that would be part of the Fortnite ecosystem, span franchises and brands from Avatar and Star Wars to ESPN and Disney Cruise Line, and enable users to create their own Disneylands and Disney Worlds, and watch and shop for Disney content and products. In parallel, Pixar, Adobe, Apple, Autodesk, and Nvidia, in partnership with the Linux Foundation, Epic Games, and Unity, also launched the OpenUSD format, which Nvidia had proposed as “the HTML of the Metaverse”—a comprehensive framework for describing, composing, simulating, and collaborating within 3D worlds.

Other updates to the book reflect reader feedback and areas of interest. *The Metaverse* now includes detailed histories of the founding of companies such as Epic Games and Oculus VR, and an examination of why it was that in 2021 the Metaverse began to surge to national headlines ([Chapter 3](#chapter3.xhtml)). [Chapter 4](#chapter4.xhtml), which unpacks my widely cited description of the Metaverse on a keyword-by-keyword basis, has been revamped for clarity and to differentiate between the “minimum” and “full-spec” Metaverse. The first edition of this book had four charts and exhibits; this revision has more than ten times as many.

The re-release also comes at a very different time in the macroeconomic cycle. Beginning in late 2022, interest rates rose faster than at any point since the dawn of the internet and to levels higher than at any point since the debuts of Amazon Web Services in 2002 and the iPhone in 2007—two events which are considered the starts of the cloud and mobile computing eras. Increases in the cost of capital and a squeeze on profits led many companies to reduce their Metaverse investments and focus instead on nearer-term business opportunities. This narrative shift has led to increased skepticism toward the Metaverse—and prompted many of the companies which once boasted the term and its ideas to substitute it for other decades-old buzzwords, such as “immersive” or “spatial.” Irrespective of the words used or sentiment, the trends are clear. The number of virtual worlds made each year, the number of people inside them as well as the money and time they spend there, and the cultural influence of those spaces all continue to grow. The deployment of real-time 3D-simulation and game-engine technology also continues to grow, as have their capabilities and business applications. These tools are increasingly used in healthcare, industrial design, civic management, automotive, aerospace, and artificial intelligence—to entertain and to improve lives and even save them. The Metaverse is a 100-year-old idea and 30-year-old word; no matter what it’s called, it gets nearer and clearer each day.

 

# [INTRODUCTION](#contents.xhtml#int1)

Technology frequently produces surprises that no one predicts. But the biggest and most fantastical developments are often anticipated decades in advance. In the 1930s, Vannevar Bush, then president of the Carnegie Institution of Washington, began work on a hypothetical electromechanical device that would store all books, records, and communications, and mechanically link them together by keyword association, rather than traditional, mostly hierarchical, storage models. Despite the enormity of its archive, Bush stressed that this “Memex” (short for “memory extender”) could be consulted “with exceeding speed and flexibility.”

In the years that followed this early research, Bush became one of the most influential engineers and science administrators in American history. From 1939 to 1941, he was vice chairman and temporarily served as chairman of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, the predecessor agency to NASA. In this position, Bush convinced President Franklin D. Roosevelt to establish what became the Office of Scientific Research and Development (OSRD), a new federal agency that would be run by Bush, who would report directly to the president. The agency was provided nearly unlimited funding, primarily for secret projects that would aid the United States’ efforts in World War II.

Only four months after OSRD was founded, President Roosevelt approved the atomic bomb program known as the Manhattan Project, following a meeting with Bush and Vice President Henry A. Wallace. To manage the Manhattan Project, Roosevelt created a Top Policy Group consisting of himself, Bush, Wallace, Secretary of War Henry L. Stimson, Chief of Staff of the Army General George C. Marshall, and James B. Conant, who headed up a subbranch of OSRD previously run by Bush. In addition, the Uranium Committee (later named the S-1 Executive Committee) would report directly to Bush.

After the war ended in 1945, but two years before he left his role as director of the OSRD, Bush wrote two famous essays. The first, “Science, the Endless Frontier,” was addressed to the president and in it, Bush called for an increase in government investments in science and technology, rather than a peacetime reduction, as well as the establishment of the National Science Foundation. The second essay, “As We May Think,” appeared in *The Atlantic* and publicly detailed Bush’s vision of the Memex.

In the years that followed his essays, Bush stepped back from public office and public view, yet his influence matured as his various contributions to government, science, and society began to converge. Starting in the 1960s, the US government funded a variety of projects within the Department of Defense, in partnership with a network of external researchers, universities, and other nongovernment institutions, that together developed the foundation of the internet. At the same time, Bush’s Memex was informing the creation and evolution of “hypertext,” which enabled nearly all online information, content, documents, and pages to be interconnected and instantly accessed through clickable text links. The HyperText Transfer Protocol would later become one of the core protocols of the Internet Protocol Suite (TCP/IP) and defining aspects of the World Wide Web, which is typically written in the HyperText Markup Language (HTML). In 1986, partly inspired by Bush’s writings, the US federal government established the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) to guide the technical evolution of the Internet Protocol Suite.

While technological progress typically occurs out of common sight, science fiction often provides the general public with the clearest view of the future. In 1968, fewer than 10% of American households had a color TV, yet the second-highest-grossing film of the year, *2001: A* *Space Odyssey*, imagined a future in which humanity had compressed these fridge-sized devices into coaster-thin displays and used them idly during breakfast. Anyone watching the film today will instantly liken these devices to iPads. As with Bush’s Memex, this imagined technology took longer to arrive than was originally anticipated. iPads appeared in stores four and a half decades after Stanley Kubrick’s groundbreaking film was released, and more than a decade after the year in which the futuristic film was set.

By 2021, tablets had become commonplace and spacefaring had begun to feel within reach, with the competing efforts of Richard Branson’s Virgin Galactic, Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin appearing on front pages and inspiring dreams of civilian space stations and multiplanetary colonization. Yet 2021 saw another fantastical vision begin to take hold—one that promised to take humanity anywhere without ever having to leave their homes, let alone terra firma; that imagined not a new planet but a new plane of existence on top; and that focused on building new universes rather than just exploring the solar system. This vision was called “the Metaverse.” And while the term was nearly 30 years old and the ideas behind it older than even Bush’s Memex, the world’s most powerful companies and executives seemed to believe it would soon arrive.

## **“A Metaverse Company”**

For most people, the heralding of the Metaverse’s arrival began the same day they first heard the term. On October 28, 2021, Facebook, one of the most widely known brands in human history, announced it would subsequently be known as Meta Platforms.^([\*](#introduction.xhtml#footnote-064)) Facebook’s founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, explained that the name change signified his commitment to transforming the 17-year-old “social media company” into a “Metaverse company,” and that he hoped the move would help rally the company’s users, partners, employees, and shareholders behind this mission.

Though some argued Zuckerberg’s announcement was little more than an attempt to shed Facebook’s controversial existing brand, the company’s pivot to the Metaverse was, in fact, already in its eighth year. In 2014, Facebook had purchased Oculus VR for approximately $2 billion—a sum twice what was paid to acquire Instagram two years earlier. By 2018, an internal report developed by Facebook’s executive team^([†](#introduction.xhtml#footnote-063)) and distributed to select board members declared that the Metaverse could be built by 2022 and was “ours to lose,” while calling on the company to “act first, and go big, or we risk being \[a\] wannabe.”^([1](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr1))

By the time of Facebook’s name change, the company had spent roughly $29 billion to develop, manufacture, and sell virtual reality (VR) headsets, augmented reality (AR) devices, brain-to-machine interfaces, and other technologies intended to build the Metaverse.^([2](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr2)) As Zuckerberg began to publicly detail these investments, he warned shareholders that the costs would reduce operating income at least $10 billion per year for several more years and that the Metaverse would not arrive for five to ten more years. But when it arrived, Zuckerberg promised, it would be worth trillions.

For many who were hearing about the “Metaverse” for the first time, Zuckerberg’s announcements were surprising. But those announcements were also backed by a decade and a half of success. Facebook was not just the sixth-most-valuable publicly listed company in the world; it was the youngest company to rank in the top 50. Facebook’s non-Metaverse businesses were generating close to $60 billion in operating cash flow—a sum that few companies had ever exceeded and that was so large it managed to make Facebook’s Metaverse investments seem modest. Zuckerberg also had a history of investing long before profits and building hundred-billion-dollar businesses out of products his rivals had considered profitless hobbies. And less than a decade ago, Zuckerberg oversaw one of the most successful platform pivots in technology history. In May of 2012, he declared Facebook would become a “mobile-first company,” and over the following five quarters, mobile’s share of Facebook’s revenue grew from between 3% and 5% to over 50%.^([3](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr3))

Zuckerberg’s repositioning of Facebook was also aided, and perhaps implicitly encouraged, by his competitors. In March of 2021, the social gaming platform Roblox had completed the largest-ever initial public offering (IPO) in the history of video gaming, finishing its first trading day at a $45 billion valuation.^([4](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr4)) In its prospectus, Roblox declared itself a Metaverse company, while highlighting that its business plan “assumed” the “adoption of the Metaverse” which, in its view, was now “materializing” after 30 years of advances in computing power, high-bandwidth internet connections, and other related technologies.^([5](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr5)) Moreover, many Wall Street analysts had argued the commonalities between *Roblox* and “2D” social networks such as Facebook, Instagram, and Snapchat. At the time of its IPO, *Roblox* had more than 40 million daily users and nearly 200 million monthly, and estimated that three-quarters of Americans aged 9–12 used the platform on a regular basis.^([6](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr6)) When Facebook purchased Instagram in 2012, the image-sharing network had fewer than 30 million monthly users; by the end of 2021, it had more than a billion monthly users. When Snapchat rebuffed a Facebook acquisition offer in 2013, it had fewer than 25 million monthly users; by the end of 2021, it had more than 500 million.

In May 2021, two months after Roblox’s record-breaking IPO, Satya Nadella, the CEO of Microsoft, the world’s second-most-valuable public company, began to talk publicly about the enterprise Metaverse that Microsoft was in the process of building. At its annual Ignite conference later that year, Nadella boasted to developers, “I can’t overstate how much of a breakthrough \[the Metaverse\] is.”^([7](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr7)) May of 2021 also saw China’s largest company, the internet gaming giant Tencent, unveil its vision of the Metaverse, which it dubbed “Hyper Digital Reality.” In early August, Krafton, the maker of the blockbuster battle royale video game *PUBG*, completed its IPO, the second largest in South Korea’s history. Krafton’s investment bankers made sure to tell would-be investors that the company would also be a global leader in the enormously valuable and inevitable “Metaverse.”

August also saw Jensen Huang, CEO and founder of computing, semiconductor, and AI giant Nvidia, which also ranked among the 10 largest public companies in the world, declare that the Metaverse was the “next evolution of the internet,”^([8](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr8)) which he later said would have an economy larger than that of the physical world.^([9](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr9)) By the end of the month, Chinese internet giants Alibaba, the 13th-most-valuable public company in the world, and TikTok owner ByteDance, a start-up whose $500 billion valuation in private markets would have made it the 11th, both began to register various Metaverse trademarks and acquire promising VR- and 3D-related start-ups.

Throughout 2020 and 2021, the Metaverse had also become a popular theme among blockchain and crypto users, developers, and investors. To many in the community, blockchain technologies were needed to build the Metaverse—or at least to build one that protected the rights of individual users and developers, rather than the preferences of whichever groups or governments might own or control the Metaverse. Others argued that, at a minimum, the rise of virtual-only currencies with trillion-dollar market capitalizations, as well as virtual-only items worth tens of millions, demonstrated that society was ready for the Metaverse. In any case, crypto’s rising value was indisputable. In the 12 months leading up to Facebook’s name change, the combined value of all cryptocurrencies and tokens had surged from $400 billion to more than $2.5 trillion.^([10](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr10))

By the end of 2021, the term “Metaverse” had appeared in more than 277 filings made with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), 86 of which preceded Facebook’s announcement.^([11](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr11)) By comparison, “Metaverse” had appeared in fewer than two dozen filings from January 2001 through October 2020, when Roblox filed for its IPO.^([12](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr12)) It took 2022 only 62 days to break 2021’s record. And it did so in its own record-breaking fashion.

## **Trillions and Trillions**

On January 18, 2022, Microsoft announced it would acquire Activision Blizzard, the largest independent video game publisher outside of China, at an enterprise value of $75 billion—making it the largest acquisition in big-tech history. Microsoft’s press release declared, “This acquisition will accelerate the growth in Microsoft’s gaming business across mobile, PC, console and cloud and will provide building blocks for the Metaverse.”^([13](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr13))

Over the following months, every institution seemed to be talking about the Metaverse, whether they made digital toys or physical ones, ran data centers or oil pipelines, crafted sandwiches or gave sermons,^([‡](#introduction.xhtml#footnote-062)) or steered global monetary policy, international peace, or worldwide police enforcement. In total, 2,934 SEC filings used “Metaverse” in 2022, more than ten times as many as in 2021.^([14](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr14))

Increased attention to the Metaverse was propelled by independent validations of the Metaverse’s market potential. The management consultancies Boston Consulting Group and McKinsey & Company estimated the Metaverse would contribute $1.3 trillion^([15](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr15)) and between $4 and $5 trillion^([16](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr16)) to global GDP by 2030, representing roughly 1.1%–4.2% of world GDP by the end of the decade and 4%–17% of growth in world GDP during it.^([17](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr17)) The investment bank Goldman Sachs projected between $2.5 and $12.5 trillion by 2030,^([18](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr18)) while Citi, another bank, and KPMG, a Big Four accounting firm, each predicted $13 trillion.^([19](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr19)) The investment bank Morgan Stanley estimated that the combined Metaverse economies of the United States and China would be worth $16 trillion annually, with other countries, markets, and territories generating trillions more.^([20](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr20))

![US Securities and Exchange Commission](OEBPS/images/pgxx.jpg)

US Securities and Exchange Commission

Governments, too, weighed in. In fact, the response from many governments predated Facebook’s name change. In May of 2021, South Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (Information and Communications Technology) announced the South Korean “Metaverse Alliance,” spanning over 450 companies, including SK Telecom, Woori Bank, and Hyundai Motor. The following year, the ministry announced a $200 million initiative for the alliance intended to make South Korea the fifth-largest Metaverse market by 2026, ranking twice as high as it does in traditional GDP measure.^([21](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr21))

Not long after Tencent publicly unveiled its vision of hyper-digital reality, the Communist Party of China (CCP) began its biggest-ever crackdown of its domestic gaming industry. Among several new policies was a prohibition on minors playing video games Monday through Thursday that also limited their play to between 8 p.m. and 9 p.m. on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday nights.^([22](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr22)) In addition, companies such as Tencent would use their facial recognition software and a player’s national ID to periodically ensure that these rules were not being skirted by a gamer borrowing an older user’s device. Tencent also pledged $15 billion in aid for “sustainable social value,” which Bloomberg said would be focused on “areas like increasing incomes for the poor, improving medical assistance, promoting rural economic efficiency and subsidizing education programs.”^([23](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr23)) Alibaba, China’s second-largest company, committed a similar amount only two weeks later. The message from the CCP was clear: look to your countrymen and women, not virtual avatars.

The Chinese government’s concerns about the growing role of gaming content and platforms in public life became more explicit in August of 2021, when the state-owned *Security Times* warned its readers^([§](#introduction.xhtml#footnote-061)) that the Metaverse is a “grand and illusionary concept” and “blindly investing \[in it\] will ultimately come back to bite you.”^([24](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr24)) Some commentators interpreted China’s various warnings, prohibitions, and taxes as confirmation of the Metaverse’s significance. For a communist and centrally planned country ruled by a single party, the potential of a parallel world for collaboration and communication is a threat, regardless of whether it’s run by a single corporation or decentralized communities.

Yet China’s approach to the Metaverse suddenly shifted in the summer of 2022. Regulators began to allow new game launches and even loosened some of its control over in-game content. China’s domestic giants, such as Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance, also resumed their talk of building the Metaverse. The first edition of this book was also approved for a local release in China, releasing within a month of its US publication, and four weeks later I was the cover story of the August 29, 2022, edition of *Bloomberg Businessweek China*.^([¶](#introduction.xhtml#footnote-060)) Alongside these apparent openings, however, was a new mandate for the Metaverse in China: it should be “independent and controllable,” while also increasing China’s influence over standards of a global Metaverse economy.^([25](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr25)) To this end, the government expanded its bans and prohibitions over blockchain technologies and similarly decentralized structures, and mandated that various national bodies, cities, and industry leaders collaborate to build Metaverse-focused computing, artificial intelligence, and 5G infrastructure.

Many of China’s stated ambitions were mirrored in Middle Eastern countries. Throughout 2022, the crown prince of Dubai, Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, spoke of his plans to make Dubai one of the top ten Metaverse economies globally, the Middle Eastern hub of the Metaverse, and a leader in the development of global standards for the Metaverse. In November, this strategy was formally presented to the nation and approved by Sheikh Mohammad bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the prime minister of the United Arab Emirates and Dubai’s ruler.^([26](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr26)) As part of this program, Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed announced plans to evaluate the country based on its “gross Metaverse product,” which “will be able to create billions of dollars in returns from Dubai without people being physically in the emirate but experiencing it in the Metaverse.”^([27](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr27))

As with the governments of China and South Korea, the European Parliament began to focus on the Metaverse in the months prior to Facebook’s name change. This interest was informed by the multiyear development of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which was officially proposed to the European Commission in December 2020. The DMA was the largest overhaul of digital regulations in the internet’s 40-year history, many of which were intended to curb the powers and reach of the largest (and typically American) tech giants, such as Apple, Amazon, Facebook, Google, and Microsoft. The DMA thus helped propel these companies’ investments in virtual, augmented, and synthetic realities.

A week before the first public rumors of Facebook’s name change in 2021, Christel Schaldemose, a Danish member of the European Parliament who had also served as chief negotiator for the European Union on the DMA, told *Politiken* that “plans for Metaverse are deeply, deeply worrying” and that the union “has to take them into account.”^([28](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr28)) Scrutiny only increased after Facebook’s plans were revealed. In February of 2022, Margrethe Vestager, the EU’s commissioner for competition, told a group of German publishers that “the Metaverse is here already” and so the EU legislature and regulators must begin to act.^([29](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr29)) In September 2022, a report from the EU’s commissioner for internal market, Thierry Breton, stated the Metaverse was “one of the \[Union’s\] pressing challenges,” arguing that action was needed to ensure the Metaverse developed and operated in a manner consistent with European values and rules and with European influence, while warning of the need to prepare European internet infrastructure for the Metaverse. “We are ready to roll out our European ambition,” concluded Breton in his note titled “Europe’s Plan to Thrive in the Metaverse.”^([30](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr30)) By March of 2022, Vestager cautioned that the EU needed to be vigilant if it wanted to avoid a Metaverse dominated by American companies.^([31](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr31))

Regulators in the United States had similar fears to those of their EU counterparts—or at least fears that the existing tech giants would be able to use their cash reserves and market influence to ensure they dominated the budding Metaverse. In July 2022, the US Federal Trade Commission sued to block Facebook’s acquisition of Within, which was announced in October 2021. At the time, Within had fewer than a million estimated active users, but the FTC argued that in acquiring the company “Meta would be one step closer to its ultimate goal of owning the entire ‘Metaverse,’ ” which “poses a reasonable probability of eliminating both present and future competition. That lessening of competition may result in reduced innovation, quality, and choice, less pressure to compete for the most talented app developers.”^([32](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr32))

## **Faster, Stronger, Harder, and Bound to Confuse**

Perhaps no technology buzzword has ever risen so suddenly, so significantly, and with such expectations as “Metaverse” in 2021 and 2022. There have certainly been more popular terms, such as “mobile,” “cloud,” “personal computing,” and “the internet,” but interest in them built more steadily and it took years after the buzz began for companies such as Chevron or Panera Bread to seek related trademarks or patents, or for governments to take such strong preemptive action.

The shocking rise in usage of the term “Metaverse” led to understandable skepticism. Indeed, the tech industry has a history of using buzzwords that are hyped for far longer than they ultimately end up lasting in the market, such as 3D televisions, or that prove to be further away than originally promised, such as VR headsets or virtual assistants.

Some journalists suggested that big tech’s sudden interest in the nebulous idea of the Metaverse was an effort to avoid regulatory action.^([33](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr33)) If governments around the world became convinced that a disruptive platform shift was imminent, then even the largest and most entrenched companies in history need not be broken up—free markets and insurgent competitors would disassemble them in due time and without the messiness of antitrust suits. Others argued that, on the contrary, “the Metaverse” is being used by those same insurgents to force regulators to open antitrust investigations into today’s big-tech companies. Various shareholders, meanwhile, feared that big-tech CEOs were using the vaguely understood term to justify billion-dollar pet R&D projects that were years from public release, probably further behind schedule, and destined for failure.

In practice, this curve primarily reflects the fact that in late 2021 and throughout 2022, many companies, including the likes of Disney and Chevron, rushed to file “intent to use” applications to try to claim the exclusive right to use Metaverse for products and services that they had not yet developed. Accordingly, 2023’s applications are mostly limited to companies that were slower to file claims or want to expand the claims they had previously filed, as well as companies that had not been formed during 2021 or 2022. ¶ US Patent and Trademark Office](OEBPS/images/pgxxv.jpg)

The drop in Metaverse trademark applications during 2023 might suggest a Metaverse bubble has popped and corporations are no longer using the term Metaverse. In practice, this curve primarily reflects the fact that in late 2021 and throughout 2022, many companies, including the likes of Disney and Chevron, rushed to file “intent to use” applications to try to claim the exclusive right to use Metaverse for products and services that they had not yet developed. Accordingly, 2023’s applications are mostly limited to companies that were slower to file claims or want to expand the claims they had previously filed, as well as companies that had not been formed during 2021 or 2022. ¶ US Patent and Trademark Office

Cynics were aided by an unavoidable truth: there seemed to be widespread confusion and/or disagreement about the Metaverse among those who touted it. Some executives argued the Metaverse was decades old (Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, whose company produced two of the best-selling franchises of all time, *Grand Theft Auto* and *Red Dead Redemption*) or had recently arrived (Satya Nadella). Others argued it was imminent (Microsoft founder Bill Gates) or would arrive by the end of the decade (Mark Zuckerberg). A final cohort cautioned against any deadline at all, instead saying the Metaverse would emerge in the coming decades (Jensen Huang, as well as Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, whose company produced *Fortnite*, and Tencent senior vice president, Steven Ma, who leads its hyperreality vision and international games business^([34](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr34))). Moreover, the Metaverse was constantly conflated with video games, VR headsets, crypto, or 3D simulations of a building (known as a “digital twin” or “virtual twin”). Some companies spoke of “the” Metaverse, while others said they were building “a” Metaverse, a semantic difference of little consequence to the average person, but one that revealed significant philosophical disagreements. The companies that raised “the Metaverse” did share one talking point: the Metaverse would, naturally, make their company more profitable, their customers happier, and their competitors less threatening.

Metaverse doubters also noted what often went unsaid by its promoters: that the term originated in dystopic literature. Making matters worse, blockchain-based Metaverse companies and platforms seemed focused on the securitization of virtual existence—selling multimillion-dollar virtual plots of land or images. Not only did this focus strike many as absurd, but it was also offensive given the many, very real problems of the “real world,” such as poverty and climate change. And the digital world as it already existed was fraught with its own issues, from online harassment, misinformation, and data collection—why would anyone need to be online more, let alone exist online? Some recalled the rise of *Second Life* in the early 2000s, which had also been declared the start of virtual existence and appeared on the cover of national magazines, only to fade from memory by the end of the decade.

The skeptics, in short, had a real basis for their skepticism. And as of early 2024, much of it seems validated. Two and a half years after Facebook’s name change, it’s obvious the buzz has receded, if not turned negative. Life isn’t that different, Metaverse revenues are hard to trace, and there are few “Metaverse products” that can be bought that weren’t available for the past decade (and fewer still that are bought). Some companies have started backing away from the term altogether.

But behind the Metaverse hype is something that is both real and distinct from hype cycles of the past. The world’s largest companies never publicly reoriented themselves around the idea of 3D TVs or driverless cars, let alone renamed themselves 3D TV Platforms or Autonomous Vehicle Networks. Nor did they invest $50 billion—and promise to invest tens of billions more—in a speculative future they admitted was five to ten years away. *Second Life* may have fallen short of expectations, but in the 23 minutes it will take the average person to read to this point in the book, more people will have logged in to *Roblox* than used *Second Life* in a month during the peak of its popularity;^([35](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr35)) indeed, more people use *Roblox* in a day than have even set up accounts on *Second Life* in the two decades since its launch in 2003.^([36](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr36))

The term “Metaverse” is not the point. In the first edition of this book, I wrote that society would likely abandon the term “Metaverse” by the time it arrived—an easy bet given the extent it was already misused, its conflation with the vision and success of a specific company (Facebook), and negative associations with blockchains, big tech, and dystopic fiction. In the months leading up to the unveiling of the Vision Pro mixed-reality headset, Apple CEO Tim Cook was asked about Apple’s plans for the Metaverse and replied, “I always think it’s important that people understand what something is. And I’m really not sure the average person can tell you what the Metaverse is.” This is right. Products and experiences matter; terms don’t. Apple never called the iPhone a smartphone, but instead “a revolutionary mobile phone” that combined with a “widescreen iPod and an internet communicator.”^([37](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr37)) It still became the defining smartphone. And the iPod was not sold as an MP3 player, which had existed for years, but “a whole new category of digital music player” that “puts 1,000 songs in your pocket.”^([38](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr38)) The Apple Watch, unsurprisingly, was not a smartwatch but “a revolutionary product that can enrich people’s lives” and “Apple’s Most Personal Device Ever.”^([39](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr39))

And for all his reluctance on using the word “Metaverse,” Cook has been unafraid to declare that humanity’s future is one surrounded by augmented, virtual, and mixed reality. Only a few days before he discussed his reservations about “Metaverse,” Cook gave an off-the-record to an Italian university in which he said, “I’m super excited about augmented reality. Because I think that we’ve had a great conversation here today, but if we could augment that with something from the virtual world, it would have arguably been even better. So I think that if you, and this will happen clearly not too long from now, if you look back at a point in time, you know, zoom out to the future and look back, you’ll wonder how you led your life without augmented reality. Just like today, we wonder, how did people like me grow up without the internet.”^([40](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr40)) Though these remarks were leaked, they were not a new position for Cook, nor a newly public one, either. As early as 2016—long before the Metaverse hype cycle—he promised that eventually, a “significant portion of the population … will have AR experiences every day, almost like eating three meals a day. It will become that much a part of you.… VR I think is not going to be that big, compared to AR. I’m not saying it’s not important, it is important.”^([41](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr41))

When Apple finally unveiled its Vision Pro headset in June 2023, the company chose to brand the device a “spatial computer,” while declaring “the era of spatial computing” had begun.^([42](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr42)) The term “spatial computing” was coined around the same time as Neal Stephenson developed “Metaverse” in the late 1980s and is typically attributed to Bob Jacobson, who co-founded the Human Interface Technology (HIT) lab at the University of Washington in 1989, and/or Tom Furness, another HIT co-founder and pioneering VR researcher. By 1992, Jacobson was using “spatial computing” as part of his start-up, Worldesign.^([43](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr43)) In January 2024, two weeks before the Vision Pro was made available for sale, Apple publicly released its guidelines for Vision Pro developers, stating that developers should “refer to your app as a spatial computing app. Don’t describe your app experience as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), extended reality (XR), or mixed reality (MR).”^([44](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr44))

David Baszucki

@DavidBaszucki

We are deeply humbled by the overwhelming support for @Roblox and our public offering today. To all those who helped us get one step closer to fulfilling our vision of the #Metaverse—thank you. #RobloxIPO

1:40 PM • Mar 10, 2021

Roblox’s Shifting Language

At the time of its October 2020 IPO filing, the term “Metaverse” had appeared in only 17 filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission since January 1, 2001.^([45](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr45)) In its filing, Roblox wrote “Metaverse” 16 times, writing that it operates in a category sometimes known as the “metaverse,” and which Roblox believed was “materializing,” with its “business plan \[assuming\] … the adoption of a metaverse.”^([46](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr46)) During the company’s pre-IPO roadshow, Roblox founder and CEO David Baszucki wrote an opinion piece as part of Wired magazine’s 2021 predictions column titled “The Metaverse Is Coming,” in which he predicted “billions would come to \[Metaverse\] platforms such as Roblox” and that the “Metaverse is arguably as big a shift in online communication as the telephone or the internet.”^([47](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr47)) Then, on the day of the company’s March 2021 IPO, Baszucki tweeted, “To all those who helped get us one step closer to fulfilling our vision of the #Metaverse-thank you. #RobloxIPO.”^([48](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr48)) In early October 2021, Baszucki continued to talk about the popularity of Roblox’s “Metaverse.”^([49](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr49)) However, the company largely stopped using the term following Facebook’s rebrand to Meta in late October 2021. Two years later, Baszucki was asked about reports that the company was distancing itself from “metaverse connotations.” Baszucki demurred, arguing the company had always used other terms such as “human co-experience” and had “evolved the terminology we use,” and claimed, “We’ve never really used the term metaverse a lot.”^([50](#notes_split_000.xhtml#introfr50)) Twitter

The future of the Metaverse may be a rebrand—to spatial computing, as Apple imagines it, the spatial internet, the 3D internet, to hyper-digital reality, as Tencent imagines it, or to a “human co-experience” platform, per Roblox. Alternatively, the concepts and ideas powering the Metaverse will just be absorbed into a term that’s already in use: the internet. But however uncertain the Metaverse’s terminology may be, the trends are clear. The number of virtual worlds made each year, the number of people inside them, as well as the money and time they spend there and the cultural influence of those spaces, all continue to grow. More importantly, the deployment of real-time 3D-simulation and game-engine technology continues to increase, as do their capabilities and business applications. These tools are increasingly used in healthcare, industrial design, civic management, automotive, aerospace, and more.

The goal of this revised edition of *The Metaverse* is to clarify what the Metaverse is, explain what’s needed to build it, why it matters—and how the way it is built, and those who build it, will affect our lives for decades to come.

# [Part I A CENTURY OF  
DEFINITIONS AND  
DEVELOPMENTS](#contents.xhtml#pt_1)

## [Chapter 1 A FICTIONAL HISTORY OF THE FUTURE](#contents.xhtml#ch_1)

At the foundation of Metaverse misunderstandings is a simple fact: the term’s creator never defined it. The first appearance of the “Metaverse” was not in a computer science magazine, a technical schematic, or even a business plan, but instead in the 1992 science fiction novel *Snow Crash*, written by Neal Stephenson. And while much of *Snow Crash* takes place in or concerns the “Metaverse,” it is never concretely explained, only described—and from the perspective of the novel’s protagonist, a part-time hacker and part-time pizza deliverer for the Mafia.

What the satirically named Hiro Protagonist describes is a persistent and three-dimensional virtual world that reaches, interacts with, and affects nearly every part of human existence and much of the physical world. It is a place for labor and leisure, for self-actualization and physical exhaustion, for art alongside commerce. Users interact with the Metaverse primarily through virtual reality and augmented goggles, in addition to two-dimensional black-and-white displays (i.e., traditional computer monitors), experience it through a first-person perspective, and are represented by avatars that need not resemble their real selves at all. In totality, the Metaverse in Stephenson’s novel is more than 2.5 times the size of the earth and with no predefined bodies of oceans or lakes, thereby resulting in a planet with more than 8.5 times the available real estate. Stretched across that entire planet is “the Street,” a hundred-meter-wide road Stephenson refers to as “the Broadway, the Champs Élysées of the Metaverse.”^([1](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr1)) At any given time, there are roughly 15 million human-controlled avatars on the Street, with “a hundred million or so of the richest, hippest, best-connected people on earth” visiting “every day of their lives.”^([2](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr2)) As a point of contrast, there were fewer than seven million total users of the internet in the real world the year Stephenson’s novel was published and fewer than one million when he began writing it. It would take until 1998, six years after *Snow Crash* published, for the internet to reach a hundred million active users total and until the next decade for there to be a hundred million daily internet users.

While Stephenson’s vision was vivid and, to many, inspiring, it was also dystopic. *Snow Crash* is set at some point in the early 21st century, years after a global economic collapse. Most layers of government have been replaced by for-profit “Franchise-Organized Quasi-National Entities” and “burbclaves,” a contraction of the term “suburban enclaves.” Each burbclave operates as a “city-state with its own constitution, a border, laws, cops, everything”^([3](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr3)) and some even provide “citizenship” based purely on race.

Stephenson never suggests that the emergence of the Metaverse prompted the aforementioned collapse, but he nonetheless suggests that the Metaverse worsened the world around it. Yes, Stephenson’s Metaverse offers opportunity and escape to millions—it is a place where a gig worker in the “real world” can be a talented swordsman with inside access to the hottest clubs—but readers are left with the unmistakable sense that it leads to further disengagement from the problems of the real world. Moreover, the technical demands of the Metaverse are so great that, at most, 16% of people can afford a computing device powerful enough to access it, and more likely, fewer than 1 in 20 can do so. Nearly all of the 100 million daily users of the Metaverse, in other words, are members of the economic or social elite.^([4](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr4)) Some Metaverse users choose to spend nearly all their waking life inside the Metaverse, entombing themselves in portable terminals, goggles, and other accessories that enable them to stay connected at all times. Stephenson calls these individuals “gargoyles” (none of whom are individually named) and writes that “nothing looks stupider,” they are “rude by definition,” “embarrassing,” and “no fun to talk to” as they just “pretend to make conversation.”^([5](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr5)) And what of the billions of people who don’t go to the Metaverse? “Most of them are making mud bricks or field-stripping their AK-47s.”

The Metaverse itself is administered by the inscrutable (and ultrarich) “Global Multimedia Protocols Group,” which owns all of the underlying virtual land of the Metaverse, as well as the machinery that enables it to exist. Access to the Metaverse, as with most global communications technologies, is controlled by the shadowy L. Bob Rife, whom many readers consider to be a riff on Scientology founder L. Ron Hubbard.

Though Stephenson never aspired to shape global policy or technology, his influence, like that of Vannevar Bush, only grows with time—even if he is and will likely remain mostly unknown to the public.^([\*](#chapter1.xhtml#footnote-059)) Conversations with Stephenson helped inspire Jeff Bezos to found the private aerospace manufacturer and suborbital spaceflight company Blue Origin in 2000 (Stephenson was also the company’s first employee and remains a senior advisor a quarter century later). As of 2023, Blue Origin is the second-most-valuable private aerospace company in the world—behind only Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Two of the three founders of Keyhole, which was acquired by Google in 2004 and renamed Google Earth, have said their visions were informed (or inspired^([6](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr6))) by a similar product described in *Snow Crash*, and that they once tried to recruit Stephenson to the company (reports differ on whether this was as an advisor or just guest).^([7](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr7)) From 2014 to 2020, Stephenson was also the “chief futurist” at Magic Leap, which is widely considered the first high-profile start-up which sought to build the augmented and virtual reality devices that enable Stephenson’s Metaverse. By 2021, Magic Leap had raised more than $7 billion from the likes of Google, Alibaba, AT&T, and Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund, the last of which acquired the majority of the company in late 2022.

Stephenson’s works have also been cited as an inspiration for dozens of projects and technologies that never appeared in *Snow Crash*. Two particularly notable novels came out in the seven years following *Snow Crash*. *Diamond Age*, published in 1995, is set in a world revolutionized by nanotechnology, operated on a “worldwide \[digital\] network that can transfer money anonymously,”^([8](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr8)) and centered on characters who have met through the virtual world and in many cases only know one another’s fictional identity. The pivotal technology of *The Diamond Age*, though, was an interactive book (a “ractive”) that generated live, CGI-based films, television series, and instruction lessons using the body movements and utterances of performers who might be tens of thousands of kilometers away. It wasn’t until 2002 that a film, *The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers*, had even captured a performer’s motions in real time as part of the still-manual process of creating a CGI character.

Stephenson’s 1999 novel *Cryptonomicon* told a tale of cryptocurrencies, cryptographic program execution, and how money stores value, as well as the establishment of offshore data havens powered by ultrahigh-capacity submarine internet cables. Bitcoin, the first mainstream cryptocurrency, debuted a decade after *Cryptonomicon*.

Despite his far-reaching impact, Stephenson has consistently warned against a literal interpretation of his works—especially *Snow Crash*. In 2011, the novelist told the *New York Times*, “I can talk all day long about how wrong I got it,”^([9](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr9)) and when asked about his influence on Silicon Valley by *Vanity Fair* in 2017, he reminded the publication to keep “in mind that \[*Snow Crash* was written\] pre-Internet as we know it, pre–Worldwide Web, just me making shit up.”^([10](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr10)) And while Stephenson coined the term “Metaverse,” he was far from the first to introduce the concept.

### **The Metaverse Before It Was “the Metaverse”**

In 1935, Stanley G. Weinbaum wrote the short story “Pygmalion’s Spectacles,” which includes the first example of what modern readers would call a “virtual reality headset.” In the story, the inebriated Dan Burke^([†](#chapter1.xhtml#footnote-058)) is approached by the mysterious Professor Ludwig,^([‡](#chapter1.xhtml#footnote-057)) who speculates that Burke’s consumption stems from the desire to “make real a dream.” Ludwig goes on to tell Burke of the teachings of philosopher George Berkeley,^([§](#chapter1.xhtml#footnote-056)) saying that all of “reality is a dream” and that “we do not see, feel, hear, taste the object, but that we have only the sensation of seeing, feeling, hearing, tasting.… \[The sensations\] are ‘mental phenomena’ and ‘interpretations.’ ”^([11](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr11)) Ludwig then promises that his device, which “vaguely resembles a gas mask,” produces a “movie that gives one sight and sound.… You are in the story, you speak to the shadows, and the shadows reply, and instead of being on a screen, the story is all about you, and you are in it.”^([12](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr12))

Eventually, Burke relents and tries on the device and is promptly stunned. After only a few moments, he loses all sense of time inside and struggles to accept that what he experiences isn’t real. Inevitably, Burke falls for an apparition, Galatea—and remains entranced even after he recognizes her name as a reference to the Greek myth of Pygmalion and Galatea. In the tale, the Cypriot king Pygmalion carves a sculpture so beautiful and lifelike that he falls in love with her, and the goddess Aphrodite eventually transforms her into a living woman, Galatea, whom the king later marries.

After finally removing the goggles, Burke is in a state “worse” than being “in love with a vision.… \[He is\] in love with a girl who had never lived, in a fantastic Utopia that was literally nowhere!”^([13](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr13)) Some months later, Burke finds Ludwig, who reveals his device was all “trick photography, but stereoscopic, as I told you—three dimensional,” with Ludwig carrying around a photographic apparatus in real time and his niece playing the part of Galatea. Ludwig remarks that its verisimilitude requires self-hypnosis, but Burke doesn’t care; an “ache had vanished; a pain was eased.” Galatea, Burke exclaims, is “attainable at last.” Ludwig, however, remains frustrated: “Fools! I bring it here to sell to Westman, the camera people, and what do they say? ‘It isn’t clear. Only one person can use it at a time. It’s too expensive.’ Fools! Fools!”

Ray Bradbury’s 1950 short story “The Veldt” continues upon (and darkens) Weinbaum’s themes. The story imagines a nuclear family living in an automated home that performs household tasks and entertains the two children, Peter and Wendy,^([¶](#chapter1.xhtml#footnote-055)) using a virtual reality nursery.^([#](#chapter1.xhtml#footnote-054)) Eventually, the parents fear that the Happylife Home’s AI has displaced them as parents and that their children might never develop self-sufficiency. After deciding to move to the country, Peter and Wendy trick their parents into the nursery, which subsequently traps and kills them. As they die, the parents realize the nursery had previously simulated, and thus prepared for, exactly this sequence of events.

Philip K. Dick’s 1953 story “The Trouble with Bubbles” is set in an era where humans have explored deep into the solar system but never succeeded in finding life. Yearning to connect with other worlds and life-forms, consumers begin to buy a product called “Worldcraft” through which they can build and “Own \[Their\] Own World,” with these worlds being cultivated to the point of producing sentient life and fully realized civilizations. Most Worldcraft owners eventually destroy their creations in a celebratory competition that Dick described as a “neurotic” “orgy of breaking” intended to “amuse some god suffering from ennui.”^([14](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr14)) The protagonist, Nathan Hull,^([\*\*](#chapter1.xhtml#footnote-053)) introduces a bill to the Directorate to ban Worldcraft on ethical grounds, while also arguing man ought to “try to find outlets that aren’t so artificial” and that “bottle-up” creative energy until it “sours.” Hull’s bill loses in a vote, 400 to 35. Not long after, an earthquake occurs, after which Hull realizes he is sentient life inside another life-form’s own Worldcraft-like product, destined to be one of the “obliterated countless millions.”

In 1956, Isaac Asimov’s novel *The Naked Sun* was published. In it, he described an alien society with long life spans, but where face-to-face interactions (“seeing”) and physical contact, including sex, are considered both wasteful and repugnant, with most socializing taking place through projected holograms and 3D televisions, and work performed by robots. By the end of the novel, the human detective Elijah Baley, who appears across Asimov’s Foundation book series, concludes the Solarian race is weak and largely incapable of exploration or cooperation. Three years after *The Naked Sun*, Dick published a novel, *Time Out of Joint*, in which the protagonist learns the paradise he inhabits is merely a constructed reality intended to protect his psyche from the fact that the planet earth is at war with lunar colonists.

In 1963, Dick wrote the short story “The Days of Perky Pat,” which was subsequently reimagined in the 1964 novel *The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch*. In the short story, humanity has retreated into remote enclaves following global thermonuclear war. Nearly all of the survivors of the war spend their time playing Perky Pat, a dollhouse-based game in which their prior lives are simulated in physical “layouts,” and use most of their scrounged supplies to improve these layouts, adding features such as an electric lawn mower to Pat’s home or automatic door to the local supermarket. The winner of the game Perky Pat is decided through money, as there is “no other criterion by which one could tell if he had won or lost.” Occasionally, the survivors feel “shame” when playing “but only fleetingly; the shame, almost at once, was replaced by the desire to play more.”^([15](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr15)) The children of the survivors consider Perky Pat to be “utterly wasteful, stupid,” and instead focus on their lives, while speculating that the “grown-ups” would die if they had to take care of themselves (“Wouldn’t that be too bad,” one of the children thinks to himself; “Sure be sad”).^([16](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr16)) In Dick’s full-length novel, the world has been destroyed by global warming, not war, and the United Nations initiates a draft to help colonize nearby planets. To adjust, these colonists begin to take the illegal drug Can-D to experience shared hallucinations while using Perky Pats, both of which are manufactured by Layouts Inc. Eventually, pseudo-religious cults of Can-D users emerge, as well as a more powerful intravenous drug, Chew-Z, which seems to give God-like powers and entrap certain users.

One of the most important contributions to the ideas of simulated existence came via nonfiction. In 1981, French philosopher and cultural theorist Jean Baudrillard coined the term “hyperreality” in his seminal treatise, *Simulacra and Simulation*. Baudrillard described hyperreality as a state in which reality and simulations were so seamlessly integrated that they were indistinguishable (just as Weinbaum had once imagined). Though many find this idea frightening, Baudrillard argued that what mattered was where individuals would derive more meaning and value—and speculated it would be in the simulated world.^([17](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr17)) Though Tencent did not mention Baudrillard when it unveiled its Metaverse vision, “hyper-digital reality,” the reference was quickly noted.

The same year Baudrillard published *Simulacra and Simulation*, the science fiction novelist William Gibson first read his short story “Burning Chrome,” which he subsequently expanded into the celebrated 1984 novel *Neuromancer*. The pair of stories popularized the term “cyberspace,” which had existed since the late 1960s but had not previously related to any digital technology. In *Neuromancer*, Gibson defined cyberspace as “a consensual hallucination experienced daily by billions of legitimate operators, in every nation.… A graphic representation of data abstracted from the banks of every computer in the human system. Unthinkable complexity. Lines of light ranged in the nonspace of the mind, clusters and constellations of data. Like city lights, receding.”^([18](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr18)) Early in the novel, the hacker Henry Case is poisoned by his employers as punishment for theft, with the mycotoxin damaging his nervous system so severely he can no longer connect to cyberspace. “For Case,” Gibson writes, “who’d lived for the bodiless exultation of cyberspace” and developed a “relaxed content for the flesh,” his body was now a prison.^([19](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr19)) When asked about Baudrillard’s influence on *Neuromancer* in 1991, Gibson said “he was a cool science fiction writer.”^([20](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr20))

As Baudrillard and Gibson were writing, the Walt Disney Company was in production on the family-rated feature film *Tron*, which released in 1982 and was written by Steven Lisberger and Bonnie MacBird, with Lisberger also directing. *Tron* focused on Kevin Flynn, portrayed by Jeff Bridges, a video game developer whose mind and body are accidentally uploaded into the virtual gameworld that he created. While trapped in his world, Flynn is forced into gladiatorial combat-to-the-death, and discovers sentient life as well as an AI dictator that has begun appropriating real-world infrastructure and programs to grow more powerful.

Though Flynn prevails, he is eventually stuck in “the Grid” for 30 years, leaving his young son fatherless. *Tron* was one of the first films to make extensive use of computer animation, with entire scenes composed exclusively of digital terrains, objects, and events, or with Bridges and a few physical items layered on top of its virtual world. The film was ultimately nominated for Best Costume Design and Best Sound at the 55th Academy Awards, but omitted in the Best Visual Effects category.^([††](#chapter1.xhtml#footnote-052)) In 2010, Joseph Kosinski, who directed that year’s sequel to *Tron*, *Tron: Legacy*, told *Vanity Fair*, “There’s an interesting irony in the fact that the original *Tron* was disqualified from the visual-effects category … because \[members of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences\] considered using a computer cheating. The movie was ahead of its time; the ideas in it were ahead of their time. The idea of a virtual avatar, a personality for yourself that exists in an online world, at that point was very unique—something people couldn’t quite comprehend then but now it’s second nature.”^([21](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr21))

Originally envisioned as a graphic novel in 1989, *Snow Crash* was ultimately (and exclusively) published as a novel in 1992. And in the years that followed, many others continued to develop its themes. One such example was the 1999 film *The Matrix*, which was the fourth-highest-grossing film of the year globally. *The Matrix* took its name from *Neuromancer*, which had called visual abstraction of cyberspace the Matrix. In the film, which was written and directed by Lana Wachowski and Lilly Wachowski, “the Matrix” refers to a persistent simulation of the planet earth as it was in 1999, but that operates in the year 2199. The purpose of this simulation is to keep the minds of the incarcerated and incapacitated human race at peace so that their bodies can be used as bioelectric batteries by the sentient, but man-made, machines that conquered the planet earlier in the 22nd century. In the Wachowskis’ original shooting script, Morpheus, having recently “awakened” the protagonist Neo from the Matrix, explains that “as in Baudrillard’s vision, your whole life has been spent inside the map, not the territory.”^([22](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr22)) The line did not make the final cut, though the film retains a shot in which Neo picks up a copy of *Simulacra and Simulation* that has been hollowed out^([‡‡](#chapter1.xhtml#footnote-051)) so it might better hide hard disks of his (illegal) hacking programs.^([23](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr23))

Another famous example came in 2011 with the publication of Ernest Cline’s *Ready Player One*, a sort of pop culture–infused version of *Snow Crash*. Set in the 2040s, the “real world” of *Ready Player One* suffers from various ecological, socioeconomic, and energy-related crises. In contrast to Gibson and Stephenson, Cline imagined that most of humanity had taken refuge in his imagined “Metaverse,” which he called the OASIS. Like the Metaverse, the OASIS was a digital and often fantastical simulation of reality that was accessed via a combination of VR headsets and various haptic peripherals, and which ran on a currency that was as valuable as those of the real world—and arguably more stable, too. The narrative of the book concerns the fight to control the multitrillion-dollar OASIS following the death of its owner, James Halladay, and keep it out of the hands of Nolan Sorrento, the CEO of IOI, which marshals a seemingly infinite number of human laborers inside the OASIS. The global film studio Warner Bros. optioned *Ready Player One* a year before its publication, with Steven Spielberg directing the 2018 adaptation.

### **A Metaverse by Any Other Name**

There is no answer for why Stephenson’s term “Metaverse” took hold while other terms from similarly popular, influential, and predictive novels did not. Having first entered the pop culture lexicon in the 1990s, perhaps “cyberspace” became popular too early to endure. Though a cult classic, *Tron* was far from a breakout success, limiting the impact of the “Grid.” The “Matrix” was probably contaminated by the R-rated themes of the Wachowskis’ hit film, as well as the term’s somewhat contradictory embrace by consumer-focused brands (in 2002, three years after *The Matrix* released in theaters, Toyota debuted the Matrix compact hatchback, which it produced for more than a decade). “Hyperreality” was likely too obscure and abstract, while “the OASIS” was too new. Moreover, it’s not yet clear—and is probably unlikely—that the term “Metaverse” will endure, even if Facebook’s new name does.

Regardless, the broader history of the Metaverse in literature makes it easier to separate its ideas from the novel in which the term originates. Shared across the works of Stephenson, Cline, Gibson, the Wachowskis, et al. is the idea of a simulated reality that never stops, pauses, or resets, that touches nearly every living person (irrespective of whether they ever enter the Metaverse), that spans myriad experiences of both realism and fantasy, for leisure and labor, and that often directly touches the real world and its economy, complementing and sometimes substituting for parts of it.

There is another shared idea: that the Metaverse is dystopic, or at least the world that embraces it is a dystopia, and if so, the situation is exacerbated by the existence of the Metaverse. This commonality led to widespread criticism of big tech’s intentions when it embraced the term. Eleven days after Facebook’s name change, Alex Blechman, a staff writer for the satirical newspaper *The Onion*, posted a particularly popular tweet:

Alex Blechman

@AlexBlechman

Sci-Fi Author: In my book I invented the Torment Nexus as a cautionary tale

Tech Company: At long last, we have created the Torment Nexus from classic sci-fi novel Don’t Create The Torment Nexus^([24](#notes_split_001.xhtml#ch1fr24))

5:49 PM • Nov 8, 2021

On a more serious note, many asked why a company such as Facebook needed, let alone deserved, more reach into the lives of its users. Others wondered whether the present-day internet had already created the dystopias described by 20th- and 21st-century science fiction authors.

Though these questions are fair, the focus on the dystopic settings of Metaverse literature is misplaced. At the root of most fiction is drama—especially human drama—and a perfect society tends to produce little of it.^([§§](#chapter1.xhtml#footnote-050)) It’s for this reason that so few books are set in utopias and that these supposed utopias later collapse or are revealed to be dystopic. The authors detailed throughout this chapter sought not to warn humanity of potential technologies but to predict and entertain through them. But more important than what various authors meant when they said “Metaverse” or “Cyberspace” or the “Grid” is what is meant by the technology executives and entrepreneurs who are trying to build it.
