## [Chapter 2 WHAT THE “METAVERSE” IS (AND ISN’T)](#contents.xhtml#ch_2)

Stephenson’s neologism “Metaverse” comes from the Greek prefix *meta* and the stem “verse,” a back-formation of the word “universe.” In English, *meta* roughly translates to “beyond” or “which transcends.” Metadata is data that describes data, while metaphysics refers to a branch of philosophy “of being, identity and change, space and time, causality, necessity and possibility,” rather than the study of “matter, its fundamental constituents, its motion and behavior through space and time, and the related entities of energy and force.”^([1](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr1)) The “meta” and “verse” are intended to be a unifying layer that sits above and across all individual, computer-generated “universes,” as well as the real world, just as the universe contains, by some estimates, 70 quintillion planets.

To some technologists, philosophers, and sociologists, the Metaverse has existed for decades using another name: “the internet.” Today, the internet, a digital layer that spans nearly every country, company, and person, is used for labor and leisure, powers much of the physical world and extends much of its users’ senses of self, and has both a unified access layer (such as the web browser) and an underlying organizational framework (IP addresses, email addresses, etc.). The Metaverse Stephenson imagined in the early 1990s, and which was set sometime in the 2010s, is very different from the internet that’s been experienced since *Snow Crash* was published, but there’s obvious merit to the argument that humanity lives in it nevertheless.

However, the Metaverse is more commonly—and best—positioned as an “evolution of” or “successor state to” the internet as it is known today, rather than a byproduct of the internet of the past 40-plus years. In particular, the “Metaverse as the next version of the internet” is the framework championed by Nvidia’s Jensen Huang,^([2](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr2)) Facebook’s Mark Zuckerberg,^([3](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr3)) Epic Games’ Tim Sweeney,^([4](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr4)) and Unity’s John Riccitiello, four central figures in the Metaverse’s development. Apple’s Tim Cook holds a similar view, though he eschews the term “Metaverse” for those of “spatial computing” and “immersive interfaces,” which make up the next great “digital era.”^([\*](#chapter2.xhtml#footnote-049)) At Microsoft’s Ignite 2021 conference, Microsoft’s Satya Nadella attempted to address confusion by stating that the term “Metaverse” “described both the new platform and a new application type; similar to how we talked about the web and websites in the early 90s,” but in this case, the Metaverse resulted from “the unification of digital networks and the physical world.” Nadella added, “The Metaverse enables us to embed \[connected\] computing into the real world and to embed the real world into computing.”^([5](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr5))

Although the successor state of the modern internet is not a literal adaptation of Stephenson’s Metaverse of 1992, it’s consistent across the relevant works of Weinbaum through Cline, each of which assumes a suite of technologies that come together to produce a new, multidimensional technological medium that spans nearly all of human existence. It’s also consistent with Stephenson’s underlying ambitions for the Metaverse of *Snow Crash*—that it would be a 3D medium more popular than the dominant medium of the 1990s (television, which has since been surpassed by the internet) and would bring “spatial arrangement to the World Wide Web.”^([6](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr6))

Regardless, anchoring the Metaverse in the internet only provides context for the Metaverse—it doesn’t explain or define it. Indeed, the claim produces a new challenge: even after decades of use, most people cannot define the internet. Instead, they can only describe their experience. And while many corporate executives understand the internet, they will only ever discuss it in the context of their business. An internet provider will talk about cables in the ground or wireless towers, or how the internet enables more people to communicate. To a media company, the internet is a direct-to-consumer channel for “streaming content.” A device manufacturer will speak of smartphones and touchscreens. A politician and day laborer, senior citizen and teen will give explanations that differ even more widely.

Of course, it doesn’t matter that the average person cannot define the internet—no part of their experience or usage of it is held back as a result. Eventually, the same will be true of the Metaverse. But without a basic understanding of how the internet works, it’s difficult to explain its still-in-formation successor state, let alone address misunderstandings. At a similarly early stage in the internet’s adoption, it was most commonly characterized as “the information superhighway,” which users “surf” with their keyboards and “mouse.” A quarter century later, it’s obvious this conception of the internet was a poor and misleading way to describe what was to come, but until most people could experience the full range of the internet, such accounts endured.

### **Breaking Down Today’s Internet**

The internet is the global system of interconnected computer networks that uses the Internet Protocol Suite (also known as TCP/IP) to communicate between networks and devices. There are interconnected networks other than the internet—such as those across a corporate or college campus—but the internet is by far the largest “network of networks.”

In total, the modern internet spans 110,000 networks across nearly 200 countries,^([7](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr7)) markets, and territories, connecting over 30 billion active devices and more than 6 billion people. Each of these users, devices, and systems can coherently, comprehensively, and consistently exchange information. More than 90% of internet users log on daily, using it for an average of more than two hours, while generating over a half trillion emails, accessing more than four million apps, and visiting many of the world’s two-billion-plus websites and many billions of webpages.

Crucially, “the internet” is not a formalized organization, collective, or even group of networks. The more than 100,000 networks that constitute this “network of networks” are almost all independently funded, operated, and otherwise autonomous. Most have no formal or financial relationship with one another. In fact, they rarely know more than a few dozen networks even exist. Despite this, many networks work in concert—broadcasting their location on the internet as well as other attributes such as their available capacity and speeds, and carrying one another’s data in accordance with the internet’s protocols. These protocols, meanwhile, have no formal licensing body or authority. Instead, they are typically steered by birds-of-a-feather working groups that recommend given processes, conventions, and standards, which the networks, alongside countless device manufacturers, application developers, wireless modem and router makers, all choose to support, too.

The internet is also aided by additional conventions that, while not part of the Internet Protocol Suite, are widely supported. For example, most internet applications support common file formats (e.g., JPEG, MP3), practices (metadata structures), and languages (JavaScript, HTML), thereby making it easier for the data shared across the internet to be widely understood. As with the Internet Protocol Suite, these so-called standards tend to be run by various consortia, working groups, and open-source communities, none of which can compel “the internet” to support one of these standards.

Despite—or indeed, because of—the internet’s decentralized architecture and collaborative principles, it has become one of the most important technological platforms in history. Though TCP/IP does not specify how it should be used or what should be built with it, nearly every part of modern life is now run through or supported by the internet. The World Bank and United Nations estimate that at least 15%–20% of world GDP is “digital,” with this segment growing two and a half times faster than the “physical” economy, and typically transforming it, too.^([8](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr8)) In many cases, the internet is used without users ever actively “logging on.” Nearly all Western point-of-sale terminals use the internet to authenticate and process payments, as do many passcode security devices, such as a building ID card, and most high-value goods are tracked through internet-connected tags. These experiences are also remarkably seamless. A user who places a video call using a Windows PC inside their apartment connected to an Ethernet cable can relocate to a restaurant across town, resume their video call on an Apple iPhone using the restaurant’s Wi-Fi or any available wireless network, continue to passively receive email and instant messages on this new device, and even resume downloads. The user and their device are instantly relocated on the internet, without interruption, obligatory fees, or even much difficulty. Several proprietary videoconferencing platforms, such as Zoom and Microsoft Teams, can call into one another, too, even if their users are on entirely different operating systems and/or using different browsers and in different countries. It should be noted, however, that while the internet is not inherently dystopic or utopic, it is doubtless used for ill and sometimes has ill effects.

### **The Next Internet**

The simplest way to describe the Metaverse is as a 3D version of the internet. Whereas Vint Cerf, one of the “fathers of the internet”; Sir Tim Berners-Lee, the inventor of the World Wide Web; and Vannevar Bush, whose Memex inspired HyperText Transfer Protocol, all imagined the interconnection of networks, devices, and documents, a “3D internet” enables interconnection of virtual worlds.

Although there are many virtual worlds on the internet today, they are precisely that—applications on the internet. These worlds, as well as the billions of users fragmented across them, cannot exchange much information or even locate one another. Instead, they operate like a hotel whose rooms can call only other rooms (and if they’re lucky, maybe sister hotels). Or contrast today’s “internet” with the first mainframe computer networks, which emerged in the late 1940s, or even the first “network of networks” that was built and deployed across the Defense Department’s Advanced Research Projects Agency (commonly known as DARPA). These early networks are distinguished from “the internet” because the internet connected nearly all devices and networks globally. It’s for this reason that internet users do not worry about whether one email account can reach another, or need to check that they can link to a specific webpage, or wonder whether a given web browser can load a given page, an internet-enabled device can technically connect to a given network, or an American-based productivity solution can send out automated email alerts based on an online database hosted in Germany. The internet reaches and connects nearly all digital life.

Those building the Metaverse aim to extend this functionality into three-dimensional virtual worlds and spatial systems. Users would be able to seamlessly jump from virtual world to virtual world, whether from a science class at Harvard into a lecture run by Yale, from the AR experience inside a shopping mall into each of its stores and then the public park outside, from the planet Hoth on Disney+ into a fitness class on Peloton. Each of these worlds, meanwhile, would support and interact with the others’ avatars and virtual goods, and integrate into shared payment systems. Industrial simulations, too, would be capable of widespread and frictionless integrations. A self-driving Tesla could access the 3D mapping data of an underground parking lot, while exchanging spatial data from the other cars in the lot. Alongside city services such as electricity, water and sewage, police, fire, and ambulance would be a “virtual platform” that real estate developers, business operators, and civilians could access and build upon in daily life.

The purpose of this chapter is not to explain those use cases, nor their benefits, but instead to explain why the current internet does not properly enable them. To return to the hotel example: individual rooms can call phones outside the hotel not just because the building’s internal telephone network connects to that of the outside world, but because there is a global organizational hierarchy and numbering system for devices that support phone calls. For the internet, this framework is managed by ICANN, which assigns IP and network addresses, as well as manages the Domain Name System (DNS) that makes it easy for a user to contact these addresses. No such structures exist for virtual worlds or spaces on the internet.

Beyond being able to identify, organize, and contact virtual worlds, there need to be common ways of expressing and recognizing this information. Whereas the 2D web has myriad standardized file formats, such as JPEG for images or MP3 for audio, 3D and spatial information lack equivalent standards. Though there’s reason for optimism given the extent to which real-world documents have been digitized, it’s far harder to digitize the real world itself. Developers will need to describe what an object looks like, how and where it’s positioned, and its material composition, surface texture, temperature, purpose, activities, and more. There must also be consistent ways of designing and interpreting these virtual worlds. A JPEG, after all, is part of a website, not the website itself, and the World Wide Web has no “template.” Accordingly, almost all websites are built using HTML, a markup (not programming) language that tells a browser how to display the page’s content—including the color, font, and arrangement of its text, the orientation and dimensions of images, and its many hyperlink connections to the rest of the web. Without similar models for the Metaverse, its worlds and objects are just “data” that’s intelligible only to those who created it.

Other limitations stem not from what has yet to be established but from that which was. Though the internet’s founders envisioned many potential use cases—and were familiar with much of the science fiction work of Weinbaum, Dick, Asimov, Gibson, et al.—they were devising its protocols at a time when there was no worldwide data network and no agreement on whether it was even possible, let alone how it might work best. Moreover, delivery of any digital information across any network was unreliable, costly, and slow. And so the internet was built around a simple use case: asynchronously transmitting a copy of one file from one device to another device, and involving only the networks in between those two devices. Decades later, the internet has far exceeded this initial objective, but it remains constrained by it.

When logging on to the internet, the user is engaging in a series of short connections to outside servers—just long enough to download the requisite information, after which the interconnection is severed. Modern terminology reflects this—users say they “load” the *New York Times* homepage, not “connect to” the *New York Times*. Even when a user spends a half hour browsing the site, the process is more like leaving a string of voicemails with the *New York Times* server than carrying out a conversation. The user “calls” the *New York Times*, connects to their voicemail, leaves a message saying “Please send me the homepage,” then disconnects. Shortly thereafter, the *New York Times* calls the user back, and details the homepage on their voicemail. The same process applies to nearly all applications, even those that seem live. When browsing a “live feed” on the *New York Times* or Facebook, the initial page loaded includes code that instructs a user’s web browser or app to reconnect to the *New York Times* or Facebook server for an update after a predefined period of time, such as 3 or 30 seconds in the future. Each of these reconnections might travel a different route (i.e., over different intermediary networks) and thus travel at different speeds and over different distances, and is partly held up by the need to initiate a handshake of sorts. The result is that nearly all of the content viewed on the internet is “old” in one way or another. Two users sitting side by side in a coffee shop who load the *New York Times* a second apart may see entirely different homepages, photos, and/or headlines.

Despite the silent friction inherent in the internet’s design, most non-live experiences on the internet still feel live because the volume of updates sent and requested is high (as in the case of instant messengers), the delivery time is typically rapid and delays often hidden behind design tricks, users don’t necessarily know when information is out of date, and update requests occur more regularly when an application is open and thus under the eye of the user. Unlike web browsing and instant messaging, however, truly live online experiences require a user’s device to establish a sustained or continuous connection to the relevant third-party server. It’s for this reason that video calls, live video streaming, and video games are not always possible, let alone reliable in performance. Yet it’s these experiences, not browsing the *New York Times*, that best reflect the data needs of the Metaverse. The Metaverse is a live world and live experience and therefore requires both live (i.e., real-time) information and a continuous connection to its source. And unfortunately, neither the internet backbone nor the Internet Protocol Suite was designed for these applications. As an example, TCP/IP’s Border Gateway Protocol, which routes traffic on the internet as it jumps from one network to another, neither routes nor prioritizes traffic that needs to arrive quickly or whose connection must be sustained. Indeed, BGP doesn’t even receive that information.

Making matters more challenging, the Metaverse is imagined as a shared and multiparticipant experience. As such, the information sent by a given user or server must be synchronized across all relevant users, networks, and devices in real time. Again, though, the internet was designed to connect no more than two devices or servers at once, and for only finite periods of time.

This structure has worked fairly well over the past 40 years because there are relatively few shared online experiences. When visiting an office cafeteria, many users are on the company’s corporate Wi-Fi, but their experiences are entirely disconnected and irrelevant to one another. When two users scroll BuzzFeed together on their respective devices, they are sharing a real-world experience, but not a digital one. In some cases, the internet is co-experienced—but these experiences are typically simple, computationally limited, and tolerant of delays. Live text chats, such as those on Twitch, are uncoordinated between users, barely customized, and unaffected by which entry appears above or below another. Google Docs are coordinated, but it’s rare that they are edited concurrently, and even rarer that the same part of the document has several simultaneous authors.^([†](#chapter2.xhtml#footnote-048)) Video calls are an exception to the above as they are both live and, by definition, multiuser experiences. Yet these applications have an important advantage: there is usually just one focal participant at any given moment, with all others serving primarily as spectators, not “collaborators” in the experience.

What makes the Metaverse particularly difficult from a networking perspective is that every additional user or device has a linear impact on the number of required continuous connections—which is already hard—and an exponential impact on the number of interactions that must be synchronized in real time. And unlike a video call or Google Doc, these interactions are not video frames or text, but contribute to a complex and dynamic computer model. Recall that the Street protocol of Neal Stephenson’s could “handle” more than ten million simultaneous users.

A related problem is that of “copies.” The Internet Protocol Suite as it exists today is designed to share copies of files. As such, every message, document, or photo that is sent is ultimately copied to various recipient devices. When a user sends a photo from their iPhone using Gmail, a copy exists on their device and Gmail account, as well as the recipient’s email service, and any number of devices they use to download it on or view it. Both users’ iCloud accounts may also store a copy of the photo, too, which may or may not sync with whether the device keeps or deletes the photo. There is no mechanism in TCP/IP that establishes, let alone manages or enforces, the canonical version of a file, ownership of it, or various access and permission rights. Instead, these properties and rights are possible—on a limited basis—only when the content remains on a single platform on the internet. If a *Roblox* user wants to trade an avatar to their friend, *Roblox* can ensure the friend receives it, the sender loses access to it, and so on. If that user were to export the avatar, then the copy problem begins. To use a “real-world” analogy, Chase Bank can reassign the rights to a $100 bill across its customers’ bank accounts, but neither Chase nor the US Treasury can control who has it, takes it, or might try to forge it when it leaves Chase Bank.

There are some bodies that administer the “canon” of the internet. The domain system managed by ICANN is a literal database which enables various agents (e.g., GoDaddy or Name.com) to register domains on behalf of private individuals and shift their websites from one domain to another, or sell their domain to another person or company. The DNS record is singular, authoritative, and dynamic, having expanded from only 7 top-level domains in 1998 (.com,.org,.net,.edu,.gov, .int, .mil) to more than 1,500 a quarter century later, but neither technical systems nor governance structures of ICANN can scale to manage infinitely expanding inventories of virtual goods worth trillions per year.

The Metaverse does not mean securitizing or canonizing all content on the internet. It’s not just okay, it’s good that many copies of a photo might exist, and that User A cannot alter a photo they sent to User B after User B received it, or take it back. But for the Metaverse to have a network-level economy for any virtual goods, or any creations, that spans more than a single platform, it requires altogether new systems for object rights and exchange.

To summarize: a basic definition of the Metaverse might be a “shared, live, and 3D version of the internet that supports an open economy of virtual goods.” [Part II](#part2.xhtml) of this book will progress from this definition to a description that better illuminates the Metaverse and its technological needs. But for the time being, this stated definition should suffice to explain the “next internet” in contrast to the current one.

### **What the Metaverse Is Not**

Having established a baseline, if still simplified, understanding of both the internet and the Metaverse, it’s helpful to address common Metaverse myths and misunderstandings. Several points should now be obvious to readers, but it’s helpful to address them directly.

#### ***Error #1: Using the singular article “a” Metaverse, plural form “Metaverses,” or possessive construction such as “Company A’s Metaverse”***

Companies such as Amazon, Apple, Facebook, Google, and Microsoft are not “the internet,” do not operate “the internet,” control the protocols of the “internet,” or have their own “internets.” Instead, these companies operate large, hardware- and software-based, horizontal and vertical platforms that are on the internet, help users access the internet, and provide things to do with the internet. And as vast and mighty as these various platforms are, they represent just a small portion of the overall internet—even when combined. This is the right way to think about the Metaverse, too.

Like the internet, the Metaverse is not any one network, platform, device, application, or even group of them. It is instead a network of myriad interconnected and interoperable networks, platforms, devices, applications, and so on. While it’s common to hear that Company A or B is building “the” Metaverse or building “a” Metaverse, they are typically just building hardware and/or applications (and maybe contributing to development of a Metaversal Internet Protocol Suite). Now, there are some important nuances to this taxonomy and philosophy.

First, there are rival efforts to build the foundational technologies of the Metaverse. Company A and Company B, for example, may envision and advocate for competing protocols and standards for the Metaverse, which would in turn affect how the Metaverse operates or is commercialized. As such, it could be argued that these two companies are contributing to the development of Metaverses (certainly, Web3 developers would say they are building a very different Metaverse than the likes of Facebook and Microsoft). History suggests that separate initiatives can endure for some time, before eventually merging or establishing a single winner. From the 1970s to 1990s there were many proposed and operating working alternatives to the internet, some of which were supported by different US federal departments even though the Department of Defense had created and still spearheaded much of the internet. Few technologists at the time expected that a single global winner would emerge from these so-called “protocol wars,” but the utility of a unified digital economy was too great, and holdouts eventually switched or integrated into the internet. It’s even less likely that over the coming decades, the common foundations of the current internet would split into multiple Metaverses.

Second, there is likely to be some regional fragmentation across “the” Metaverse. The so-called “Chinese internet” uses the same Internet Protocol Suite (TCP/IP) as the rest of the world, yet the experience of using the internet in China is unmistakably different due to various regulations, firewalls, software giants, and cultural norms. If the Metaverse proves as essential and valuable as many predict, it’s likely the Chinese Metaverse will be even more distinct from that of the rest of the world than the internet is today (as mentioned in the introduction, the Chinese government has already stated that its domestic Metaverse should be “independent” and “controllable”). Still, the Chinese Metaverse will be built on top of the Internet Protocol Suite, likely leverage many of the same technologies that are also used for the Metaverse outside China, and interoperate into parts of the non-Chinese Metaverse. As such, the “Chinese Metaverse” is best described as a regional expression or variation of the Metaverse, rather than a wholly different Metaverse.

Third, one company may still establish effective control over the Metaverse by designing and/or operating its protocols or access devices. Though the foundations of the internet are both open and without an owner, it has become increasingly closed and commercialized over the past 40 years—and the Metaverse is likely to exacerbate this trend, rather than reverse it. This dynamic is discussed throughout this book and is a point of focus in [Chapters 3](#chapter3.xhtml) and [10](#chapter10.xhtml).

#### ***Error #2: Conflating the Metaverse with a virtual or augmented reality headset, operating system, or experience***

Technically, the term “virtual reality” refers to computer-generated simulations of three-dimensional objects or environments with seemingly real, direct, or physical user interaction.^([9](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr9)) The underlying mechanics of processing and rendering computer-generated simulations do not fundamentally differ based on the type of screen they’re viewed through, or how the user’s inputs are collected. In current usage, however, virtual reality refers to a computer-generated simulation that is rendered on a screen contained within a headset, rather than a TV screen or monitor, with the user interacting with the simulation using a mix of facial or body movements, rather than typing on a keyboard or operating a controller. VR headsets provide a greater sense of immersion inside a computer-generated simulation, and greater ease of use, as the user’s senses (i.e., their eyes and ears) are enveloped in the device, and they can interact as they do in the real world (e.g., look right to shift the camera angle right, turn body right to turn the character right).

In contrast to VR devices, augmented reality devices layer computer-generated simulations on top of the real world, rather than replace it altogether. For example, an AR device worn in a supermarket might layer floating, 3D labels above produce that identify various items and estimate their ripeness. As with VR, AR does not require a headset. Many applications provide rich AR experiences today through a standard smartphone camera and screen. Popular examples include Snapchat (which enables users to capture videos wearing AR costumes and makeup), *Pokémon Go* (which enables users to “see” and interact with Pokémon that appear to exist in the real world), and Google Maps (which can help users find their way by placing directional arrows on top of landmarks and streets). As with VR, it is assumed that wearable headsets are the most intuitive way to use AR functionality, just as glasses are easier to use than monocles stored in pockets.

VR and AR devices are often conflated with the Metaverse because of their role in novels such as *Neuromancer*, *Snow Crash*, and *Ready Player One*, as well as their centrality to Facebook’s Metaverse strategy. There is also a widely held belief that VR/AR headsets will eventually become the “best,” “most popular,” and “preferred” way to access the Metaverse. Regardless, the Metaverse is not a device, nor a specific interface or type of experience.

To better understand the relationship between VR/AR devices and the Metaverse, consider the relationship between touchscreen smartphones and the internet. Neither the internet nor even the mobile internet requires either a touchscreen or the use of apps—users could, if they preferred, use BlackBerry-style clickwheels and physical keyboards. In fact, no part of using the internet even requires a visual interface; billions of people globally can and do occasionally access the internet simply by saying “Siri” or “Hey Google” or “Alexa.” Apps are another good example. Though the most popular way to access digital content and experiences, users could mostly just use a single app to engage with the internet: a web browser.

Though the internet does not require touchscreens, smartphones, or apps, it’s generally recognized that they are the best way to access it and have been key to expanding who uses the internet, for what, and how often. Without a touchscreen, keyboards would take up half of a smartphone’s display and there would be little ability to tailor any interface to a specific application—whether the user was playing a game, accessing a medical record, or scrolling TikTok, they would need to use an alphanumeric keyboard, a half dozen symbol-based keys, and some form of trackwheel or thumbpad, rather than benefit from a tailor-made touch user interface (UI). This limitation would have made general-purpose smartphones ill-suited to many specialized tasks and kept many children and senior citizens from adopting the devices in the first place. Though most internet products and services are available via web browser, most users prefer to access these products and services via apps, which are purpose-built for these products and services and therefore offer substantial performance, stability, and interface-related improvements. VR/AR headsets will likely play a similar role to touchscreens and apps in the Metaverse.

All that said, traditional or “flat 2D” devices have proved surprisingly capable at enabling users to interact in 3D spaces. In 2022, Neal Stephenson wrote a series of tweets intended to answer a commonly asked question: Did the Metaverse he envisioned require an AR or VR headset?

> The assumption that the Metaverse is primarily an AR/VR thing isn’t crazy. In my book \[*Snow Crash*\] it’s all VR. And I worked for an AR company \[Magic Leap\]—one of several that are putting billions of dollars into building headsets. But I didn’t see video games coming when I wrote *Snow Crash*.… Thanks to games, billions of people are now comfortable navigating 3D environments on flat 2D screens. The UIs that they’ve mastered \[keyboard and mouse for navigation and camera\] are not what most science fiction writers would have predicted. But that’s how path dependency in tech works. We fluently navigate and interact with extremely rich 3D environments using keyboards that were designed for mechanical typewriters. It’s steampunk made real. A Metaverse that left behind those users and the \[developers\] who build those experiences would be getting off on the wrong foot.… My expectation is that a lot of Metaverse content will be built for screens (where the market is) while keeping options open for the future growth of affordable headsets.^([10](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr10))

#### ***Error #3: Conflating the Metaverse with a video game platform such as*** **Fortnite*,*** **Minecraft*, or*** **Roblox**

As with AR/VR, this mistake is understandable. Nearly all of the top popular multiplayer video games of 2024 are shared, live, and 3D and boast some form of internal goods economy. In addition to these attributes, *Fortnite*, *Minecraft*, and *Roblox* each operate networks of tens of millions of virtual worlds, all of which are underpinned by an extensive technology suite that covers identities, avatars, virtual currencies, and communications, and can be accessed through nearly every mainstream computing device globally, are used for both work and play, and have millions of individual contributors supporting hundreds of millions of users as part of their multibillion-dollar economies.

Though there is a structural similarity between the Metaverse and these platforms, characterizing the former as the latter would be akin to saying Facebook is the World Wide Web. Yes, Facebook is a large, device-agnostic platform that spans billions of interconnected pages, with standardized identifiers (accounts rather than IP addresses), formats, conventions, and so on. And for some users, Facebook is most of what they do on the internet. Yet Facebook is a fraction of the overall internet, predominantly leisure focused, and entirely separate from the actual protocols of the internet. *Roblox*, *Minecraft*, and *Fortnite* are likely to be part of the Metaverse, resemble much of it, and pioneer some of its standards and user behaviors, but they are not a Metaverse, let alone the Metaverse.

 

#### ***Error #4: Conflating the Metaverse with Web3, blockchains, cryptocurrencies, or NFTs***

A recurring theme in this book is the difficulty of fully separating various technological eras, waves, or models. Nevertheless, technologists, sociologists, and investors typically differentiate between the early stage of the internet, so-called “Web 1.0,” which began with the creation of the World Wide Web in 1989, and “Web 2.0,” which started around 2004 or 2005, following the launch of Facebook and YouTube. Webs 1.0 and 2.0 can be broadly differentiated in terms of content, user activity, the role of platforms, and the technologies used.

During the Web 1.0 era, content was not strictly limited to text, but limitations in broadband speeds and computer processing power meant that images were scarce and low resolution, while audio was typically available only in excerpts and low quality, and video was hard to find and even harder to watch. The content creator typically hosted this content themselves on servers they owned, and these ran open-source operating systems such as Linux. The content itself was usually produced or displayed using common standards (e.g., JPEG, GIF, JavaScript, HTML), and distributed through open platforms (the World Wide Web, web browsers, Microsoft Windows, email protocols, etc.). Although the Web 1.0 era was the first time most people could widely distribute their content—and without intermediation by a publisher, producer, retailer, and so on—almost no internet users created content during Web 1.0. They just consumed it.

During Web 2.0, it became common to create, distribute, and access high-quality media formats, including live video and interactive media. Billions of users also established comprehensive internet-based identities (e.g., a Facebook account), as well as their own internet-based networks (e.g., adding friends on Facebook). The advent of cloud data centers meant a developer or user could easily hire a company like Amazon or Microsoft to host and manage their website or app versus buying, setting up, and maintaining their own server. Apple, Google, and Facebook, among other technology companies, made it easier for individuals to create, discover, share, or monetize a piece of content, page, application, and so on. These many advances led to a surge in online creation. Rather than just view the internet, as was the case in Web 1.0, nearly all users of the Web 2.0 internet also contribute to the internet. Some of these contributions are just an occasional social media post, but millions of independent developers and creators now earn a living through their social media pages, video channels, apps, and websites, while millions more work in the digital “gig economy.”

Despite these benefits, many in the tech community worried about the underlying trade-off of Web 2.0: though more prosperous and participatory, it was also becoming more closed and privately owned. Identities and networks were established not on TCP/IP (e.g., email or IP addresses) or other open protocols but instead on private databases and systems (e.g., Facebook log-ins). If a developer published a website to the World Wide Web, they could freely shift it from one host to another, change their domain, or shift their customer and mailing lists to a different provider, but on Facebook or YouTube, most of the user’s content, identity, and followers were stuck. The major mobile operating systems also dictated what sorts of apps could be distributed, using which technologies, and through which business models they could be monetized—and took 15%–30% of an app’s digital revenues, too. Though nominally still “open,” the World Wide Web was intermediated by web browsers that were also tightly controlled by mobile operating systems (i.e., iOS and Android); a search engine with 95% market share and a desire to foster its ecosystem, collect data, and sell ads (Google); and algorithmic social feeds that were even more opaque and represented the majority of time spent online for billions of users (Facebook, Twitter, TikTok, etc.).

The overarching goal of Web3 is to continue to expand and enrich the number of contributors to the internet, while also returning the internet to the decentralized principles upon which it was founded, and reducing the power of big-tech platforms and aggregators. The supposed result would be a “healthier” internet that gives more rights to the individual user, offers more profits to the independent developer, and reduces the influence and controls of the various big-tech platforms that typically sit between users and developers.

Specifically, Web3 advocates argue this dream is best enabled by (or at least most likely through) blockchains, which also use cryptocurrencies and tokens to compensate users who help “run” these blockchains. In this sense, a Web3 internet is one in which regular users not only consume the internet and create content on the internet, they also help to operate it and have an economic stake in it, too. Advocates of “Web 3.0” (note the small terminological difference from “Web3”) share similar aims, but do not see blockchains as necessary (or even useful) to achieving them—or to the need to securitize the internet’s operations. Vint Cerf says he has some skepticism about blockchains and the Metaverse, but believes that revising and expanding the Internet Protocol Suite, which has gone largely unchanged since the early 1990s, is key to the internet’s long-term health.^([11](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr11)) Sir Tim Berners-Lee, who believes the Metaverse is “going to be part of the future,” has called Web3 a “marketing hijack” that should be “ignored,” but insists that “Web 3.0” is “the real thing … a mid-course correction to take \[the internet\] back.”^([12](#notes_split_002.xhtml#ch2fr12))

The confusion between “Metaverse” and “Web3/Web 3.0” has several causes. Most obviously, the two terms rose to prominence at the same time and both are considered “successor states” to the internet as it’s known today. The evolution of online media formats from Web 1.0 to Web 2.0 also suggests that the embrace of a 3D/spatial internet would mean transitioning to Web3/Web 3.0. Some also believe blockchain technologies are required to actually run the Metaverse (though some Metaverse pioneers believe blockchains have no future at all), while others believe the Metaverse must emerge for the many blockchains and cryptocurrencies to justify their multitrillion-dollar combined valuation.

Despite their occasional similarities, the Metaverse and Web3/Web 3.0 remain definitionally distinct. The former does not require further decentralization of the internet (in fact, it would likely emerge more slowly as a result), while the latter does not require the development of a 3D internet. Regardless, the principles of Web3/Web 3.0 would likely produce a healthier Metaverse, even if it’s not technically required.

 

#### ***Error #5: Considering the Metaverse a “replacement” to today’s internet, applications, and devices***

Believing in the Metaverse does not require one to believe that society will stop using PCs or smartphones, abandon 2D applications and interfaces, or perform all digital labor and leisure inside 3D or spatial simulations.

Consider usage of the internet today. Though the “mobile and cloud” era of computing and networking is doubtless here, non-mobile devices such as laptops and PCs are still in use, “traditional” phone calls are common, most files are stored on local devices, billions still work “in person,” and restaurant, live sporting, and concert revenues have never been higher. And while more than half the traffic on the internet both originates and terminates on a mobile device, and over two-thirds of data is stored in the cloud, nearly all transmission of this data occurs via wired, not wireless, infrastructure, using a version of the Internet Protocol Suite that remains mostly unchanged since its formalization decades ago.

As was the case with the rise of both mobile networking and computing and cloud networking and computing, the Metaverse will likely result in new software, services, behaviors, use cases, and even hardware. In some cases, these new technologies will fully substitute for their predecessors. But more often, they will complement existing behaviors.

## [Chapter 3 WHY NOW?](#contents.xhtml#ch_3)

If the ideas behind the Metaverse are nearly a century old, if the Metaverse evolves from a technology more than a half century old, and if the term itself is 30 years old, it’s natural to wonder why the Metaverse came into focus in 2021—and to wonder when it might arrive.

New technological eras do not have launch dates. It’s possible to identify when a certain technology began development, when that technology first performed a given task, completed a public demonstration, or passed a sales milestone. But eras? They lack a singular starting moment. Instead, they emerge and are named only when the maturation of ecosystems proceeds to the point where sociologists, technologists, and regular people can identify widespread change. A great way to understand this dynamic is by considering the history of mobile computing.

### **Dialing Back**

The first mobile (i.e., cellular network) phone call was placed in New York City in 1973 using a Motorola cellphone. It’s difficult to argue the mobile computing era began that year, but the development of the two-and-a-half-pound prototype Motorola DynaTAC is nonetheless an essential starting point, in retrospect. To build its device, Motorola had to not just establish a new category but also make advances in portable, miniaturized, and rechargeable batteries and help establish new standards for long-range wireless data transmission. And the success of the first phone call, which was placed by Motorola researcher Martin Cooper as he walked between 53rd and 54th Streets on Sixth Avenue in Manhattan, also prompted companies such as Bell and NTT to build the wireless towers and networks that device manufacturers would need to be able to sell usable phones and, later, smartphones too.

In 1991, Norway launched the first “2G” network—the first network to support wireless data, rather than just voice communications (which powers SMS). The following year, IBM unveiled the first smartphone, the IBM Simon, which was made available for sale in 1994. That year also saw the release of Apple’s first portable computer, the Newton, though the device lacked a mobile networking chip and predated the creation of Wi-Fi by three years and, as such, could receive and send data only through physical cables and chips. By the late 1990s, Research in Motion’s various BlackBerry models had begun to take hold in governments, large enterprises, and information-focused businesses (e.g., finance, healthcare), with RIM going public in 1998. In 1999, the Wireless Application Protocol, or WAP, debuted, enabling a primitive version of the World Wide Web to be accessed from most phones—smart or not.^([\*](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-047)) Though not part of the Internet Protocol Suite, WAP was the first mobile-specific protocol to see widespread adoption and facilitate widespread access.

In October 2001, a year and a half after the dotcom crash, Japan premiered the first commercial 3G network. The speeds enabled by 3G made it practical for smartphones to download more than text-based emails and WAP webpages, which in turn expanded the device’s appeal to consumers rather than just business users, and led to the development of the first major mobile-only media companies. December 2002, for example, is considered the start of the “ringtone” industry, after a Japanese wireless carrier launched its “Chaku-Uta” service, which let customers pay to download 45 clips of select songs, which could then be used instead of a traditional phone ringer. Mobile game downloads followed soon after.

As 3G internet speeds and coverage expanded, and more mobile services and games debuted, smartphone sales began to surge. From 1991 through 2003, roughly 70–80 million total smartphones were sold worldwide. In 2004 and 2005, nearly 100 million more were sold.

![Benedict Evans, IDC, TechCrunch, Matthew Ball](OEBPS/images/pg37.jpg)

Benedict Evans, IDC, TechCrunch, Matthew Ball

Although smartphone sales hit additional records in the years that followed, there’s a reason that most industry observers and smartphone owners consider the smartphone era to have truly begun sometime between the second half of calendar year 2007 and the end of 2008. In July of 2007, the first iPhone launched, with Apple releasing an updated 3G model as well as its now-famous App Store in the summer of 2008. In September of 2007, Google released the first version of Android, which would later become the most popular operating system in human history. Two months later, the International Telecommunication Union unveiled 4G, which offered speeds practical for video, just as 2G enabled text and 3G enabled audio and images. These many convergent innovations established a brand-new curve for smartphone adoption, which grew from 100 million units sold in 2007 to over 250 million in 2010, 500 million in 2012, and a billion in 2013.

Still, it’s strange to say mobile had “arrived” in 2007, in 2008, or even by 2012. It took until 2014 for half of Americans to own a smartphone and it wasn’t until 2020 that half of the world had one. Until these milestones, most Americans and most people globally were not part of the mobile era. And during the interim years, there was an increase not just in the number of people using smartphones but in what smartphones could do, how often they were used, and for what purposes.

### **How Many Years Does It Take to Turn On a Lightbulb?**

Another case study—a personal favorite—is the process of electrification, which began in the late 19th century and ran into the mid-20th century, and focused on the adoption and usage of electricity, skipping past the centuries-long effort to understand, capture, and transmit it. Electrification was not a single period of steady growth, nor a process through which any one product was adopted. Instead, it consisted of two separate waves of technological, industrial, and process-related transformation. The first wave began around 1881, when Thomas Edison stood up electric power stations in Manhattan and London. Yet while Edison was quick to commercialize electricity—he had created the first working incandescent light bulb only two years earlier—demand for the resource was low. A quarter century after the first stations, an estimated 5% to 10% of mechanical drive power in the United States came from electricity (two-thirds of which was generated locally, rather than from a grid). But then, rather suddenly, the second wave began. Between 1910 and 1920, electricity’s share of mechanical drive power quintupled to over 50% (nearly two-thirds of which came from independent electric utilities). By 1929, it stood at 78%.^([1](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr1))

![Benedict Evans, IDC, TechCrunch, Matthew Ball](OEBPS/images/pg39.jpg)

Benedict Evans, IDC, TechCrunch, Matthew Ball

The difference between the first and second waves was not the portion of American industry that used electricity but the extent to which that portion did—and designed around it.^([2](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr2))

When factories first adopted electrical power, it was typically used for lighting and to replace the on-premises source of power (usually steam). Owners did not rethink or replace the legacy infrastructure that would carry this power throughout the factory and put it to work. Instead, they continued to use a network of cogs and gears that were messy and loud and dangerous, were difficult to upgrade or change, were either “all on” or “all off” (and therefore required the same amount of power to support a single operating station or the entire plant, and suffered from countless “single points of failure”), and struggled to support specialized work.

But eventually, new technologies and understandings gave owners both the reason and the ability to redesign factories end to end for electricity, from replacing cogs with electric wires to installing individual stations with bespoke and dedicated electrically powered motors for functions such as sewing, cutting, pressing, and welding.

The benefits were wide-ranging. The same factory now had considerably more space, more light, better air, and less life-threatening equipment. What’s more, individual stations could be powered individually (which increased safety, while reducing costs and downtime), and they could use more specialized equipment, such as electric socket wrenches.

Factory owners could configure production areas around the logic of the production process rather than hulking equipment, and even reconfigure production areas on a regular basis. These two changes meant that far more industries could deploy assembly lines (which had first emerged in the late 1700s), while those that already had such lines could extend them further and more efficiently. In 1913, Henry Ford created the first moving assembly line, which used electricity and conveyor belts to reduce the production time per car from 12.5 hours to 93 minutes, while also using less power. According to the historian David Nye, Ford’s famous Highland Park plant was “built on the assumption that electrical light and power should be available everywhere.”^([3](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr3))

Once a few factories began this transformation, the entire market was forced to catch up, thereby spurring more investment and innovation in electricity-based infrastructure, equipment, and processes. Within a year of its first moving assembly line, Ford was producing more cars than the rest of the industry combined. By its 10 millionth car, it had built more than half of all cars on American roads.

The “second wave” of industrial electricity adoption didn’t depend on a single visionary making an evolutionary leap from Thomas Edison’s core work. Nor was it driven merely by an increasing number of industrial power stations. Instead, it reflected a critical mass of interconnected innovations, spanning power management, manufacturing hardware, production theory, and more. Some of these innovations fit in the palm of a plant manager’s hand, others needed a room, a few required a city, and all depended on people and processes. In aggregate, these innovations enabled the “Roaring Twenties,” which saw the greatest average annual increases in labor and capital productivity in a hundred years, and helped power the Second Industrial Revolution.

### **Back to the Future**

In June of 2021, Epic Games’ founder and CEO Tim Sweeney tweeted a screenshot of code from Epic’s first 3D game, *Unreal*, with the caption “October 1997.” In a pair of follow-up tweets, Sweeney wrote, “\[Users\] could go into portals and travel among user-run servers when Unreal 1 was released in 1998. I remember a moment where folks in the community had created a grotto map with no combat and were standing in a circle chatting. This style of play didn’t last for long though. Epic has had Metaverse aspirations for a very, very long time … but only in recent years have a critical mass of working pieces started coming together rapidly.”^([4](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr4))

At the time of Sweeney’s post, the Metaverse was already years behind not only the fictional forecasts of *Snow Crash*, which supposed that the Metaverse was fully operational and inhabited by more than a hundred million people by the early 2010s, but also the real-world hopes of many tech entrepreneurs. But as the histories of mobile computing and electrification remind us, eras begin when many different technologies converge and ecosystems are built up around them. And by the early 2020s, there was growing consensus that the Metaverse was about to hit its version of the 1910s in electricity or the 18-month period that followed the iPhone’s debut in 2007. The modern history of virtual worlds, real-time graphical simulation, head-mounted displays, human culture and pastimes, and AI also helps to explain this belief, too.
