### **Synthetic Worlds**

Most accounts of the history of the Metaverse begin in the 1970s, with the advent of Multi-User Dungeons (or MUDs), a sort-of software-based version of the role-playing game Dungeons & Dragons, but which was experienced purely through text and the internet. Using text-based commands that resembled human languages, MUD players could interact with one another, explore a fictional world populated by non-playable characters and monsters, attain power-ups and knowledge, and eventually retrieve a magical chalice, defeat an evil wizard, or rescue a princess.

The growing popularity of MUDs inspired the creation of Multi-User Shared Hallucinations (or MUSHs) and Multi-User Experiences (MUXs). Unlike MUDs, which asked players to carry out specific roles in the context of a specific and usually fantastical narrative, MUSHs and MUXs enabled participants to collaboratively define the world and its objective. Players might choose to set their MUSH in a courtroom, while taking on roles such as defendant, attorney, plaintiff, judge, and members of the jury. One participant might later decide to transform the relatively mundane proceedings into a hostage situation—which would then be defused by a poem mad-libbed by the other players. As late as 1993, traffic analysis suggested that 10% of data transmitted on the internet was for MUDs, MUSHs, and MUXs—a remarkable figure given that these simulations transmitted little data in each message compared to emails, financial files, and research reports.^([5](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr5))

The next great advance came in 1986 with the release of the Commodore 64 online game *Habitat*, published by Lucasfilm, the production company founded by *Star Wars* creator George Lucas. *Habitat* was described as “a multi-participant online virtual environment” and, in a reference to Gibson’s novel *Neuromancer*, “a cyberspace.” Unlike MUDs and MUSHs, the world of *Habitat* was graphical, thereby allowing users to actually see virtual environments and characters, though only via pixeled 2D. It also afforded players far greater control over the in-game environment. “Citizens” of *Habitat* were in charge of the laws and expectations of their virtual world, and had to barter with each other for necessary resources and avoid being robbed or killed for their wares. This challenge led to periods of chaos, after which new rules, regulations, and authorities were established by the player community to maintain order.

Though *Habitat* is not as widely remembered as other 1980s video games, such as *Pac-Man* and *Super Mario Bros.*, it transcended the niche appeal of MUDs and MUSHs, ultimately becoming a commercial hit. The title was also the first game to repurpose the Sanskrit term *avatar*, which roughly translates to “the descent of a deity from heaven,” to refer to a user’s virtual body. Decades later, this usage has become convention—in no small part because Stephenson reapplied it in *Snow Crash*.

In the 1990s, virtual world platforms began to transcend the flatness of 2D text and imagery. *Web World*, released in 1994*,* was the first open-ended virtual world platform that was rendered in “2.5D.”^([6](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr6)) This graphics approach produced the illusion of 3D through the use of isometric art styles,^([†](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-046)) mathematically precise distortions in the virtual world’s map and objects, and tilting the virtual world’s map and/or the camera angles a player used to see it. In 1995, Worlds, Inc., brought true 3D to the category and was expressly focused on all forms of virtual socializing, rather than game-like objectives.^([7](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr7)) That same year saw the debut of *Activeworlds*, the first virtual world platform that enabled multiple users to build a given world at the same time using 3D drag-and-drop objects, rather than just commands and code.^([8](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr8)) Notably, *Activeworlds* also had the express purpose of building Stephenson’s Metaverse and asked players to both enjoy its virtual world and help expand and populate it.^([9](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr9)) In 1998, *OnLive! Traveler* launched with spatial voice chat, allowing users to hear where other players were positioned relative to other participants, and for an avatar’s mouth to move in response to the words spoken by the player.^([10](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr10))

In 1999, Intrinsic Graphics, a 3D gaming software company, completed the spin-off of Keyhole, whose titular product was a virtual production of the entire planet earth. Five years later, Google acquired the company after concluding that more than a quarter of Google Search queries were for geospatial information, such as the location of a supermarket or the directions to it.^([11](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr11)) In 2005, Google renamed Keyhole “Google Earth” and made it available for free to consumers worldwide. In the ensuing 20 years, Google’s many upgrades to Google Earth brought the product ever closer to the “Earth” application of Stephenson’s *Snow Crash*, which had inspired at least one of Keyhole’s founders to start the business. In 2007, Google began its Google Street View project, which eventually enabled Google Maps users to view 360-degree photos staged every few feet (in cities) or dozen meters (rural areas) on nearly every street in the world. By 2020, Google was updating these photos every year (cities) or three (rural areas). In 2008, Google added live traffic information across its mapping products. At first, Google’s data set relied on licenses to traffic sensors owned by various governments and private infrastructure operators, but the company eventually factored in data generated by the billions of smartphone-based Google Maps users, which provided greater insight into real-time transit, scheduled transit, and typical patterns. In 2012, Google Earth launched a 3D mode for select cities, such as Manhattan and Paris.

For many, especially those in Silicon Valley, the idea of a parallel virtual existence was not seriously contemplated until the arrival of the aptly named *Second Life* in June 2003 (two months before the debut of the 2D social network MySpace). In its first year, *Second Life* attracted over one million regular users, and shortly thereafter, numerous real-world organizations rushed to add their own businesses and presences inside the platform. This included for-profit corporations such as Adidas, BBC, and Wells Fargo, as well as nonprofits such as the American Cancer Society and Save the Children, and even universities, including Harvard, whose law school offered exclusive courses inside *Second Life*. In 2007, a stock exchange was launched on the platform with the aim of helping *Second Life*–based companies raise capital using the platform’s Linden Dollars currency.

Unlike most virtual worlds before and after *Second Life*, its developer Linden Labs did not intermediate transactions between players, nor actively manage what was made or sold. Instead, transactions were made directly between buyers and sellers and based on perceived value and need. Overall, Linden Labs operated more like a government than a game maker. The company did provide some user-facing services, such as identity management, ownership records, and an in-world legal system. But its focus wasn’t on building out the *Second Life* universe directly. Instead, it enabled a thriving economy via ever-improving infrastructure, technical capabilities, and tools that would attract more developers and creators who would then create things for other users to do, places for them to visit, and items for them to buy—attracting more users and therefore more spending, which would in turn attract more investment from developers and creators. To this end, *Second Life* also offered users the ability to import virtual objects and textures made outside the platform. By 2005, just two years after it launched, *Second Life*’s annualized GDP exceeded $40 million.^([12](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr12)) By 2009, it exceeded half a billion dollars, with users cashing out $55 million into real-world currency that year.^([13](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr13)) Over *Second Life*’s first decade, a total of $3.2 billion in player-to-player transactions took place, with an average of more than 1.2 million individual transactions per day.^([14](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr14))

For all the success of *Second Life*, it was the rise of virtual world platforms *Minecraft* and *Roblox* in the 2010s that brought Linden Labs’ ideas to mainstream audiences. In addition to offering significant technical enhancements compared to their predecessors, *Minecraft* and *Roblox* were far easier to use, too, due to their focus on children and teenage players. The results have been astounding.

By the end of 2021, more than 150 million people were using *Minecraft* each month—more than six times as many as in 2014, when Microsoft bought the platform—with the title also becoming the best-selling game in history. Despite this, *Minecraft* was far from the size of the new market leader, *Roblox*, which had grown from fewer than 5 million to 225 million monthly users over that same period. Put together, the two platforms were averaging more than 6 billion hours of monthly usage, with more than 100 million different virtual worlds having been created, and more than $1 billion in royalties paid to *Roblox* developers alone. The second most popular virtual world on *Roblox*, *Adopt Me!*, was created in 2017 by two hobbyist players under the age of 25; in 2021 alone, *Adopt Me!* received more than 10 billion visits—more than seven times the average number of global tourism visits in pre–COVID-19.^([15](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr15))

In addition to being popular, the virtual worlds of *Roblox* and *Minecraft* consistently achieved new creative highs and made their presence felt in the “real world,” too. On a recurring basis, fans of franchises such as *Game of Thrones* or *Star Wars*, or sports teams such as Real Madrid or Manchester City, would spend weeks reproducing major locations brick by brick—such as the Santiago Bernabéu Stadium or even the 500 square miles of the fictional King’s Landing. One video game streamer, Aztter, constructed an original cyberpunk city out of an estimated 370 million *Minecraft* blocks, having worked an average of 16 hours per day for a year.^([16](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr16)) In 2015, Verizon built a cellphone inside *Minecraft* that could browse the web and even complete live (though blocky) video calls with people in the “real world.”^([17](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr17))

As the COVID-19 virus spread across China in February 2020, a community of Chinese *Minecraft* players rapidly re-created the 1.2-million-square-foot hospitals built in Wuhan as a tribute to the “IRL” (“in real life”) workers, receiving global press coverage.^([18](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr18)) One month later, Reporters Sans Frontières (also known as Reporters Without Borders) commissioned the construction of a museum within *Minecraft* that was composed of over 12.5 million blocks assembled by 24 virtual builders in 16 different countries over some 250 hours combined.^([19](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr19)) The Uncensored Library, as it was called, allowed users in countries such as Russia, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt to read banned literature, as well as works promoting free speech and detailing the lives of slain journalists such as Jamal Khashoggi.

Despite the enormous growth in *Minecraft*’s and *Roblox*’s audiences and developer communities, many other platforms emerged and grew in the second half of the 2010s. In the summer of 2016, Niantic released *Pokémon Go*, which shared the core mechanics of most *Pokémon* titles—finding, capturing, training, and battling Pokémon—but required players to leave their homes and traverse a virtual map layered atop the real world. To catch a Pokémon that swam in the ocean, for example, a player would need to visit an ocean-side beach; to find a bumblebee-styled Pokémon, they would need to wander a local park in the summer. Once the *Pokémon Go* application noticed the player was close to a Pokémon, a battle would trigger, in which the user could see a 3D version of the creature through their smartphone screen and camera, then throw an animated pokéball to capture the creature, which would also try to evade the player. By visiting various virtual locations set around physical landmarks, the user could also train their Pokémon, and battle other players at “gyms” based on key locations such as museums or statues. After six months, *Pokémon Go* amassed more than half a billion downloads and half a billion in revenue. By its sixth anniversary, lifetime revenue exceeded $6 billion with monthly players averaging between 75 and 150 million. The title was praised for its promotion of physical activity, helping local businesses grow as a result of increased foot traffic, and fostering in-person connection among players who didn’t know one another. Notably, Niantic was a spin-off from Google’s Geo division, which oversaw Google Maps, Google Earth, and Google Street View. Niantic’s CEO, John Hanke, had run the division until the spin-off, having joined with the sale of Keyhole, where he was co-founder and CEO.

In 2017, Epic Games launched *Fortnite*, which quickly established itself as a platform for mass culture, rather than just a virtual pastime. In 2018 and 2019 (the last years with publicly available data), *Fortnite* collected more than $9 billion in net revenue—mostly through the sale of virtual apparel that had no performance-related or competitive value. These sales exceeded those of storied fashion houses and brands such as Dolce & Gabbana, Saint Laurent, J.Crew, Prada, and Lacoste. Unlike these physical labels, however, *Fortnite* had only design costs, rather than manufacturing and shipping/fulfillment expenses, making Epic one of the most profitable apparel makers globally. By the end of 2023, brands such as Nike, Balenciaga, LVMH, Moncler, and Ralph Lauren had released exclusive virtual apparel inside *Fortnite*, as well as complementary physical editions with prices that ran into the thousands. Before passing away from cancer at the age of 41, Virgil Abloh, the founder and CEO of Off-White and creative director of Louis Vuitton menswear, announced the creation of a virtual-only fashion label, saying, “I want to make virtual clothes to paint pictures physical clothes cannot, and let buyers access a new dimension of their personal style—no matter who they are, where they live, and the virtual worlds they love.”^([20](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr20))

![In both 2018 and 2019, the only years in which revenues have been publicly disclosed, Fortnite generated more net revenue in a 12-month period than any other game in history—even though the entirety of the game was free-to-play. Nearly all of the title’s revenue came from the sale of in-game cosmetics that had no effect on gameplay but were instead used to restyle the player’s avatar, or from season passes that players purchased in order to unlock cosmetics that were not available for à la carte purchases. The revenues generated from these cosmetics exceeded those of many of the top clothing companies in the world—and in contrast to “real” clothing, these virtual goods had nearly 100% gross profit margins. ¶ Epic Games, The Verge, The Companies, Matthew Ball](OEBPS/images/pg49.jpg)

In both 2018 and 2019, the only years in which revenues have been publicly disclosed, Fortnite generated more net revenue in a 12-month period than any other game in history—even though the entirety of the game was free-to-play. Nearly all of the title’s revenue came from the sale of in-game cosmetics that had no effect on gameplay but were instead used to restyle the player’s avatar, or from season passes that players purchased in order to unlock cosmetics that were not available for à la carte purchases. The revenues generated from these cosmetics exceeded those of many of the top clothing companies in the world—and in contrast to “real” clothing, these virtual goods had nearly 100% gross profit margins. ¶ Epic Games, The Verge, The Companies, Matthew Ball

In 2018, Epic launched *Fortnite Creative*, its own riff on *Minecraft*’s and *Roblox*’s world-building modes, with brands such as Nike and Coachella, as well as the Estate of Martin Luther King Jr., establishing a presence. The following year, *Fortnite* hosted a live, interactive, and canonical prologue to the Star Wars film *The Rise of Skywalker*, which also included a live interview with director J. J. Abrams. The year after that, hip-hop star (and Kardashian family member) Travis Scott hosted a concert that was attended live by over 12 million players, with millions more watching live on social media. As a point of contrast, fewer than 9 million Americans attended *The Avengers: Endgame*, which holds the record for highest single-day ticket sales in American history, during its first 24 hours of release. The track Scott premiered during the concert, which featured Kid Cudi, debuted at #1 on the *Billboard* Hot 100 charts a week later, was Cudi’s first #1 track, and finished 2020 as the third-largest US debut of the year. In addition, several of the tracks Scott performed from his two-year-old *Astroworld* album returned to the *Billboard* charts after the concert, with the official event video accumulating more than 200 million views. *Fortnite* would go on to host live shows with artists such as Steve Aoki, Ariana Grande, and J Balvin; exclusively premiere trailers to films such as Christopher Nolan’s *Tenet*; host film festivals; and tie in with the 75th anniversary of the NBA.

In the history of the Metaverse from MUDs to *Fortnite*, a few points are clear. Efforts to build a parallel virtual existence span decades rather than just a few buzzy years. As graphical capability, experiential diversity, and the number of internet users grew, so did the popularity of the top virtual worlds. Moreover, growth seems likely to continue in the years to come. But to understand why so many companies declared for the Metaverse in 2020–22, it’s necessary to examine the technical side of the history detailed above. Recall Sweeney’s 2021 observation: not only has a “critical mass of working pieces started coming together,” it is “coming together rapidly.” The best place to start is with live graphical simulation technologies.

 

### **Real-Time Graphical Simulation**

The first attempts to build a “computer game” or “video game” emerged in the 1940s. The 1947 “cathode-ray tube amusement device” is considered the first interactive electronic game, but it did not use a computer or any form of memory device or program. Instead, the player adjusted various knobs to change the trajectory of a CRT beam so that it would align with plastic targets overlaid on the device’s screen.^([21](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr21)) In 1948, the celebrated mathematician, computer scientist, and cryptanalyst Alan Turing began development of Turochamp, which was intended to play a full game of chess with a human player, but the code proved too complex for even military computers of the era.

In 1950, the Canadian inventor Josef Kates unveiled Bertie the Brain, a nearly four-meter-tall computer that, for all its immensity, could play just a single game that spanned only two different inputs and nine total decisions: tic-tac-toe. Bertie was incapable of producing computer graphics; the moves of both the player and Bertie’s AI were represented by the turning on and off of various lightbulbs.^([‡](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-045)) *OXO*, a 1952 tic-tac-toe title which was developed at the University of Cambridge as part of a research study, added on-screen computer graphics and ran on a general-purpose computer rather than purpose-built one (though this meant the computer was the size of the room, rather than an everyday storage cabinet).

Until 1958’s *Tennis for Two*, all “video games” had been made to test computer-programming capabilities or evaluate human-computer interactions rather than for entertainment. Still, *Tennis for Two* had no leisurely origin story—and it still required several hundred pounds of professional equipment.^([22](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr22)) The title was created by William Higinbotham, an American physicist working at Brookhaven National Laboratory, which had been established by the US Atomic Energy Commission following World War II, and was based on research used to simulate the trajectory of missiles under various wind conditions. Specifically, *Tennis for Two*’s display ran on an oscilloscope, which graphically displayed voltage-based signals as waveforms. Higinbotham programmed his oscilloscope for three different voltage inputs—one each for the tennis court, its net, and a ball—that cycled so rapidly that a human player would see all three at the same time. The ball, meanwhile, was adapted from the missile arcs. As the name suggests, *Tennis for Two* was also a multiplayer title—the first in history. It was also the first video game whose graphics were in a constant state of change. Earlier titles with computer-generated graphics, such as *OXO*, changed only when a move was made.

The video game sector shifted from its infancy to childhood in 1962 following the release of the multiplayer combat title *Spacewar!* Originally created at MIT by Steve Russell and fellow members of the school’s Tech Model Railroad Club, *Spacewar!* became the first video game that was playable outside a single research institute and to be installed on multiple computers. In fact, Russell promptly open-sourced the title’s codebase, inspiring other computer scientists and hobbyists to use his creation to build their own.

The 1970s saw four major innovations in graphics-based simulations. The first was the release of the first video game console, 1972’s Magnavox Odyssey. For only $99.95 (equivalent to roughly $750 in 2024), a family could purchase an easy-to-use, shoebox-sized computer designed to play 28 games, including *Pong*, each of which was limited to white shapes on blank black screen and no sound. The second and third innovations came via MUDs and MUSHs, which pioneered both user-generated virtual world creation and the ability for multiple users to co-experience that world over the internet. The fourth advance was “3D,” though these early efforts focused on producing the sensation of 3D rather than “true 3D.” The first such example was *Maze*, which debuted in 1973 and was made by high school students Steve Colley, Greg Thompson, and Howard Palmer during a study program at NASA’s Ames Research Center.^([23](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr23)) *Maze* was a first-person-perspective title in which players navigated through a labyrinth of seemingly endless, identically designed hallways. Though users could move forward or backward, or take a left or right to travel down an intersecting hallway, their perspective was always straight ahead, with no ability to look up or down (vertical axis) or to the side (horizontal). When the player did make a turn, the very next frame would place them in the center of the new hallway, rather than show the user’s eyeline as it shifted across a doorframe and from one pathway to another. And if the player wanted to move forward or backward, they could do so only in fixed one-step increments. In truth, the maze didn’t even have a 3D model. Instead, it was composed of coordinate-based intersections of green lines that provided the illusion of angles and three dimensions.

In 1980, Atari released *Battlezone*, which let users take control of a tank viewport as they navigated a large two-dimensional map, that included various pyramid- and block-shaped obstacles, and fought enemy combatants. In contrast to *Maze*, players could look right and left, but the underlying mechanics were similar. Opponents and obstacles looked like they were 3D thanks to their geometric green outlines and 360-degree rotations, but this was an illusion similar to that produced by quickly flipping through a stack of papers that, sheet by sheet, portrayed a tank rotating from left to right. And while enemy tanks and hazards were often wider at the base than at their top, the tank could only ever shoot straight ahead and its shells, unlike the balls of 1958’s *Tennis for Two*, had no gravity-like arcs. As such, the varying widths were of purely aesthetic value (in fact, the game could have been played with only a single horizontal row of pixels). *Battlezone*’s background hills, meanwhile, would enlarge and shrink as the players moved backward or forward, but could never be reached.

A Reproduction of the 1973 Game Maze (also known as Maze War)

![Steve Colley, Greg Thompson, and Howard Palmer](OEBPS/images/pg53.jpg)

Steve Colley, Greg Thompson, and Howard Palmer

In 1991, John Carmack, Adrian Carmack (no relation to John Carmack), Tom Hall, and John Romero founded id Software, which released the groundbreaking *Catacomb 3-D* in 1991, *Wolfenstein 3D* in 1992, and *Doom* in 1993. Though these titles seemed to be 3D—and offered full-color maps and models—they are not typically described as “true” or “full” 3D.

Imagine playing the classic *Pac-Man* arcade game, but with the camera (and all in-game assets) swung down 90 degrees from a bird’s-eye view into first person. The player, as Pac-Man, would see hallways dozens of feet long, several feet tall, and several feet wide, and be able to travel freely forward and backward, while also turning right or left at an intersection. Though this might seem 3D, the game’s ghosts, pellets, and fruit would still be flat 2D models with no sides or backs, let alone angles. These objects would sit squarely in the center of view at all times, too, and could not be ducked under or jumped over when moving forward. Meanwhile, the level itself would remain flat, with no stairs, hurdles, or even inclines or declines, with the player also unable to tilt their camera up or down. And because tilting the camera angle does not add any more detail to the map, moving forward or backward would, from a visual perspective, resemble zooming in or out from a given perspective (not unlike zooming in or out on a Google Street View image, which either tightens or widens the view, with the image blurring or sharpening accordingly).

id’s *Catacomb 3-D* effectively pioneered the *Pac-Man* example described above and, in doing so, created a thrill ride that felt not only 3D but new. The title was a fast-moving action shooter with large maps, swappable guns, depleting health and ammo meters that could be replenished through in-game items, secret doors the player could push through to reveal hidden pathways, and the ability for players to move “naturally” across its map, rather than jump across preset chess- or checkers-like positions.

In 1992, id debuted *Doom*, which maintained the 3D approach of 1991’s *Catacomb 3-D*, but seemed to offer players the ability to travel to higher and lower levels. Mechanically, it was akin to visually elevating half of a *Pac-Man* maze. The titular hero might seem to fall down from or jump up to this higher level, but there would be no real interaction between the two layers, and the process of moving from one to another was just an in-game animation. In the case of *Doom*, a player sitting on the top of a ledge would still be shooting straight, but their bullets would hit an enemy down below as though they were standing side by side. And if the player were below the ledge, they could not “shoot” up, just straight into the wall. And above the wall was just more wall that looked like the top of the ledge. Though these were tricks, the result was still stunning—especially given that *Doom*, unlike *Catacomb 3-D*, supported local and internet-based multiplayer.

In 1996, id released its “first true 3D” game, *Quake*, which boasted full 3D models, uneven terrain, the ability to look up and shoot artillery that would follow gravity-like arcs when shot—and even as these explosives ricocheted among walls, columns, and other obstacles. Though *Quake* was another landmark for the gaming industry, id’s earlier achievements had already convinced many of its peers that the era of real-time 3D had arrived. One of the first to subscribe to this view was Epic Games.

Epic had been founded by Tim Sweeney in 1991, the same year as id, but the company initially focused on 2D games, such as *ZZT*, *Jazz Jackrabbit*, and *Jill of the Jungle*. According to Sweeney, the release of “Wolfenstein and DOOM … changed everything. The titans were busy building huge 2D games and Epic took a huge leap of faith on 3D.”^([24](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr24)) In the months after *Wolfenstein*’s release, one of id’s business leads, Mark Rein, joined Sweeney as a co-founder, and by 1995, Epic had merged all of its smaller teams working on 2D games into one focused on a true 3D game—1998’s *Unreal*.

Like *Quake*, *Unreal* was a “true 3D” sci-fi multiplayer shooter and an instant hit. It achieved an 89% average review on GameRankings (the predecessor to Metacritic),^([25](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr25)) was the 14th-best-selling PC game of the year,^([26](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr26)) sold 1.5 million units by its fourth anniversary,^([27](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr27)) and led to a direct sequel in 2003, as well as four multiplayer-focused spin-offs (*Unreal Tournament* in 1999, *Unreal Tournament 2003*, *Unreal Tournament 2004*, and *Unreal Tournament 3* in 2007). As discussed at the start of this chapter, *Unreal* was also Epic’s first effort to build a “proto-Metaverse,” though it was limited to “text chat” and “300-polygon strangers.” Despite the success of the game, *Unreal*’s greatest legacy was the technology that powered it.

*Unreal* had cost about $3 million to produce ($6 million in 2024 dollars), most of which was spent on its engine, dubbed “Unreal Engine,” rather than gameplay or artwork. Most game developers at the time could not afford such investments and those that could weren’t guaranteed an equally useful result, either. And so in 1996, two years before *Unreal* was even released to the public, Sweeney bet he could build a business around its engine. Though licensing UE meant aiding Epic’s rivals, some of whom produced directly competitive titles such as *Duke Nukem*, it netted the company $250,000–$350,000 in up-front payments and 5%–7% in royalties in each case.^([28](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr28)) It also enabled Epic to further its investment in UE and to benefit from the R&D of its licensees, too. In September of 1998, Sweeney told *Maximum PC*: “The big goal with the *Unreal* technology all along was to build up a base of code that could be extended and improved through many generations of games.”^([29](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr29))

In 1996, id had begun selectively licensing its Quake Engine, too—and saw early success when Valve produced its 1998 blockbuster title *Half-Life* using a modified version of the Quake Engine—but most developers opted to build on UE. And while *Unreal* was inspired by the early 3D games of id Software, the Unreal Engine’s source of inspiration was Epic’s very first game, the 2D puzzler *ZZT*.

In 1989, Sweeney had begun building a text editor,^([§](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-044)) because he didn’t like those available on PCs at the time. Eventually, he transformed the cursor into a smiley face, then designed and inserted other characters into the application, followed by labyrinth-like walls, the ability to collect ammo and shoot enemies, discovery keys used to unlock doors, and so on, until he had produced a colorful 2D action-adventure puzzle game. After encouragement from friends, Sweeney decided to release *ZZT* publicly in January 1991.^([30](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr30)) By November, the 20-year-old Sweeney was generating over $3,000 in monthly sales from *ZZT* (equivalent to $6,700 in 2024 prices). Less than a year later, monthly sales exceeded $25,000 ($58,000).^([31](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr31))

A Screenshot of the Homescreen for Epic Games’ ZZT

![Tim Sweeney, Epic Games](OEBPS/images/pg57.jpg)

Tim Sweeney, Epic Games

Due to its origins as a text editor, *ZZT*’s “graphics” were actually just made up of the 256 characters that constituted the ASCII standard, each of which was one byte in size, and spanned the numbers 0–9, lower- and uppercase versions of all 26 English letters, various mathematical symbols such as π and + as well as select punctuation like !, shading blocks like ![](OEBPS/images/pg58-1.jpg)or ![](OEBPS/images/pg58-2.jpg), and other signs like ↑ and ![](OEBPS/images/pg58-3.jpg). While ASCII had been popular in the 1960s and 1970s, it had largely fallen out of style as computers gained the ability to render individual pixels, which led to the rise of more specialized in-game art. As such, *ZZT*’s visuals were inferior to those of titles as old as 1978’s *Space Invaders* or other maze-focused games like *Pac-Man*—and the title fell particularly short of other 1991 releases, such as *Sonic the Hedgehog* and *The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past*. Yet *ZZT*’s technical foundations provided the title with a key advantage.

In addition to its fun and intuitive gameplay, *ZZT* thrived because of Sweeney’s decision to include a customized version of the very software he used to make it, thus allowing users to build their own levels using his ZZT-OOP scripting language. *ZZT* was not the first video game to support or encourage “user-generated content”—MUDs were based on that very premise and dedicated game-creation software had been released throughout the 1980s for consoles such as the Commodore 64 or Atari ST. However, *ZZT*’s origins as an editing program and Sweeney’s interest in such functionality meant that *ZZT*’s tools were far easier to use than those afforded by other titles. In contrast with other game creators, *ZZT* was also downloaded over the internet, rather than purchased via cartridge or disk. Accordingly, users could easily (and freely) share their mazes with other users online, which helped grow awareness of *ZZT* while also deepening its gameplay.

Eventually, Sweeney announced a contest in which users could submit their mazes to his company, then known as Potomac Computer Systems. The winning entries were then packaged in the 1992 sequels *Best of ZZT* and *ZZT’s Revenge*, with their creators receiving gift certificates and/or honorable mentions in the game’s credits (six creators even won jobs at the newly renamed Epic MegaGames).^([32](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr32))

Sweeney credits *ZZT* with convincing him to start a gaming company and setting its “core philosophy.… We both build games ourselves and we share all the results of our work with the world to build their own games.”^([33](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr33)) And as the company shifted its focus to 3D in the mid-1990s, Sweeney aspired to produce a 3D engine that was as easy to use as it was powerful, thereby enabling creative teams to spend more of their time making a game, not building the tools needed to do so, or learning how to use those same tools. To Sweeney, *ZZT* was “sort of a prototype Unreal Engine 0.”^([34](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr34))

The development of easy-to-use, cross-company tools such as UE are key to establishing the Metaverse. Previously, building a virtual world required a developer/creator to acquire deep technical expertise and design their own tools, just like Epic Games or id Software, or build within a platform, such as *Second Life* or *ZZT*. The former approach constrained how many virtual worlds were created, and led to technical fragmentation that made interoperation difficult. The latter approach, meanwhile, produced networks within an application, rather than a network of applications.

In the quarter century since its debut, the Unreal Engine (now UE5) has become the most widely used “high-fidelity” engine for 3D games. Unity, a rival engine that launched in 2005, powers more than 50% of mobile games. And these engines are increasingly used outside of gaming, too.

Although the first few dozen virtual worlds were designed for scientific purposes, such as Turochamp, Bertie the Brain, *OXO*, *Tennis for Two*, *Spacewar!*, and *Maze*, nearly all of those created since were designed for video games. This skew is partly why so many liken the Metaverse to such experiences. It’s also a contrast with the traditional adoption curve for advanced computing and networking technologies.

The first computers were too large, expensive, and power intensive for anyone but governments and major enterprises to afford, let alone use. Moreover, these devices were too difficult for the average person to use and their utility was limited to (slowly) solving complex calculations that were relevant only to research labs and governments. Accordingly, it was more than 50 years until half of computers were owned by consumers and longer still for most usage to be noncommercial. The arc of the internet was similar. Over its first 20 years, bandwidth was too limited and latency too great for the internet to support consumer use cases such as photo sharing, let alone video calls or streaming, but it was more than capable of sharing word documents, spreadsheets, and messages, which were of immense value to the “information economy” and far superior to using couriers and postal services. And while early smartphones could barely play *Snake*, let alone support color displays, businesses and governments considered push email to be orders of magnitude more helpful than pager notifications or live phone calls.

In contrast to the path of computers and the internet, 3D simulations have limitations that historically prevented their adoption by industry and government services and instead confined them to consumer-focused implementation. All a “game” needs from simulation is to create a sense of fun; the physics of a building on fire, a car crash, or a shotgun pellet do not need to be realistic—and are sometimes better because they’re fantastical. Military personnel, surgeons, and infrastructure operators, meanwhile, need far greater fidelity. And it’s only over the past few years that this has been possible.

By the start of the 2020s, a company that had access to enough computing power could run large-scale, real-time simulations down to the particle level, enabling precise readings of heat absorption, transference, and dissipation, the effects of vibrations, the flow of sound, the reflection of light, the accumulation of radiation, and so on. The engines behind these simulations recently became “deterministic,” too—able to generate the identical outcome each time they were run, rather than nondeterministic, in which outcomes are largely but not precisely alike.

The many advances in real-time 3D simulation have resulted in new usages. In 2019, the Hong Kong International Airport produced a digital twin using the Unity Engine that simulates critical airport activity in real time, from passenger movement to planes and vehicles on the runway, as well as inbound traffic and their dependencies. This information is then used to predict and address potential backups and gate changes, and to prepare for and respond to emergency situations. In other cases, entire cities have been re-created and then connected to real-time data feeds for vehicular traffic, weather, and civic services, such as police, fire, and ambulance response. The goal of a digital twin is to enable city planners to make more informed decisions about zoning, construction approvals, and more. How would a new commercial mall affect travel times for emergency medical or police services? How might a specific building design adversely affect wind conditions, urban temperatures, or downtown light?

A good way to understand the practical potential of city-scale digital twins, unsurprisingly, came from video gaming. In December 2021, Epic Games released *The Matrix Awakens*, a playable technical demonstration that was intended to show off the functionality of the forthcoming Unreal Engine 5 when running on the newly released PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S|X, which kicked off the “ninth generation of video game consoles” (the 1972 Magnavox Odyssey was first gen). *Matrix Awakens* was set in a procedurally generated and photorealistic city that was 16 square kilometers in area, spanning 7,000 buildings, 260 kilometers of drivable roads with 1,250 intersections, 50,000 cars (nearly all of which could be walked up to and driven), and 40,000 pedestrians.^([35](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr35)) “Players,” if one could call them that, could change the city’s time of day in real time and watch the sun’s rays shift and bounce across various buildings and windshields, as well as modify the number of pedestrians and cars, and then watch how the flow of traffic and people altered as a result. Some masochistic users even orchestrated traffic accidents so severe that hours later, they could observe how traffic jams had spread throughout the city.

In September of 2022, job postings at Tesla revealed the company was working to make Epic’s demonstration a reality by producing a live 3D model of the city of San Francisco using the Unreal Engine.^([36](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr36)) Unlike Epic’s demo, Tesla’s simulation doesn’t need to run on a single, consumer-brand video game console. Instead, it can be operated on Tesla’s private supercomputer cluster, or on the data centers of cloud computing giants such as Amazon and Microsoft. And Tesla’s virtual San Francisco is not made by designers or generative models, but assembled and maintained using the myriad real-time lidar scans and positional pings generated by the network of San Franciscan Teslas. The resulting simulation would aid city planning, autonomous driving software, and human navigation.

Tesla wasn’t the only tech giant to imagine a living Metaverse version of Google Street View; Google, too, was hard at work. In June of 2023, the company launched its Geospatial Creator tool, which let users create 3D/augmented reality experiences that could be “anchored” to real-world locations inside Google’s various mapping programs for other users to see and experience. To commemorate the launch, Google announced an AR-based reinvention of the 1978 hit video game *Space Invaders*. Unlike the arcade classic, however, the titular enemies would rain down not from the top of a CRT-display but from the skies of major cities such as Rio de Janeiro and New York, and they would be repelled not through joysticks and buttons but by smartphone-wielding citizens throughout the city. Nvidia, meanwhile, announced it was building “Earth-2,” a live digital twin that would model “the physics, chemistry and biology of the atmosphere, waters, ice, land and \[aggregate\] human activities” of the earth down to the “meter-scale resolution \[that\] is needed to simulate \[as an example\] clouds that reflect sunlight back to space.”^([37](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr37))

### **Head-Mounted Displays**

As the field of graphical simulation progressed, so too did efforts to build “head-mounted displays” capable of realizing “Pygmalion’s Spectacles.”

In 1955, the American cinematographer Morton Heilig wrote a famous paper, “The Cinema of the Future,” declaring that “pandemonium \[reigned\] supreme in the film industry,” with studios “hastily converting to its own ‘revolutionary’ system—Cinerama, Colorama, Panoramic Screens, Cinemascope, Three-D, and Stereophonic Sound,” which were used to “lure” customers with (false) promises of a “sensational new experience.”^([38](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr38)) Worse still, Heilig argued, “art” had fallen behind “science” and “industry” in using contemporary technology and research into the human mind to make its products more “effective.”^([39](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr39)) In many cases, art failed to achieve “active participation” from a spectator—and without it “there can be no transfer of consciousness, no art.”^([40](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr40))

The remedy, to Heilig, was to activate four of the human species’ five primary senses (sight, hearing, smell, and touch), which contemporary research suggested “monopolized man’s attention” to 99% (respectively, 70%, 20%, 5%, and 4%, with taste making up the remaining 1%).^([41](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr41)) Due to sight’s share, he also argued that all of a spectator’s visual field must be filled with a screen, rather than the 5% offered by contemporary movie theaters, the 7.5% of widescreen-equipped theaters, the 18% of Cinemascope, or the 25% of Cinerama.^([42](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr42)) Ideally, the screen would offer “true and not illusory depth … another essential element of man’s consciousness” which would be achieved by “electronic and optical means,” rather than the tricks of polarized glasses, which first emerged in the late 1800s and were popularized by the 1930s.^([43](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr43)) Not long after his paper, Heilig got to work.

In 1960, the cinematographer-turned-inventor patented the “Telesphere Mask,” which would give spectators “a complete sensation of reality, i.e. moving three dimensional images which may be in colour, with 100% peripheral vision, binaural sound, scents and air breezes.”^([44](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr44)) The device looks astonishingly similar to modern HMD patents and supported stereoscopic (3D) and widescreen TV and true stereo sound (though no motion capture).^([45](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr45))

Two years later, Heilig patented the Sensorama, an “Experience Theater” designed to fully realize his vision of the Cinema of the Future.^([46](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr46)) This time, the “device” was an arcade-sized cabinet equipped with a screen, surround-sound system, fans, odor emitters that reproduced smells such as that of pizza and petroleum, and a moving chair—all of which were timed to specific events in movies that had also been produced by Heilig. Though the Sensorama was considered a marvel for decades after its unveiling, Heilig, like Professor Ludwig, was unable to find backers for his pioneering device and returned to traditional filmmaking by the 1970s.

Morton Heilig’s Telesphere Mask

![Heilig’s 1960 patent for a head-mounted display capable of stereoscopic 3D video and audio bears a remarkable resemblance to modern HMD patents. ¶ US Patent and Trademark Office, Morton Heilig](OEBPS/images/pg64.jpg)

Heilig’s 1960 patent for a head-mounted display capable of stereoscopic 3D video and audio bears a remarkable resemblance to modern HMD patents. ¶ US Patent and Trademark Office, Morton Heilig

In 1961, the Philco electronics company developed the first head-mounted display, the Headsight, which had a dedicated screen for each eye, as well as a magnetic motion detector that was connected to an external camera that moved with the user’s head. Though notable for its form factor, the Headsight was never intended to represent virtual reality, but instead to allow military users a live, first-person view of areas that were too dangerous to physically access.^([47](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr47))

In 1965, Ivan Sutherland detailed “The Ultimate Display,” a concept document that continues to guide VR research decades later. Sutherland’s objectives included the creation of a synthetic digital world that was photorealistic, supported 3D sound, provided haptic feedback, was fully interactive, and endured beyond the user’s personal experience inside the display. Moreover, Sutherland imagined this display being worn in a physical location that complemented his virtual world but was also controlled by the same computer. As he wrote, “A chair displayed in such a room would be good enough to sit in. Handcuffs displayed in such a room would be confining.” More alarmingly, Sutherland imagined “a bullet displayed in such a room would be fatal,” though “with appropriate programming,” he argued, the room and display paired together “could literally be the Wonderland into which Alice walked.”^([48](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr48)) By 1968, Sutherland had converted his theorizing into a real HMD, commonly known as the “Sword of Damocles.”^([¶](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-043)) Sutherland’s device could not control a physical space, but it is considered the first HMD able to generate its imagery via computer, rather than just relay the live video feed from a camera or play back prerecorded video. As one might expect, the Sword of Damocles did not have an onboard computer, but instead connected to a computer that was nearly as large as a typical American bedroom.

Morton Heilig’s Sensorama

![This 1962 patent filing for the Sensorama shows the booth, as well as its synthetic odor emitters, which are automatically activated at specific times during a Sensorama film. ¶ US Patent and Trademark Office, Morton Heilig](OEBPS/images/pg65.jpg)

This 1962 patent filing for the Sensorama shows the booth, as well as its synthetic odor emitters, which are automatically activated at specific times during a Sensorama film. ¶ US Patent and Trademark Office, Morton Heilig

Through the 1970s and 1980s, HMDs continued to progress, with a particular focus on simulating flight for professional pilots and other aviators. In 1989, NASA created project VIEW (Virtual Interface Environment Workstation), an HMD that could display an “artificial computer-generated environment or a real environment relayed from remote video cameras.”^([49](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr49)) In addition to the display, operators would wear a “DataGlove” that used fiber-optic cables and sensors that could reproduce their hands inside the VIEW, as well as a similarly functional “DataSuit,” which was also programmed to understand gestures.^([50](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr50)) The 1990s saw both Nintendo and Sego release VR headsets and gloves, though neither was a success.

After decades of unsuccessful tinkering from toy makers, inventors, and public research labs, big tech began to plow billions into the HMD field in the early 2010s. In 2010, Rony Abovitz, who previously founded MAKO Surgical Corp., which designed and manufactured robotic arms to aid live patient surgery, launched Magic Leap, which designed and manufactured mixed-reality devices primarily aimed at industrial and governmental applications. By the time Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund acquired a majority stake in Magic Leap in 2022, the company had raised more than $4 billion (though reports suggested it sold for less than that sum). Also in 2010, Microsoft started development of HoloLens AR platform,^([#](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-042)) which also focused on enterprise usage, with the first model releasing in 2016 and a follow-up in 2019, and Google kicked off its Google Glass smart glasses, which were designed for consumer users. The first Google Glass Explorer was released in 2013, with an enterprise-focused unit launching in 2019 and a reconceived and rebranded design publicly field-tested in 2022. Google’s Cardboard VR platform debuted in 2014, with Google’s second VR platform, Daydream, coming two years later. Sony PlayStation began development of its VR platform in 2011, and the PS VR came to market in 2016. In 2014, Snap acquired Vergence Labs, an AR glasses start-up that had been founded in 2011, and served as the foundation for the Snap Spectacles, which premiered in 2016, with the Spectacles 2, Spectacles 3, and Spectacles 4 releasing over the following five years. Amazon began development of its Alexa-based AR glasses sometime in 2016 or 2017. The first Echo Frames were released in 2019; the second edition arrived two years later.

NASA’s Project VIEW and DataGlove

![NASA’s VIEW could show a live video feed from remote cameras, or a computer-generated environment. DataGlove used fiber-optic cables and sensors to translate hand movements inside the VIEW. Not pictured is the complementary DataSuit. NASA](OEBPS/images/pg67.jpg)

NASA’s VIEW could show a live video feed from remote cameras, or a computer-generated environment. DataGlove used fiber-optic cables and sensors to translate hand movements inside the VIEW. Not pictured is the complementary DataSuit. NASA

As Magic Leap, Microsoft, and Google started their HMD divisions, Palmer Luckey, an HMD designer at the University of Southern California Institute for Creative Technologies, began developing a VR device that later became known as the Oculus. At the time, Luckey was rumored to own the largest personal collection of HMDs in the world, and his goal for the Oculus was to build a device more capable than any other available in the market at the time but also cheaper. At the time, John Carmack, the id Software founder, had also been investigating the HMD field and heard about Luckey’s work. After trying a prototype Oculus in late 2011, Carmack began to help Luckey with his research, and at the 2012 E3 video game convention in Los Angeles, the “father of 3D graphics” gave the first public demonstration of the Oculus (which was visibly held together by duct tape) and announced *Doom 3* would be ported to the device. The following year, Carmack joined Oculus as chief technology officer and left id shortly thereafter. A year after that, Facebook purchased Oculus VR for $2 billion, with Carmack staying on until 2022, when he left to found Keen Technologies, an artificial general intelligence start-up.

Despite the tens of billions spent on VR and AR HMDs by mid-2020, the lifetime sales of these devices were fewer than $30 million combined.^([51](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr51)) But then, suddenly, these investments seemed to mature.

In June 2020, neurosurgeons at Johns Hopkins performed America’s first and second surgeries on a live patient using an FDA-approved AR device. The first was a spinal fusion surgery, during which six screws were inserted into the patient’s spine, while the second concerned the removal of a cancerous tumor on another patient’s spine. In both cases, the surgeon used a head-mounted AR device that rendered a 3D model based on a CT of the patient’s spinal column and internal bone structures, which displayed, in real time, the surgeon’s tools and insertions, plus the patient’s vitals. By the end of 2022, Dr. Timothy Witham, who performed Johns Hopkins’s AR surgeries and is the director of the hospital’s Spinal Fusion Laboratory, had completed more than 150 live patient surgeries using an AR device, with dozens of other such surgeries taking place across the United States.^([52](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr52))

In September of 2020, Mercedes-Benz announced it would deploy Microsoft’s HoloLens 2 AR device across its nearly 400 dealerships throughout the United States to local technicians performing complex repairs.^([53](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr53)) Specifically, the device would provide technicians with on-screen schematics, automatically highlight the parts that needed testing or repairs, and guide installations and removals, while also warning of key risks, such as the potential for a burn. Technicians could also use the device to video-call Mercedes’s own centralized experts, who would be able to instruct the local technicians while watching their efforts in real time from the HoloLens’s front-facing camera.

Throughout 2020 and 2021, each of the ten largest upstream oil and gas companies began to incorporate VR devices into their training programs, especially for those who would be stationed on oil rigs and platforms. Not only are these facilities entirely foreign to most new hires, but they are in remote locations and dangerous; in the United States, oil rig and platform fatality rates are 25–30 per 100,000 (45–50 for drill workers), more than seven times the national average.^([54](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr54)) One oil and gas executive reported that beyond reduced training time and accident rates, the use of VR devices in workplace onboarding had even led to new safety signage, placements, and instructions after eye tracing revealed that many trainees struggled to locate (or otherwise missed) emergency information in test scenarios.

In March 2021, the US Army announced a deal to buy up to 120,000 customized AR HoloLens devices from Microsoft over the following decade. This contract was valued at $22 billion—nearly $200,000 per headset (this sum includes hardware upgrades, repairs, bespoke software, and other Azure cloud computing services). In a press release, Master Sergeant Marc Krugh, who supported the army-Microsoft AR partnership since its inception, said the device would enable soldiers “to rehearse and train in more realistic scenarios.”^([55](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr55)) The army-specific HoloLens unit, called IVAS (Integrated Visual Augmentation System), used HoloLens’s technology, while adding thermal imagery, additional sensors, GPS, and night vision to provide situation inputs and live training data to soldiers. Users could see where they were on the battlefield, as well as what and who was around them, by “projecting holographic images, three-dimensional terrain maps and a compass onto their field of vision.” Microsoft boasted that IVAS would enable users to shift their view to the simulated “vantage point of combatants” and evaluate not just their prospect for success but how they might be affected by daylight, moonlight, rain, and so on. The army was particularly keen on the ability to minimize the risk of friendly fire and improve the ability to escape a firefight. When paired with a weapon sight, IVAS allowed soldiers to see as their rifle might see, thereby providing the ability to “safely look around corners.”

Alongside the rapid deployment of commercial HMDs was an equally sudden, and even larger, surge in consumer demand. In May of 2019, Facebook released the Quest 1, the sixth VR device released by its Oculus division. Over its first 14 months on sale, fewer than 1 million total units were shipped. The Quest 2, which released in October 2020, sold 1 million units in under 100 days and crossed 10 million by its one-year anniversary. Moreover, the Quest 2’s sales figures were comparable to those of Microsoft’s Xbox S|X console, which had sold roughly 12 million units since its debut in November 2020, and not far off from the 16 million units sold by PlayStation 5, which also came to market in November 2020. The Quest 2’s growth over the Quest 1 also recalled the second iPhone, which outsold the first iPhone three to one and ushered in the smartphone era. In 2022, Mark Zuckerberg revealed that it was the success of the Quest 2 that inspired him to publicly unveil Facebook’s Metaverse ambitions and rename the company.^([56](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr56)) By the end of 2022, annual spend on VR applications was estimated at more than a billion dollars per year, three-quarters of which was billed through Facebook’s Quest Store.^([57](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr57))

For many, the clearest signal that the age of mixed-reality headsets was imminent came on June 6, 2023. At its Worldwide Developers Conference, Apple unveiled its long-awaited Vision Pro headset at its Cupertino, California, headquarters, with an average of 725,000 people watching the more than two-hour-long video.^([58](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr58)) The Vision Pro represented Apple’s most significant product launch since 2007’s iPhone, with tens of billions in R&D invested and more than 5,000 patents behind what the company called “the most advanced personal electronics device ever” and the start of a “new era of computing … spatial computing.”^([59](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr59)) Among the many use cases demonstrated were virtual movie theaters, mixed-reality school lessons, and immersive 3D “memories.”

Given the attention paid to the new 3D-focused devices, it has been easy to overlook the investments that added spatial functionality to traditional 2D form factors. In 2016, Apple released its first iPhone model with two rear cameras, enabling apps to focus on two fields of depth at the same time. Starting in 2017, the standard-issue iPhone came equipped with two rear cameras, with that year’s model also adding infrared (IR) sensors to the front-facing camera that could track and recognize 30,000 points on a user’s face in real time. To support this new hardware, Apple introduced ARKit, a software frame that helped developers build AR apps using the iPhone’s many cameras, computer and graphics processors, and motion sensors. The results were immediate.

In 2015, Snap launched AR filters, which used a phone’s camera and processor to understand a face and contextually layer on top a 3D effect, such as sunglasses, a beard, or blue eyes, all in real time. At the time, all filters were produced by Snapchat. Two months after the 2017 launch of Apple’s ARKit and IR-enabled iPhone X, Snap launched Lens Studio, which enabled third-party developers and eventually users to create their own lenses. Two years later, the company reported that users had created more than 600,000 AR lenses, with 142 million using at least one AR lens daily;^([60](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr60)) by April 2021, Snap said it had 200 million daily users of its AR lenses, with over a million AR lenses having been created.^([61](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr61))

Apple’s AR investments, which were rapidly replicated by Google’s Android operating system and ecosystem of device manufacturers, also enabled *Pokémon Go* to embrace “true AR.” Upon its release in July 2017, *Pokémon Go*’s “AR” was really just a 3D character or object layered overtop whatever the user’s camera was pointed to and without reference to what it saw, or its implications. A Pikachu might be seen on top of a user’s back lawn, but if the user tilted their camera to the sky or underground, Pikachu would still be there and not seem to know that fact, either. But starting three months after Apple’s ARKit and iPhone X, Niantic began a series of contextual AR upgrades. Now, Pikachu would be layered correctly on top of the user’s backyard, and if the user looked elsewhere, Pikachu would stay where it was. By 2020, Niantic had begun to roll out “occlusion,” whereby Pokémon might even hide behind a tree in the backyard, and a Pokéball thrown at Pikachu would appear to hit the tree and bounce away, rather than pass through it to the popular character.

In 2019, Apple added a third rear camera to its iPhone Pro line and also began to include ultra-wideband (UWB) transmitters and receivers into its full iPhone line, which enabled the devices to “see” through sound—just as a bat might. Specifically, Apple’s UWB transmitters were capable of emitting and processing up to a billion radar pulses per second. In doing so, these devices could generate spatial maps of a user’s home or workplace, precisely place itself within any preexisting map (whether generated by the user or available through a mapping app, such as those of Google or Apple), identify the location of other UWB devices within a few centimeters, and enhance the accuracy and safety of proximity-based smart home functionality (e.g., automatically unlock a home door when the user was approaching from outside but not when they were walking by inside the home).

Beginning with 2020’s iPhone 12 Pro, high-end iOS devices were also equipped with lidar scanners that enabled users to create high-fidelity 3D models by photographing real-world objects (a process called photogrammetry). The iPhone’s lidar-based photogrammetry capture is so powerful that many design and engineering professionals now use the device instead of $20,000–$30,000 dedicated lidar cameras. By the end of 2022, tens of thousands of private owners had used the device to produce high-resolution, immersive models of their homes, with the models then uploaded to real estate sites to better attract home buyers, or to furniture websites to help with interior decorating.

In May of 2021, Google announced Project Starline, the company’s efforts to reinvent the stodgy telepresence booth using photorealistic 3D models and machine learning software. The “magic” of traditional telepresence hardware, which first emerged in the early 1990s, was rooted in hardware and context. A corporate executive would feel as though their peers were sitting across from them in the boardroom because they (as well as their peers) were staring at a series of life-size monitors stationed on the other side of a circular table that had been cut in half. Moreover, the camera trained on each participant would be angled according to their placement on-screen (e.g., someone on the far right screen would sit to the left of the camera pointed at them, rather than head-on). As with its spiritual predecessors, Starline depended on hardware—in this case, a dozen depth sensors and cameras (together producing seven video streams from four viewpoints and three depth maps), four spatial audio speakers, and a fabric-based, multilayered light-field display. These many components, mixed with Google’s suite of computer vision and machine learning AI technologies, enabled participants to be captured and then rendered using volumetric data, rather than flattened 2D video.^([62](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr62)) In effect, viewers were looking at a live 3D model (or a “photorealistic avatar”) of their family member, friend, or colleague, rather than 30 still images played per second. Though Google did not make Starline publicly available, the company’s internal research boasted about Starline’s improvements over traditional video calls. Starline users focused 15% more on those they were speaking to (based on eye-tracking data), displayed significantly greater nonverbal forms of communication (e.g., ~40% more hand gestures, ~25% more head nods, and ~50% more eyebrow movements), and had 30% increases in memory recall when asked to remember details from their conversation or meeting.^([63](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr63)) In testing against the peer-reviewed Zoom Exhaustion & Fatigue Scale, Google found Starline users had 31% lower fatigue compared to those on traditional 2D calls, and exhibited 12% faster response times when completing cognitive tasks after the call.^([64](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr64)) For those skeptical of why the internet needs broad 3D, or who have found Zoom, Microsoft Teams, or Google Meets exhausting or alienating, Starline offers one answer.

An Annotated Look at the 2021 Google Starline without Its Enclosure
