### **Human Culture and Pastimes**

While simulation technologies and devices increased in number and effectiveness, so too did the cultural embrace of 3D environments and socialization. As the world moved on from the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022, supposed “pandemic darlings” such as Zoom, Shopify, and Peloton began to shrink. Although many had predicted their categories were forever “pulled forward” by the global lockdowns of 2020 and 2021, this acceleration was illusory. In 2019, e-commerce constituted roughly 10% of total US retail spend and 15% of addressable retail spend. This share had grown in a fairly linear fashion from approximately 3.5% and 6% since 2009, gaining an average of 0.65 and 0.9 percentage points annually. In 2020, those sums surged to about 17% and 23% (+7 percentage points and +8 percentage points year over year). By 2023, however, e-commerce’s share was well below the level experienced in both 2020 and 2021, with roughly 15.5% and 22% (representing a decline of 1.5 and 1 percentage points over a three-year period). Furthermore, e-commerce’s share of retail sales in 2023 was almost exactly where pre-COVID trendlines would have predicted.^([65](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr65)) Digital’s share of ad spend looks similar. *Roblox*, in contrast, continued to see new highs. Every quarter since the pandemic, *Roblox* exhibited year-over-year (if not quarter-over-quarter) increases in users and usage. Moreover, *Roblox* was adding more users and user hours each quarter than ever before.

![Roblox, Matthew Ball](OEBPS/images/pg75.jpg)

Roblox, Matthew Ball

It’s likely that *Roblox* experienced smaller-scale pullbacks as the pandemic eased. Some users probably played less frequently, or for less time, or stopped playing altogether. Yet the platform was benefiting from generational changes, too. Each year, 140 million people globally turn nine, entering the *Roblox* demographic for the first time. This generational shift, which e-commerce began to experience in the 1990s, also helps to explain why *Roblox*, a platform that launched in 2006, took a decade to take off.

Think back to the first two years following the release of the iPad. As the device’s sales grew, it became common to see press reports and viral YouTube videos of infants and young children who would pick up an “analog” magazine or book and try to “swipe” its nonexistent touchscreen. Today, those one-year-olds are thirteen to fourteen. A four-year-old in 2010 is well on her way to adulthood. These media consumers are now spending their own money on content—and some are already creating content themselves. And while these once unintelligible young people now understand why adults found their futile efforts to pinch-to-zoom a piece of paper so comic, older generations are not much closer to understanding how the worldviews and preferences of the young differ from their own. Most adults look at *Roblox* and see an uninteresting and rudimentary “game.” Kids see something much different: a milieu. Just as prior generations grew up talking on the phone for hours after school and loitering in malls, or on text chats and message boards or, later still, social media, younger Gen Zs and all of Gen Alpha look to platforms such as *Roblox* to socialize and make friends. Certainly, *Roblox* benefited from various technological improvements since its release, not the least of which was the launch of consumer-friendly portable computers, but it’s no coincidence that *Roblox*’s core users are the very children who grew up “iPad native” and expect everything they touch to be fully interactive. Fortunately for *Roblox*, this cohort grows by nearly 400,000 people every day.

Although many Metaverse pioneers believe blockchain and cryptocurrency technology have no place in the Metaverse (and potentially no future at all), the growth in these technologies during 2020, 2021, and 2022 reinforced society’s embrace of virtual existence.

In 2021, the combined value of all cryptocurrencies crossed $2.9 trillion,^([\*\*](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-041)) with the Bitcoin blockchain processing a remarkable $4.7 trillion in bitcoin transaction value that year, and Ethereum managing $3.6 trillion in Ether.^([66](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr66)) Though these sums fell short of credit card giants Visa ($10.4 trillion) and MasterCard ($6 trillion), they were more than American Express ($1.2 trillion), and more than the combined payments volume of Stripe, PayPal, Square, and Shopify ($1.3 trillion)—even though nearly all crypto payments are for virtual-only assets, currencies, securities, and tokens, rather than groceries, cars, travel, and so on. In 2022, Bitcoin and Ethereum transfer value declined (−13% and −56% respectively), but average daily transfers were largely flat (−3.3% and +3.7%), with the gap largely due to the declining price of bitcoin and ether throughout the calendar year.^([67](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr67)) In contrast, the US dollar inflated by an average 8% in 2022. Throughout 2021, over $40 billion was spent buying Ethereum-based NFTs alone,^([68](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr68)) only 11% shy of the $50 billion spent on physical art globally,^([69](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr69)) with 2022 sales hitting roughly $25 billion^([70](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr70)) against $68 billion.^([71](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr71)) MetaMask, the most popular crypto wallet, reported that its monthly active users grew from fewer than 500,000 in September 2020 to 10 million a year later, crossing 30 million by March of 2022.^([72](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr72))

Included in these multibillion- and multitrillion-dollar headlines were a number of significant cultural achievements, too. In July of 2021, the state of Wyoming legalized blockchain-based decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) as a corporate entity, having also been the first state to recognize the LLC business structure back in 1977.^([73](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr73)) The following month, several thousand outdoor enthusiasts used a DAO to purchase a 40-acre plot of land near Yellowstone National Park, which the collective promptly turned into a public park funded and operated by its membership.^([74](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr74)) Three months later, a crypto collective named ConstitutionDAO was formed after Sotheby’s announced that one of 13 surviving first editions of the United States Constitution was set for auction and expected to sell for between $15 and $20 million. Though ConstitutionDAO lost to Ken Griffin, the billionaire founder of the multinational hedge fund Citadel, it raised roughly $47 million in cryptocurrency from nearly 20,000 anonymous contributors in less than a week—none of which required a legal contract, lawyer, or even bank account.

### **Artificial Intelligence**

A final area that saw sudden, multifaceted advances at the end of the 2010s and the early 2020s was artificial intelligence, which had been in active development longer than not just the Metaverse but the internet, too.

As early as the 1930s, philosophers and mathematicians began to debate whether a machine that processed logic through shuffling symbols as basic as 1 and 0 could be said to “deduce” or “reason.” In 1948, the University of Manchester unveiled the Manchester Mark 1, one of the first computers capable of storing (and thus recalling) a program, prompting the press to refer to the device as an “electronic brain.” As discussed earlier in this chapter, it was possible to play games such as tic-tac-toe against an AI by 1950, with checkers following in 1951.

In 1955, American computer scientist John McCarthy coined the term “artificial intelligence,” and in 1956, IBM researcher Arthur Samuel created one of the first adaptive computer programs, the Samuel Checkers-Playing Program, which improved its checkers performance by playing against itself. The year 1956 also saw the debut of Logic Theorist, the first automated reasoning program, which was developed by Allen Newell, Herbert A. Simon, and Cliff Shaw and is considered the first “true” AI. To test the device, its creators had Logic Theorist attempt to prove the first 52 theorems of Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell’s *Principia Mathematica*. It successfully proved 38 (or 74%) of them, and even established several new—and shorter—proofs than had been created by any human mathematician at the time.^([75](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr75)) In 1958, McCarthy began development of the LISP programming language, which spent decades as the preferred language in the AI field, and is now the second-oldest high-level programming language still in use.^([††](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-040)[76](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr76)) In 1959, Samuel coined the term “machine learning.”

The first industrial robot, Unimate, was invented in 1950 by George Devol and debuted on a General Motors assembly line in 1961. Five years later, Unimate joined Johnny Carson’s *Tonight Show* to hit a golf ball (which, tragically, lipped out) and pour a beer (done to perfection). In 1966, MIT computer scientist Joseph Weizenbaum unveiled ELIZA, the first publicly demonstrated “chatbot” that understood natural human language and could credibly attempt the Turing Test.^([‡‡](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-039)) Weizenbaum named his program after the ingenue Eliza Doolittle in George Bernard Shaw’s *Pygmalion*, which took its name from the same Greek myth Stanley Weinbaum had referenced in “Pygmalion’s Spectacles.” In Shaw’s play, the working-class Doolittle is successfully trained to pass as a member of high society, after which the phonetician Henry Higgins^([§§](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-038)) deems her a successful experiment.

In 1986, the German professor Ernst Dickmanns unveiled the first autonomous car, a reengineered Mercedes-Benz van called VaMoRs, equipped with cameras, sensors, and a computer capable of real-time computer vision as well as steering, throttling, and braking. By 1987, the Benz’s computer vision was capable of processing enough imagery to drive at 60 miles per hour.^([77](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr77))

In 1996 and 1997, the IBM chess computer Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov across two six-game matches, winning 4–2 and 3½–2½. Deep Blue’s victories came nearly a half century after Turing had tried to create a program that could just play a game of chess but could not find a computer powerful enough to even test Turochamp’s code. The year 1997 also saw the release of British programmer Rollo Carpenter’s Jabberwacky (named after the famous nonsense poem “Jabberwocky” from Lewis Carroll’s *Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There*), which became the first popular internet-based chatbot. The express purpose of Carpenter’s Jabberwacky was to develop artificial intelligence by learning from interactions with humans rather than just applying a predefined ruleset and finite knowledge base. Later that year, Dragon Systems unveiled NaturallySpeaking 1.0, the first consumer product to offer continuous speech recognition, and by the end of the decade, various speech-recognition systems had surpassed the vocabulary of the average American.

In 2001, ActiveBuddy, Inc., launched SmarterChild, the first natural language chatbot that was integrated into messaging platforms such as AOL Instant Messenger (AIM) and MSN Messenger and given a distinct personality. Within its first year, nine million users added SmarterChild to their friend list (roughly 2% of all internet users at the time), with a quarter of a million engaging with it daily to look up information, play word games, and pass time.^([78](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr78)) Six years after the launch of SmarterChild, Microsoft acquired ActiveBuddy.

By 2011, information-based bots had progressed to the point where IBM’s Watson was able to handily defeat all-time *Jeopardy!* champions Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings in a live competition. That same year, Apple launched its Siri digital assistant across its hundreds of millions of iOS devices, which users could access simply by holding down the home button. Apple had acquired the start-up behind Siri in 2010; its origins could be traced to a DARPA-funded AI project led by the nonprofit Stanford Research Institute. Siri’s speech recognition engine was provided by Nuance Communications, which had acquired Dragon Systems four years after the launch of NaturallySpeaking (Microsoft would go on to buy Nuance in 2021 for nearly $20 billion). Google’s Siri competitor, Google Now, launched in 2012, with Microsoft’s Cortana and Amazon’s hardware-centric Alexa coming in 2014. Google’s self-driving car investments had begun in 2009 and by 2012, its Waymo division had passed the Nevada driver’s test. In 2015, Tesla began to roll out its self-driving capabilities, the same year Elon Musk helped to co-found OpenAI. A year later, Musk announced another start-up, Neuralink, which focuses on implantable brain-computer interfaces.

Sales and usage of digital assistants continued to grow in the second half of the 2010s, with Amazon’s Alexa line selling an estimated 250–300 million units that decade, and iOS and Android users making billions of voice-based queries each year through smartphones. However, these AI rarely provided much intelligence. Instead, they primarily reported the weather or time, put on a song, or answered a trivia question. But during the first years of the 2020s, AI seemed to cross a key threshold—especially in natural language processing.

In 2017, eight computer scientists and researchers who worked at (or who would soon join) Google released a paper, “Attention Is All You Need,” which proposed a new deep learning architecture they called a “transformer model.”^([79](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr79)) According to the *Financial Times*, the paper “kick-started an entirely new era of artificial intelligence: the rise of generative AI.”^([80](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr80)) Within a year, OpenAI had refocused its development on transformers and released its first attempt, a large language model dubbed the “generative pre-trained transformer,” or GPT for short. In 2019, OpenAI released GPT-2, with GPT-3 following a year later, GPT-3.5 debuting in March 2022, and GPT-4 launching publicly a year later.

OpenAI’s models demonstrated substantial improvements with each release. The company’s GPT-3 was first detailed in May 2020, with the enhanced GPT-3.5 submodel unveiled in March 2022 in advance of OpenAI’s public release. A year later, GPT-4 was launched and boasted comprehensive improvement over its predecessor. According to OpenAI, GPT-4 ranked in the 88th percentile in the US Law School Admission Test (LSAT) versus GPT-3.5’s 40th percentile, and 90th percentile in the Uniform Bar Exam versus 10th.^([81](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr81)) In an independent study performed by researchers at Cornell University, on the 2022 Plastic Surgery In-Service Training Exam GPT-4 ranked 99th percentile, up from GPT-3.5’s 3rd percentile placement, and 88th percentile on the 2021 exam, up from 8th.^([82](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr82)) On a custom oncology exam, the Cornell researchers found that GPT-3.5 averaged 53%, human medical physicists averaged 63%, and GPT-4 managed 75%.^([83](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr83))

In the lead-up to GPT-4’s public release, OpenAI released ChatGPT in November of 2022, a chatbot based on its GPT-3.5 model. Within 40 days, the product surpassed 10 million daily active users—the fastest a new consumer application had ever crossed that threshold—and became the 17th-most-visited website in the world, ranking alongside quarter-century-old brands such as Amazon.com and Yahoo, and passing Netflix and Microsoft Office. Although its popularity was partly due to novelty, it also reflected the unprecedented utility of OpenAI’s transformer model, which could not just engage in factual and detailed conversations but also carry out complex requests intended to aid actual work creation rather than just information retrieval. For example, a user might ask a GPT model to “write a 1,500-word essay outlining the top five causes of World War I” (as well as variations on that question), or detail the 17 precedential cases relevant to a legal dispute around agricultural water rights in California and why. ChatGPT’s sister product DALL-E, which had released a few months earlier, also let users instantly translate their thoughts into a vivid high-resolution image that could imitate specified styles (e.g., pointillist, impressionist, charcoal) and be automatically updated on command (e.g., change the black roof to brown, remove the clouds, cut the lawn). In April 2022, OpenAI released DALL-E 2, which substantially enhanced the realism and accuracy of its generative imagery, with DALL-E 3 following in September 2023 and available inside the ChatGPT application. OpenAI’s Codex, which rolled out during 2021 and 2022, enabled users to ask for the code required to carry out specified tasks (e.g., make a *Pong* game, copy the headline article text from NewYorkTimes.com every hour and paste it into a spreadsheet) in the specified language (C#, JavaScript, PHP, Ruby, SQL). In February 2024, OpenAI unveiled Sora, an adaptation of its DALL-E image technology but which generated high-definition videos based on a user’s text prompts. Many technologists believe Sora has been trained primarily on Unreal Engine–based simulations, with Sora receiving considerable praise for its ability to simulate complex particle interactions such as waves crashing through a building, snow bouncing off puppies as they wrestled, and light bouncing between windows and puddles in a nighttime street in Tokyo.^([84](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr84))

![OpenAI](OEBPS/images/pg82.jpg)

OpenAI

Remarkably, OpenAI was not alone in its advances. Many considered the text-to-image capabilities of Midjourney, a ten-person start-up founded in 2021, superior to those of OpenAI’s DALL-E. Several other start-ups, such as Cohere (co-founded in 2019 by Aidan Gomez, one of the eight authors of the “Attention Is All You Need” paper) and Anthropic (founded in 2021 by OpenAI’s former vice president of research), were also gaining on OpenAI’s GPT models. Facebook’s GPT competitor, meanwhile, LLaMa (Large Language Model Meta AI), was another powerful and potentially more efficient model. And unlike the models of OpenAI, Facebook opted to open-source LLaMa 2 in 2023 and make it available free of charge—even for commercial usage—thereby democratizing access to powerful AI tools. Not long after, Nvidia publicly launched its suite of generative AI solutions and integrations that could create 3D objects and even the foundations of entire 3D worlds, rather than just memos and 2D images. In December 2023, artificial intelligence start-up Runway announced it was adding “general world models” to its audio-visual offering.^([¶¶](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-037)) “A world model is an AI system that builds an internal representation of an environment, and uses it to simulate future events within that environment,” Runway’s co-founder and CTO Anastasis Germanidis wrote. “Research in world models has so far been focused on very limited and controlled settings, either in toy simulated worlds (like those of video games) or narrow contexts (such as developing world models for driving). The aim of general world models will be to represent and simulate a wide range of situations and interactions, like those encountered in the real world.”^([85](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr85))

Alongside the leaps in transformer-based AI were equally impressive, if less heralded, achievements in neural networks. One example is neural radiance fields (NeRFs), which were originally developed at Google in 2019 and 2020. NeRFs use neural computing networks to produce large-scale, realistic immersive models out of a few dozen 2D photos, with the network filling in the many unseen angles and elements, such as the underside of a wood table or a partly obscured stove. In 2023, Google announced its NeRF system would be used to supplement its Google Maps and Street View solutions with full immersive models of major cities, and the interiors of popular destinations such as particular restaurants or museums, as well as the ability to “time slide” through different weather and traffic conditions in order to aid trip planning.

As is reviewed in detail throughout [Chapter 12](#chapter12.xhtml), AI is a critical aspect of the Metaverse and serves several functions. From a philosophical perspective, it reflects and accelerates the multidecade trend toward synthetically aided existence. It is also required to overcome many of the physics-related challenges to building the Metaverse. In May 2023, for example, Google announced that advances in AI had enabled it to shrink its two-year-old Starline device from the size of an enclosed restaurant booth to that of a midsize TV sitting atop a minifridge, while also shifting from a dozen high-end cameras and sensors to only a “few standard” ones.^([86](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr86)) As a result, Google promised, the device would be both easier and cheaper to deploy but would still maintain its performance benefits versus traditional 2D displays. In other instances, improvements in AI will enable computer processors to “beat” the speed of light and better contend with unreliable and low-capacity networks (detailed in [Chapters 5](#chapter5.xhtml) and [6](#chapter6.xhtml)) by predicting what transmitted data will tell it to do before it arrives.

AI will also enable there to be more and better virtual worlds across the Metaverse. In 2022, *Roblox*’s roughly 275 million average monthly users created nearly 5.5 million worlds, though nearly all fall short of what users imagined. *Roblox* co-founder and CEO David Baszucki believes generative AI will enable users to type or speak entire worlds into existence by 2028.^([87](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr87)) And difficult though the creation of purely fictional worlds is today, it’s even more difficult to translate the ever-changing “real world” into virtual assets. With solutions such as NeRF and photogrammetry, it may soon be possible to produce an “Earth 2.0” that covers nearly every square meter seen by humankind.

Just as AI can help generate and operate virtual worlds, it will also help interoperate between them—enabling otherwise incompatible file formats, coding conventions, and systems to seamlessly interconnect with one another without needing human developers to conform to a single standard or produce endless permutations of every world, asset, or data set they built.

Another related role for AI is in populating virtual worlds. Transformer models from companies such as OpenAI and Facebook are now being used to create virtual agents, characters, and entire communities with detailed personalities that grow with their experiences and can serve as friends, colleagues, or mentors. Lastly, humanity will rely on AI systems to operate large-scale digital twins and simulations, as they can process more information and make more decisions than any human could, and guide users through them.

### **Why the Metaverse Matters**

When Ray Bradbury, Isaac Asimov, and Philip K. Dick began to build upon the ideas of Stanley Weinbaum and Vannevar Bush, virtual worlds were limited to single-purpose computers, played by single users, rendered in barely changing 2D monochrome, and were accessed by no more than a dozen scientists and researchers a year. Today, there are vast cloud-based networks that span tens of billions of dynamic virtual worlds that reach more than half a billion people on a regular basis and operate multibillion-dollar economies. And in the decades to come, these worlds will continue to grow in realism, diversity, functionality, economic value, and cultural influence. Meanwhile, the technologies behind these worlds will improve in capability, expand in deployment, and more deeply integrate into the physical. Precisely when “the Metaverse” arrives is a philosophical question; that it’s coming faster than ever can be said with certainty.

Another certainty is the many wars for supremacy in and over this new computing era. They will be fought between tech giants and insurgent start-ups via hardware, technical standards, and tools, as well as content, digital wallets, and virtual identities. The wars will be motivated by more than just revenue potential or the need to survive the “pivot to Metaverse.”

In 2016, a year before his company’s release of *Fortnite* and long before the term “Metaverse” entered public consciousness, Epic’s Tim Sweeney told reporters: “This Metaverse is going to be far more pervasive and powerful than anything else. If one central company gains control of this, they will become more powerful than any government and be a god on Earth.”^([88](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr88)) It is easy to find such a statement hyperbolic.^([##](#chapter3.xhtml#footnote-036)) The history of the internet, however, suggests that it may not be.

The foundation of today’s internet was built over several decades and through a variety of consortiums and informal working groups composed of government research labs, universities, and independent technologists and institutions. These mostly not-for-profit collectives typically focused on establishing open standards that would help them share information from one server to another, and in doing so make it easier to collaborate on future technologies, projects, and ideas. The internet’s decentralized design also reflected the philosophies of individuals such as Vannevar Bush, who hoped to exchange rather than control data, and the necessities of the era during which it was built, the Cold War, which prompted the adoption of transmission protocols and technologies that could operate even if substantial portions of the network were destroyed or commandeered.^([89](#notes_split_003.xhtml#ch3fr89))

The benefits of this approach were far-ranging. For example, anyone with an internet connection could build a website in minutes and at no cost using pure HTML, and even faster using a platform like GeoCities. A single version of the site could be accessed by every device, browser, and user connected to the internet. In addition, no user or developer needed to be disintermediated—they could produce content for, and speak to, anyone they wanted. The use of common standards also meant that it was easier and cheaper to hire and work with outside vendors, integrate third-party software and apps, and repurpose code. The fact that so many of these standards were free and open-source meant that individual innovations often benefited the entire ecosystem, while placing competitive pressures on paid, proprietary standards, and helping to check the rent-seeking tendencies of platforms sitting between the web and its users (e.g., device manufacturers, operating systems, browsers, and internet service providers).

Importantly, none of this prevented businesses from making a profit on the internet, deploying a paywall, or building proprietary technology. Rather, the “openness” of the internet enabled more companies to be built, in more areas, reaching more users, and achieving greater profits, while also preventing pre-internet giants (and, crucially, telecom companies) from controlling it. Openness is also why the internet is largely considered to have democratized information, and why the majority of the most valuable public companies in the world today were founded (or were reborn) in the internet era.

It’s not difficult to imagine how different the internet would be if it had been created by multinational media conglomerates to sell widgets, serve ads, harvest user data for profits, or control users’ end-to-end experience (something AT&T and AOL both tried but failed to pull off). Downloading a JPG could cost money, and a PNG could cost 50% more. Video calls might have been possible only through a broadband operator’s own app or portal—and only to those who also had that same broadband provider (imagine something like, “Welcome to your Xfinity Browser™, click here for Xfinitybook™ or XfinityCalls™ powered by Zoom™; Sorry, ‘Grandma’ is not in our network, but for $2, you can still call her …”). Imagine if it took a year or a thousand dollars to make a website. Or if websites worked only in Internet Explorer or Chrome—and users had to pay a given browser an annual fee for the privilege of using it. Or maybe the user would have to pay their broadband provider an extra fee to read certain programming languages or use a given web technology (“This website requires Xfinity Premium with 3D”). When the United States sued Microsoft in 1998 for alleged antitrust violations, it centered its case on Microsoft’s decision to bundle Internet Explorer, the company’s proprietary web browser, with the Windows operating system. Yet if a corporation had created the internet, is it conceivable that it would have even allowed a competing browser? If so, would it have allowed users to do whatever they wanted on these browsers, or access (and modify) whichever sites they chose?

A “corporate internet” is the current expectation for the Metaverse. The internet’s nonprofit nature and early history stem from the fact that government research labs and universities were effectively the only institutions with the computational talent, resources, and ambitions to build a “network of networks,” and few in the for-profit sector understood its commercial potential. None of this is true when it comes to the Metaverse. Instead, it is being pioneered and built by private businesses, for the explicit purpose of commerce, data collection, advertising, and the sale of virtual products.

What’s more, the Metaverse is emerging at a time when the largest vertical and horizontal tech platforms have already established enormous influence over people’s lives as well as the technologies and business models of the modern economy. Their power is bolstered by the profound feedback loops of the digital era. Metcalfe’s Law, for example, states that the value of a communication network is proportional to the square of the number of its users, a relationship that helps to keep large social networks and services growing and presents a challenge to upstart competitors. Any business based on artificial intelligence or machine learning benefits from similar advantages as its data sets grow. The primary business models of the internet—advertising and software sales—are also scale-driven, as the companies that sell another ad slot or app encounter almost no incremental cost from doing so, and both advertisers and developers focus primarily on where consumers already are, rather than where they might be.

But to secure their user and developer bases while also expanding into new areas and blocking potential competitors, the tech giants have spent the past decade closing their ecosystems. They’ve done this by forcibly bundling together their many services, preventing users and developers from easily exporting their own data, shutting down various partner programs, and stymying (if not outright blocking) for-profit and even open standards which might threaten their hegemony. These maneuvers, mixed with the feedback loops that come from having comparatively more users, data, revenue, devices, and so on, have effectively closed much of the internet. Today, a developer must essentially receive permission and provide payment. Users have little ownership of their online identity, data, or entitlements.

It is here that fears of a Metaverse dystopia seem fair, rather than alarmist. The very idea of the Metaverse means an ever-growing share of people’s lives, labor, leisure, time, wealth, happiness, and relationships will be spent inside virtual worlds, rather than just extended or aided through digital devices and software. It will be a parallel plane of existence for millions, if not billions, of people, that sits atop the digital and physical economies, and unites both. As a result, the companies that control these virtual worlds and their virtual atoms will likely be more dominant than those who lead in today’s digital economy.

The Metaverse will also render more acute many of the hard problems of digital existence today, such as data rights, data security, misinformation and radicalization, platform power and regulation, abuse, and user happiness. The philosophies, cultures, and priorities of the companies that lead in the Metaverse era, therefore, will help determine whether the future is better or worse than the current moment, rather than just more virtual or remunerative.

As the world’s largest corporations and most ambitious start-ups pursue the Metaverse, it’s essential that we—users, developers, consumers, and voters—understand that we have agency over our future and the ability to reset the status quo. Yes, the Metaverse can seem daunting and scary, but it also offers a chance to bring people closer together, to transform industries that have long resisted disruption and that must evolve, and to build a more equal global economy. Everything depends on how it’s built.
