# [Part II BUILDING  
THE METAVERSE](#contents.xhtml#pt_2)

## [Chapter 4 A GUIDE TO THE “FULL-SPEC” METAVERSE](#contents.xhtml#ch_4)

Part i of this book is dedicated to the history of the Metaverse, as well as its current state. [Part II](#part2.xhtml) focuses on its future. These chapters explore the various technologies, solutions, and agreements that will be needed to build the Metaverse—and the individuals and companies, philosophies and hypotheses, and complexities and histories that are behind each one.

With the above in mind, it’s helpful to move beyond the high-level definition of the Metaverse provided in [Part I](#part1.xhtml) and instead provide a description of a “fully realized” Metaverse. The Metaverse is …

“A massively scaled and interoperable network of real-time-rendered immersive virtual worlds that can be experienced synchronously and persistently by an effectively unlimited number of users with an individual sense of presence, and with continuity of data, such as identity, history, entitlements, objects, communications, and payments.”

The rest of the chapter explains this description in detail.

### **“Virtual Worlds”**

The Metaverse is made up of virtual worlds. The term “virtual worlds” refers to any computer-generated simulated environment. A virtual world can be presented in 2D (e.g., *Pac-Man*) or 3D (*Fortnite*), be purely virtual (*Super Mario*) or layered on top of the “real world” via augmented reality (*Pokémon Go*), or even be text-based (as in the case of a MUD). Some argue a virtual world need not be graphically rendered at all and instead can be limited to code (think of Neo viewing the Matrix in *The Matrix*). Stylistically, a virtual world can reproduce the “real world” exactly (this is typically called a “digital twin,” “virtual twin,” or “3D twin”) or represent a fictionalized version of it (e.g., the fantastical, quarter-scale Manhattan of PlayStation’s 2018 game *Marvel’s Spider-Man*), or represent an altogether fictional reality in which the impossible is commonplace (*Fortnite*). The graphics of this world may be “photoreal,” cartoonish, or stylized to imitate the works of Vincent van Gogh, Picasso, or any other artist, including one’s infant daughter.

The purpose of a virtual world can be “game-like,” which is to say there is an objective such as winning, killing, scoring, defeating, or solving, or the purpose can be “nongame-like” with objectives such as educational or vocational training, commerce, socializing, meditation, fitness, or operating physical spaces using a digital twin. In some cases, a virtual world has no individual users (as in the case of a Pixar film or when virtually simulating a closed ecosphere in a biology class), a single user (*The Legend of Zelda*), or many concurrent ones (*Call of Duty*).

The devices used to affect a virtual world vary: a keyboard controller, or motion sensor, network of cameras, voice, and more. The virtual world may run only on specialized hardware (e.g., a high-end supercomputer), a subset of broadly available computing platforms (e.g., PlayStation, but not Xbox), or across most possible endpoints (which likely involve large variations in the user’s experience by device).

Operationally, a virtual world may have a predefined run-time, after which it is fully reset (a level of *Super Mario*) or run in perpetuity (*EVE Online*), or it may operate somewhere in the middle, with only part of its world reset after a game or event (*World of Warcraft*). As with the real world, governance models vary widely. Most virtual worlds are centrally controlled by the person or group that developed and operates the world, which means they have unilateral control over its economy, policies, and users. In other instances, users self-govern through various forms of democracy. Some blockchain-based games aspire to operate as close to autonomously as possible after launch.

All virtual worlds face constraints. The most obvious is the difficulty and cost of development, operation, and updates. Any reduction to these barriers results in more worlds, with greater diversity, and more potential applications, which leads to a larger, more valuable, and more used Metaverse. Another constraint, which underpins much of this chapter, is the availability of computing resources (local or in the cloud). Naturally, an increase in these resources affects the virtual world’s cost structure, but it also determines the sophistication of its underlying simulation. In a simplified sense, one can think of a virtual world as having a maximum number of available “operations per second.” These operations can be used on graphical detail (i.e., shifting from low-fidelity graphics to photorealism), physics (e.g., simulating precise light reflections or damage to a car), environmental complexity (increasing the number of cars in an intersection from two to ten), the number of simultaneous users (which leads to more interactions produced per second), increasing the world’s level of persistence (discussed later in this chapter), computer vision (to understand the “real world” or a user’s hands), and so on. The “full-spec” Metaverse will simulate and include anything that an individual user or business might want to simulate and in whatever quality or fidelity is desired.

### **Immersive (or 3D or Spatial)**

The Metaverse is an immersive medium that enables users to do more than just surf “on” a page or look at an app. Instead, they will exist within it. As discussed in [Chapter 2](#chapter2.xhtml), these experiences do not require the user to adopt new form factors, such as a headset, but such devices would probably be an aid to adoption, usage, and functionality. Billions may be adept at using keyboards and controllers to navigate 3D spaces, but billions of others find those inputs impossible to use—and these inputs cannot match the precision, ease of use, or flexibility of a human hand or eye. Accordingly, companies such as Apple and Facebook are developing devices as wide-ranging as motion-tracking cameras and tracking rings, even sensors that can detect electrical signals traveling across skeletal muscles, and neural implants to read brain activity. Regardless, today’s devices, from smartphones to smartwatches, will also need additional and better sensors. The world will too. While digital twins and city-scale simulations can transform the world into the greatest software development platform in the world, fleets of Internet of Things (IoT) sensors and data pipelines will be required to both track the world in real time and translate it into 3D reproductions.

New development suites (such as the aforementioned iOS ARKit), software languages, and standards (discussed later in this chapter) will also be needed. Google’s Starline device is a great illustration of the utility of 3D, but it requires novel software and AI not just to create a realistic live avatar but also to share it. Starline creates many gigabits of data per second, several times greater than the average US household can download per second. Accordingly, Google developed a new compression algorithm that rapidly shrinks this data by more than 100 times and is still compatible with the common WebRTC standard. And to use with 3D interfaces, developers will need to create new interaction models and design principles, just as Apple pioneered user experience (UX) elements such as “pinch-to-zoom” and “swipe-to-unlock.”

Not all use cases or applications will benefit from spatial, immersive, or 3D implementations, nor will those that do benefit do so in all cases. Yet many examples are already clear, including Google’s Starline, VR training for dangerous work environments, and AR-assisted surgery or repairs. It’s also evident that among those native to devices such as the iPad or video game consoles, 3D/AR socializing is often preferred to 2D alternatives whether based on text, image, or video. But there is particular hope that a 3D internet will enhance categories that have historically resisted digital disruption.

For decades, theorists have expected education to be transformed by the internet—that Harvard University would offer online-only degrees that rivaled its in-person equivalents in both imprimatur and test scores, yet was available at a fraction of the cost and to far more students. Harvard has abstained from such a model in part due to brand- and legacy-related concerns, but no effective alternative has emerged. Indeed, the COVID-19 pandemic revealed the value of the classroom and peers-based learning just as it demonstrated the inadequacies of learning through large video calls, on-demand videos, multiple choice, and even interactive e-books. Between 2020 and 2023, the National Center for Education Statistics reported that average reading and math scores for American children fell 5 points in their standardized testing rubric (220 to 215), the largest drop since 1990, while math scores fell by 7, the first-ever-reported drop.^([1](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr1)) Among 13-year-olds, scores fell by 4 (260 to 256), more than double the largest-ever-recorded drop, and 9 (280 to 271), the second-ever-recorded drop and three times larger than the first.^([2](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr2))

The suddenness of the shift to remote education is partly to blame, but for all the power of computers and the internet, the educational sector has seen no measurable productivity improvements since the internet and PCs. Students are not taught in less time, nor are more students taught effectively per instructor. Student outcomes have not seen substantial improvements, either. In comparison to 1999, the average reading score for 9-year-olds had grown only from 212 to 220 and math grew from 232 to 241; scores for 13-year-olds saw even smaller gains, with reading increasing from 259 to 260 and math from 276 to 280.^([\*](#chapter4.xhtml#footnote-035)) Since 2012, ACT scores have routinely hit two-or-three-decade lows.^([3](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr3)) In fact, no other sector has seen greater increases in costs, with college tuition and fees up more than 825%,^([4](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr4)) while the second-closest sector, medical care and services, is up 450%,^([5](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr5)) versus 210% for the Consumer Price Index overall.^([6](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr6)) Worse still, there have been few improvements in education equality or access.

 ![National Center for Education Statistics](OEBPS/images/pg98.jpg)

National Center for Education Statistics

At-home or at-distance education will never fully substitute for in-person experience, or for the effects of geography or income on learning. But the gap is likely to close for the same reasons VR training is so impactful in industries such as automotive repairs and oil and gas rigging: humans learn best by doing and through physical instruction. Immersive simulations enable virtual classrooms to be accessed worldwide, while also affording participants the ability to be “present” in these classrooms and to make eye contact with a teacher or peer. Furthermore, the virtual classroom can be stocked with infinite and no-cost Bunsen burners to light and frogs to dissect. The classroom need not exist at all, either. Instead, students could learn on the surface of the moon or the right ventricle of the heart. Everything once imagined in *The Magic School Bus* becomes virtually real—and it will be staffed by live versions of Miss Frizzle, motion-captured recordings of other teachers and instructors, and a suite of personalized AI assistants.

To be clear, education-related use cases are not a necessary part of any Metaverse description (nor are any comparable examples in fields such as healthcare, engineering, and so on). But for the Metaverse to be “the Metaverse,” it needs more than just technological enablers to be in place. Developers must also produce new experiences out of whole cloth for it which are subsequently adopted by society.

### **Real-Time Rendered**

For a virtual world to be visible, it must be “rendered.” Rendering is the process of generating a visible 2D or 3D object using a computer program. The goal of this program is to “solve” an equation made up of many different inputs, data, and rules to determine what should be rendered and when, and by using various computing resources, such as a graphics processing unit (GPU) and central processing unit (CPU). As is the case with any math problem, an increase in the resources available to solve it (in this case, time, the number of CPUs and GPUs, and the power of these CPUs and GPUs) means that more complex equations can be tackled, and more detail provided in the solution.

Take the 2013 Pixar film *Monsters University*, which not only boasted beautiful graphics and vivid worlds but was designed to look great even on an IMAX screen more than 125 feet tall and 70 feet wide. Even when using a top-of-the-line industrial-grade computing processor, Pixar concluded that the film’s 120,000-plus frames would require an average of 29 hours each to be rendered. In total, the film would therefore require two years to be rendered, assuming no single rendering was redone, let alone any scene changed. In response to this conclusion, Pixar built a data center of 2,000 conjoined industrial-grade computers with a combined 24,000 cores that, when fully assigned, could render a frame in roughly five seconds.^([7](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr7)) Most companies, of course, can’t afford such a powerful supercomputer and therefore spend more time waiting. Many architectural and design firms need to wait overnight to render a highly detailed model. An alternative approach is to render a less complex or detailed image, object, or scene.

Prioritizing visual fidelity is sensible if one is creating a Hollywood blockbuster that will be shown on the silver screen, or selling a multimillion-dollar building renovation. However, experiences set in virtual worlds require real-time rendering. Without real-time rendering, the size and visuals of virtual worlds would be severely constrained, as would the number of participating users and the options available to each user. Why? Because experiencing an immersive environment through pre-rendered images requires every possible sequence to have been pre-made—just as a choose-your-own-adventure novel can offer only a handful of choices, rather than infinite ones. In other words, the cost of greater visuals is less functionality and agency.

Compare, for example, navigating the Roman Colosseum in a video game versus doing the same on Google Street View. Both provide 360-degree views and multiple dimensions of movement (look up or down, move left or right, backward or forward), but the former severely limits one’s choices—and if a user decides to look closely at a given stone, all they can do is zoom in on an image not designed for such scrutiny. It will be blurry, and the view angle is fixed.

Although real-time rendering enables a virtual world to be “alive” and to respond to input from a user (or a group of users, for that matter), this requires each visual frame to be rendered in a fraction of a second, rather than several seconds, let alone days. Moreover, more frames per second are needed depending on the screen that’s used and content that’s displayed. Whereas most movies, such as those of Pixar, have only 24 frames per second, most games require at least 30.^([†](#chapter4.xhtml#footnote-034)) Titles that are more dynamic and require more precise input, such as *Call of Duty*, aspire for a minimum of 60 frames per second. For head-mounted displays (e.g. virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality headsets), many experts believe at least 120 and as many as 240 frames per second are needed to avoid nausea, disorientation, and related sensations.^([8](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr8)) According to a study from VRHeaven and compiled by Goldman Sachs, 7 percent of men and 23 percent of women who had tried virtual reality headsets in June 2020 reported that they “Frequently” experienced motion sickness when using these devices, and another 14 percent and 23 percent responded “Sometimes,” and 29 percent and 20 percent said “Rarely.”^([9](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr9)) Only 50 percent of men and 35 percent of women said “Never.”^([10](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr10)) At the time, nearly all VR headsets were limited to 75 fps or fewer. The incidence of nausea stems from many unique attributes of headset-based experiences, such as proximity of the device’s screen to the wearer’s eyes (2–5cm), the overall sense of immersion in the device (which means the user’s sense of balance is not necessarily “anchored” to the real world), and the use of head and body movements as an input (which can result in a disagreement between the brain’s sense of balance or “inner ear” and the experienced viewed on the display).

In totality, non-real-time-rendered films and real-time-rendered virtual worlds face the same resource constraints, but the latter requires far more, at far greater speeds, and at lower cost than the former. Whereas a Pixar film might have roughly 1,440 frames (24 frames per second × 60 seconds), a real-time-rendered world needs 1,800 (+25%) to 14,400 (+900%). It’s okay for Pixar’s frames to take seconds, minutes, or even days to render, but a real-time-rendered world’s frames cannot be rendered in advance and must therefore be produced between 99.5% and 99.999% faster. Pixar gets to use a world-class supercomputer that costs tens of millions to construct, but to reach the entire smartphone population, a virtual world needs to run adequately on a $100 Android device.

A Pixar film, like a video game, looks better as resolutions increase. A 2K display offers twice the detail of a 1K display, making circles sharper and smiles richer whether they are predetermined or interactive. And in both cases, a doubling in resolution doubles the frames required. But while the math is linear, the difficulty is not, given the aforementioned limitations on time, cost, and available resources. Furthermore, head-mounted displays require even greater resolutions than typical displays because the user’s eyes are only an inch or two away; the pixels of a 2K television are imperceptible from seven feet, but enormous when a user’s nose is pressed up to the screen.

### **Interoperable Network**

As with the internet, the term “Metaverse” does not describe any single system or even a group of systems. It instead describes a network of systems—and these systems are interoperable with one another. “Interoperability” refers to the ability for independent, autonomous, and heterogeneous systems to exchange and make use of one another’s data.

Interoperation requires network participants to adopt common technologies, such as the Internet Protocol Suite. These shared technologies are usually steered by nonprofit groups whose recommendations must then be voluntarily adopted by the various network participants. The Internet Protocol Suite is managed by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), a nonprofit with no formal membership or requirements and whose work is funded by its contributors and project sponsors.

Typically, network participants work to establish and/or support additional common standards and working conventions that aid the exchange of data. HTML, for example, is not part of the Internet Protocol Suite and thus does not, strictly speaking, enable the exchange of data. However, the widespread use of HTML ensures that most devices, users, and developers are able to coherently understand, consistently display, and easily use one another’s data. The widespread support of formats such as JPEG and MP3, meanwhile, ensures that most photo and audio files can be used on most websites and applications, irrespective of which website or application created them. Moreover, interchange solutions and frameworks emerged which helped convert between different formats, such as JPEG and PNG. To make the internet easier to use for consumers, rather than just for servers and networks, organizational hierarchies and registries were also established, such as the Domain Name System (which effectively converts an IP address into a text name like www.google.com). HTML is managed by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), a public-interest not-for-profit organization; JPEG by the Joint Photographic Experts Group, a not-for-profit committee in partnership with the United Nations’ International Telecommunication Union; MP3 by the Fraunhofer Society, a for-profit research organization which licenses the MP3 format; and DNS is managed by the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), a not-for-profit multi-stakeholder group which also oversees IP and network addresses.

The healthiest instantiation of the Metaverse is likely one in which as many underlying protocols and standards are managed or guided by birds-of-a-feather groups, rather than by corporations or other private entities. This may take time. The easiest pathway to standards development is for a single party, especially one that already operates at scale, to lead said standards’ development and deployment. The IETF was originally established by the US federal government, which also developed the majority of TCP/IP in the first place, but by 1993, the organization had become fully independent. A related concern is how many protocols and standards are established; the internet could operate on fewer, but would likely benefit from more.

Although Neal Stephenson’s Metaverse was a protocol-based interoperable network, he imagined the Metaverse as having a unified and standardized experiential layer, whereas modern interpretations tend to assume it would not. In *Snow Crash*, the entirety of the Metaverse is contained on a single, geographically organized planet with a literal main street (and related benefits and real estate costs to the locations of various businesses), commutes to and from a user’s home, and programmatic regulations on the dimensions of avatars, buildings, and so on.

Individual platforms and experiences inside the Metaverse may resemble standardized “hub worlds,” such as Tesla’s San Francisco simulations, Apple’s AR mapping solutions, or a future version of *Grand Theft Auto*. But the overall Metaverse is likely to lack such a uniform expression, directory, or gateway—just like the internet. The World Wide Web, for example, is exhaustively organized and indexed, with sites claiming “namespaces” that are reached at assigned server addresses that are located at assigned network addresses, yet there is no “starting point” for the web other than an empty browser, users do not need a website to surf to one, and there is no required pathway between one page and another. If a user wants to go directly to a given page, they simply type in the address or click a hyperlink that takes them there directly. Smartphones offer a unified view of a user’s apps and a directory of all apps, but there’s rarely any experiential link among them, only minimal standardization across them. And while both *Roblox* and *Fortnite* enable users to jump between worlds through portals and doors, most users access various worlds through 2D interfaces that more closely resemble a streaming video service than the Street.

Not only would a planet-based organizational model for the Metaverse be frustrating, but it’s also probably impossible. Many simulations, such as those of Tesla, Apple, and a city’s own digital twin, will cover the same user and real-world location and often interconnect, but will otherwise run in parallel. Fortunately, this model has many technical benefits as well. By splitting users or data across platforms, rather than building a virtual planet with billions of concurrent users and quadrillions of objects, many of the technical challenges discussed throughout this chapter, such as rendering, synchronization, and persistence, are greatly simplified.

### **With Continuity of Data, Such as Identity, History, Entitlements, Objects, Communications, and Payments**

Although establishing an interoperable network requires participants to exchange some data (e.g., identifier, address, location, etc.), it does not specify what data is then exchanged, let alone supported across its vast network. In general, visions of the full-spec Metaverse involve interoperable identities, histories (or records), entitlements (i.e., things a user owns or has the right to access), objects (e.g., virtual goods, avatars, or asset models), communications (just as emails work across all networks, domains, devices, etc.), and payment systems (required for virtual “trade”). Without such a suite, it’s argued there would be no “Metaverse,” just an internet with a growing number of 3D applications. A more 3D-capable internet has value, but it’s less likely to produce a true “parallel plane of existence” or produce an economy that might rival that of the “physical world” (while also underpinning much of it).

Interoperability is also essential to user rights and, in turn, the health of the Metaverse overall. If a user’s virtual entitlements or creations are locked to a given platform, then that platform’s de facto control over the user will grow as time passes and the user’s investment increases. For similar reasons, it will become increasingly difficult for any other platform, new or emergent, to compete with that platform. Interoperability is also needed to ensure that investments (time, money, energy, memories) in the Metaverse endure should a single virtual world or server within it be shut down. In the “real world,” consumers do not contend with these sorts of problems. Many underlying interoperable services and registries are government owned and non-excludable (e.g., passports, national identity numbers, currencies), individuals take physical possession of goods (unlike most digital goods) and these goods don’t disappear if their manufacturer closes, interoperability is physics based (a J.Crew belt works with Gap pants irrespective of any coordination between the two companies or permission from one), intermediaries are not required for most exchange (e.g., USD to Euro, a hat for a T-shirt), and so on.

There are many obstacles to establishing these standards. One is the current state of fragmentation. Almost all the most popular virtual worlds today use their own different rendering engines (many publishers operate several across their titles), with individualized scripting languages, tools, frameworks, and related services. The practical consequences of these engine-by-engine variations can be hard for non-developers to appreciate, but the depth of these differences is demonstrated by how the two most popular engines “disagree” on coordinate axes. In Unity, the *y*\-axis in an X/Y/Z-based 3D model refers to up/down, while Unreal uses the *z*\-axis for up/down and maps the *y*\-axis to left/right. It’s easy for middleware to convert such practices, but the technical variations extend into how code is structured, inputs processed, particles simulated, and so on, rather than just the order of information.

Beyond the underlying logic and rules of these worlds is how the information that runs inside them is structured. There are no “JPEGs,” “MP4s,” “.XLS,” or “PDFs” for 3D objects, let alone environments or player data. As such, parties save their objects, textures, and player data into entirely different file formats and with only the information that they expect to need. Solving this requires not just a format but the philosophy around it. Take the idea of an “interoperable avatar.” It’s relatively easy for developers to agree on the definition of an image and how to present it, and as a static 2D unit of content made up of individually colored pixels, the process of converting one image file type (say, PNG) to another (JPEG) is straightforward. However, 3D avatars are a more complex question. Is an avatar a complete 3D person with an outfit, or is it made up of a body avatar plus an outfit? If the latter, how many articles of clothing are they wearing and what defines a shirt versus a jacket that goes over shirts? Which parts of an avatar can be recolored? Which parts must be recolored together (is a sleeve separated from a shirt)? Is an avatar’s head a complete object, or is it a description of dozens of sub-elements like individual eyes (with their own retinas), eyelashes, noses, freckles, and so on? In addition, users expect an anthropomorphic jellyfish avatar and a box-like android to move in different ways. The same applies to objects. If a tattoo is placed on the avatar’s neck, it should stay fixed to their skin irrespective of any movement they make—but a tie hung around that neck should move with (and also be affected by) the avatar. And it should move differently than a seashell necklace, which should also move differently than a feather necklace. Just sharing the dimensions and visual detail of an avatar is not sufficient. Developers need to understand, and agree on, how they work—then build code to support it.

Other areas are less ontological, but just as tricky. Interoperable economies—that is, virtual currency exchanges, goods trading, and so on—have complex tax implications, as well as regulatory burdens relating to money-transfer licenses, customer identification, securities licenses, capital reserves, and so on. For a virtual object on one platform to interoperate on another, systems are required to manage permissions and policies required to manage related liabilities. Harder still, architectures are required to sort exactly what happens (and doesn’t happen) to the relevant data and how. If a player buys an outfit on Platform A and wants to use it in Platform B, does Platform A send the outfit’s ownership record and files to Platform B, which manages it until it’s needed elsewhere, or does Platform A indefinitely manage the outfit and provide Platform B temporary rights to use it? If so, how does Platform A compensate? If the player sells the outfit to a Platform B user who doesn’t have a Platform A account, which company even processes the transaction? If the user alters the item from within Platform B, or adds an item to it from Platform B, how is the record on Platform A altered? If users have virtual items scattered across multiple titles, how do they ever know what, altogether, they own and where what they own can or cannot be used? Solutions are needed that not only establish and maintain an authoritative record but can transfer it to outside parties and provide authenticated access to that record and allow permitted parties to alter it, too.

Standards development is often considered the toughest hurdle faced by Metaverse builders because it is primarily a human process, not a technical one. Moore’s Law, which observes that the number of transistors on a microchip doubles every two years, charts predictable improvements in computing power and cost, while 6G mobile network specifications are already in early development and will doubtless be widely deployed, and the global internet backbone is constantly being expanded and upgraded.^([11](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr11)) Standards have no set timeline, inevitabilities, or obvious answers. They are agreed upon, not discovered, and therefore rely on debates and concessions, which are shaped by competitive leverage and deployment, produce unintended side effects, and sometimes result in rival standards that worsen fragmentation rather than reverse it.

Take the widely popular GIF format, first introduced in 1987. Although GIFs often compress their source video file to the point that many individual frames are discarded and the remaining frames have lost much of their visual detail, file sizes remain quite large. There are many alternatives to the GIF—from MP4 to APNG (animated PNG) and WebM—which are typically five to ten times lighter and provide far greater video clarity and detail, in addition to other benefits, such as the ability to be streamed. Despite this, GIF remains the more popular and most widely deployed form of moving image file, which makes it tough for any site or application to reject, thereby ensuring it endures. Yet this endurance has led to extra bandwidth use, more time waiting for files to load, and worse experiences overall. Given the intensity of the Metaverse’s computational and networking-related needs, such suboptimizations add up quickly.

On occasion, it’s clear which prospective standard is “best” before any one alternative sees wide adoption. Even so, the companies that steer or own a lesser alternative will typically resist embracing this rival for strategic reasons—and some of those who have already adopted the lesser alternative will continue to use it simply to avoid the burden of making a shift.

As one reviews the past four decades of the internet, it’s easy to imagine better structures or declare better formats. But the internet’s extensive interoperability was fostered by an irreplicable advantage: its foundational protocols, conventions, and formats were set long before it was commercialized. Accordingly, the internet of today did not need for-profit rivals to agree, let alone concede to, a rival’s proposal. And while many for-profit products on the internet are largely closed or use proprietary protocols, such maneuvers required the development of a product with benefits that far exceeded network effects. While many internet businesses opt out of data sharing or use proprietary protocols and services, the cost is a reduction in network effects and thus success largely depends on producing a product worthy of this trade-off. Instant Messaging services have routinely met this burden by offering greater security, functionality, speed, and reliability over SMS, but no closed alternatives to email have been able to do the same (even though companies such as Google and Microsoft might aspire for a world where all such messages ran through their systems). Conversely, today’s virtual worlds were all built without the intent, let alone ability, to interoperate. As such, opting in to such a model requires substantial technical shifts (or concessions) that provide, at least to start, only marginally greater network effects.

### **Massively Scaled**

For the internet to be “the internet,” it’s generally accepted that it must have a seemingly infinite number of websites and applications, and there must be myriad individual developers behind these pages, too. The Metaverse is similar. It must have a massively scaled number of virtual worlds if it is to be “the Metaverse.” Otherwise, it is more like a digital theme park—a destination with a handful of carefully curated attractions and experiences that can never be as diverse as, or contend with, the outside (real) world.

To most advocates, the size of the Metaverse will far exceed the overall size of the internet today—and the physical world, too. In 2021, Tim Sweeney told the *LA Times*, “Just as every company a few decades ago created a webpage, and then at some point every company created a Facebook page, I think we’re approaching the point where every company will have a real-time live 3D presence.… That’s starting to happen now. \[And\] it’s going to be a much bigger thing than these previous generational shifts.”^([12](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr12)) Jensen Huang imagines the Metaverse having countless compounding simulations; the US government might have a national simulation, with cities, building operators, and stores within the United States running their own partly overlapping and partly interconnected simulations. The larger the Metaverse, the more used and useful, but also the more difficult the problems of rendering, synchronization, standardization, persistence, and more.

### **Persistence**

In virtual worlds, “persistence” refers to the permanence of events, activities, or data. Most video games today are only selectively persistent. Throughout a match of *Fortnite*, players build or destroy various structures, set fire to forests, or kill wildlife, and so on, but after the roughly 20-to-25-minute match concludes, all of these changes are effectively deleted by Epic Games. The map once enjoyed and affected by 100 players will never be re-experienced, or even accessible, again. In fact, even within a given match, *Fortnite*’s virtual world is only partially persistent. A bullet mark on an indestructible rock might appear for only 30 seconds before it, too, is deleted, and thus also any evidence that combat had even taken place at that location. Although the world of *World of Warcraft* is “continuous,” in contrast to the match-based model of *Fortnite*, it operates similarly. If a player enters a specific part of the *World of Warcraft* map, defeats their enemies, leaves, and returns, they’ll typically find that those enemies have respawned. An in-game tradesman who sold a player a rare item only a day earlier might offer them a second as though it would be their first. The worlds of *Fortnite* and *World of Warcraft* can have lasting changes only when their developers deploy an update—and the players have little to no control over whether a given choice or event endures indefinitely.

Persistence is partly a creative challenge. The goal of most virtual worlds is entertainment, and most large-scale entertainment products are tightly produced and managed. By limiting persistence, a game’s developer can better predict what might happen and ensure it’s “fun,” as well as plan future updates that will keep the title both fun and fresh. However, persistence is a technical challenge, too. When a tree is cut down in the physical world, there is no concern for whether or not the systems of Mother Earth can handle such an event or remember it, or whether anyone else might be able to see the felled tree at a later date or interact with it. Physics adhere to their own laws, but they never run out of “processing power.” The production, operation, and memory of a virtual world are all confined by what the relevant computers can store, render, compute, and synchronize. Moreover, the effects of persistence compound. In a simple case, a tree being felled means that it is no longer there. But what of its stump? Does it remain? And does the trunk of the tree now lie on the ground? If still visible, do other users see which side it was chopped from, or just that it was generically cut? And does it “biodegrade”? If so, how—generically, or in response to its local environment? How should the tree affect other items which occupy its same space?

These questions of what should persist and how are not philosophical. A programmer (or AI) must make a decision and build the technology to support it. The answer also determines what a user can and cannot do, as well as the computing resources available for other tasks in the simulation, which affects what the world can and cannot do. In games, the answers might seem trivial, but many of the most popular social platforms, such as *Roblox*, thrive in part due to their comparatively high levels of persistence, which effectively add a fourth dimension (time) to play, and enrich the contributions of any additional user. Digital twins, such as those for a city or factory floor, have particularly high persistence and detail requirements (recall that such models might precisely simulate light, heat, sound, etc.). Networked simulations are also limited by the lowest common denominator of persistence across their network—a good reason for every participant to store as much data as possible, but that also means they must process, render, and synchronize it, too.

### **Synchronous**

For the Metaverse and its individual experiences to be shared, every relevant participant, network, and device must be synchronized in real time. This requires the user to maintain a continuous^([‡](#chapter4.xhtml#footnote-033)) (i.e., sustained and uninterrupted) connection to a virtual world’s server (both to and from) and that can deliver vast volumes of data (“high bandwidth”) in near real time (“low latency”).

These may not seem like outlandish requirements. After all, there are a hundred million people streaming high-definition video at any given moment, while much of the global economy ran via live and synchronous videoconference software throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. And broadband providers improve the availability, bandwidth, and latency of their networks each year, with internet outages becoming less common each day. However, the internet works so well today because of the many tricks deployed to cover up moments of low bandwidth, high latency, and dropped connections. Spotify, for example, used to start a track’s progress bar immediately after a user selected the track, leading them to believe it was playing even though it had yet to even load.

Although the playback of a Netflix stream is continuous, the company is sending users distinct batches of data, many of which travel through different network paths from the server to that user. By using excess bandwidth to send the user data before it’s needed—such as minutes 45 and 46 when the user is only on minute 44—Netflix can ensure playback continues in the event the user’s device loses its connection to a local Wi-Fi router or cell tower, or if there’s congestion somewhere along the route between Netflix’s server and the user. Because Netflix receives video files anywhere from months to hours before they’re made available to audiences, it is also able to analyze these titles to determine what information can be discarded in the event a user’s bandwidth suddenly drops. Specifically, Netflix’s machine learning systems will scan each frame to simplify its elements—a background sky might be composed of 500 shades of blue which, though beautiful, could be simplified to 200, 50, or 25 without significantly harming the viewer experience. The streamer’s analytics even do this on a contextual basis—recognizing that scenes of dialogue can tolerate more compression than those of faster-paced action, and that the size and resolution of the viewer’s screen matter too. In addition, Netflix will preload content at local nodes. When a user asks for the newest episode of *Stranger Things*, it might be just a few blocks away and therefore arrives immediately.

These approaches work only because most Netflix content is prerecorded; it’s not possible to “pre-do” anything that has yet to occur. It’s for this reason that live video is substantially less reliable than on-demand streams. And even streaming services that deliver live video have tricks. In most cases, transmissions are delayed by 2 to 30 seconds, which means there’s still the opportunity to pre-send content in case of temporary congestion. Commercial breaks can also be used by both the content provider’s server, or the user, to reset the connection in case the prior one proved unreliable. Most live videos require only a one-way continuous connection—for instance, from CNN’s server to the user. Sometimes there is a two-way connection, as in the case of a Twitch chat, but only a sparse amount of data is being shared (the chat itself) and it’s not of critical importance, as it does not directly affect what’s happening in the video (remember, it probably happened 2 to 30 seconds earlier).

Overall, very few online experiences require high bandwidth, low latency, and continuous connectivity other than real-time-rendered, multiuser virtual worlds. Most experiences just need one or, at most, two of these elements. High-frequency stock traders (and especially high-frequency trading algorithms) want the lowest possible delivery times, as this can be the difference between buying or selling a security at a profit or a loss. However, the orders themselves are straightforward, are data light, and don’t require a server connection to be sustained for seconds, let alone hours.

The major exception is videoconferencing, which involves many people receiving and sending high-resolution video files, all at once, and participating in a shared experience. Yet these experiences, too, can take advantage of software solutions that don’t work for real-time-rendered virtual worlds—and work even when these solutions fall short.

As with all networking activities, the data packets that make up a video call occasionally arrive late due to network congestion or temporary connectivity loss. In the case of videoconferencing, this means that at least one member of the call (if the network error occurred near their device) or many (if it happened near the speaker) might miss a few of the speaker’s words or receive a garbled version of them. This usually doesn’t matter, as humans are adept at deducing the speaker’s overall point (and potentially the exact words they said), but modern videoconferencing software, such as Zoom and Microsoft Teams, now deploys machine learning solutions to help out. If a user loses their connection, the application’s server will send the requisite audio once they regain connectivity, which is then played at roughly 1.5-times speed and with pauses programmatically edited out, so that the user can still hear what they missed and then catch up to being “live.” And because videoconferences have a single active participant and many passive viewers, this disruption typically happens without any other members of the call even knowing. Should the connectivity issues affect the speaker, everyone is affected, but another member of the call can take over or everyone can wait until the speaker reconnects. Everything is fine. If this issue continues, the application will usually stop uploading or downloading video from various members of the call, in order to prioritize what matters most: audio. And in the case of varying latency—that is, members of the call are receiving “live” video and audio a quarter, half, or even full second behind or in front of each other—it’s likely that users are annoyed, but with a little patience, they can figure out how to proceed.

In contrast to a video call, virtual worlds send more complex data, which is needed on a far timelier basis, both to and from a larger set of users, and with greater consequences resulting from network hiccups. Imagine, as an example, a multiplayer shooter game. If Player A lags 75 milliseconds behind Player B, they might shoot in a location where they believe Player B to be, but Player B and the game’s server know Player B has already left. This discrepancy means the virtual world’s server must decide whose experiences are “true” (that is, which should be rendered and persist across all participants) and whose experiences must be rejected. And if the user lags too frequently, or for too long, the server operating the virtual world might kick them out of the match altogether in order to preserve the experience of other players (though as any fan of team sports knows, the expulsion of a player disrupts the rest of the match regardless of why they were ejected).

The Metaverse is not a game, let alone a fast-moving shooter with gameplay that’s decided by as little as a single pixel or hundredth of a second. Yet the Metaverse’s synchronization requirements and obstacles are far greater. Unlike a match of *Call of Duty*, there might be millions of synchronized devices, users, sensors, and equipment, rather than just a few dozen. Users are more likely to be spread around the world, rather than between 10 and 1,000 miles apart, thereby elongating the travel times. There is also more data to synchronize and it’s of greater consequence and more likely to persist as well. Furthermore, human interaction is incredibly sensitive; a smile that happens a bit too late (or not at all) or misaligned gazes can quickly exhaust, alienate, or creep out users.

The Metaverse can’t really function as a parallel plane for human existence if many of those within it experience conflicting (and then invalidated) versions of it. But at present, only three-quarters of American broadband households can reliably participate in high-fidelity real-time-rendered virtual worlds. Fewer than one-quarter of broadband households in the Middle East can, and fewer than one in ten in India.^([13](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr13)) To improve these figures, many solutions are needed. As discussed in [Chapter 2](#chapter2.xhtml), the Internet Protocol Suite does not currently acknowledge, let alone prioritize, real-time transmission across the internet. Another obstacle is the physical internet backbone, which is shaped not to minimize delivery time, but by geographic, environmental, political, and economic realities. Indeed, even the speed of light is limiting.

### **Unlimited Users and Individual Presence**

“Concurrency,” or the number of active users at a given moment, is one of the foundational problems for the Metaverse, and for a fundamental reason: it leads to exponential technical burdens. Take synchronization as an example. It’s obvious that as more users join a simulation, there is more “work” to be done and more potential points of network failure. Yet adding a third user to a two-user simulation does not increase synchronization requirements by 50%, but by over 100%. In the first case, User A’s actions must be synchronized with User B’s, and User B’s inputs with those of User A, but in the latter case, User C must be synced with Users A and B, and each must be synchronized with C. Synchronization points grow from two to six. Adding a fourth user doesn’t increase synchronization work by a third but by more than double, as each of Users A, B, and C must sync with a third user and User D must sync with each of them, too. And as users increase, the number of events/actions to simulate per second tends to increase and their predictability decreases. This reduces computing resources available for logic processing, rendering, and persistence management.

Today, even virtual worlds that have no persistence, span fewer than ten square kilometers in surface area, tightly control user activities, and are operated by some of the most technically capable companies in the world can struggle to sustain more than 50 to 150 users at the same time. What’s more, 150 concurrent users is possible only because of how these titles are creatively designed.

In *Fortnite*, up to 100 players can participate in a richly animated virtual world, and each player controls a detailed avatar that can use more than a dozen different items, perform dozens of dances and maneuvers, and build complex structures tens of stories tall. However, *Fortnite*’s roughly five-square-kilometer map means that only one dozen to two dozen players will encounter one another at once—and by the time players are forced into a smaller portion of the map, most players have been eliminated and turned into data on a scoreboard. During *Fortnite*’s social events, such as its famous 2020 concert with Travis Scott, players converge on a much smaller portion of the map and cannot be eliminated. Accordingly, the title’s standard cap of 100 players per instance was halved, while many items and actions, such as building, were disabled, thereby further reducing the workload.

While Epic Games can rightly say that more than 12.5 million people attended this live concert, these attendees were split across 250,000 separate copies of the event (meaning, they watched 250,000 versions of Scott) that didn’t even start at the same time.

Another good example comes from *World of Warcraft*. To play, users must first pick a “realm”—a discrete server that manages a complete copy of the roughly 1,500-square-kilometer virtual world, and from which they cannot see or interact with any other. In this sense, it may be more accurate to call the game “Worlds” of Warcraft. Users can move between realms, thereby philosophically uniting these many worlds into a single “massively multiplayer online game,” but each realm is capped at several hundred participants, and if there are too many users in a specific area, the game creates several distinct and temporary copies of this area, while splitting groups of users among them.

The best example, though, is CCP Games’ *EVE Online*, a technical marvel that debuted months before *Second Life* or MySpace. Save for occasional downtime for maintenance or updates, *EVE Online* has run continually since its debut on May 6, 2003, and its virtual world has never reset. This virtual world is also enormous, spanning nearly 8,000 star systems and nearly 70,000 planets. And unlike *Fortnite* or *World of Warcraft*, all of its users are in the same game and at the same time, with no distinct matches or realms.

The scale of *EVE Online* is possible due to its innovative systems architecture, as well as its brilliantly flexible creative design. The virtual world of *EVE Online* is essentially just empty three-dimensional space with wallpaper backgrounds that look like a galaxy. Users cannot truly visit a planet and activities such as mining are more akin to setting up a Gmail account than constructing a virtual rig. As such, the persistence of *EVE Online* primarily concerns a relatively modest set of “entitlements” (an industry term), such as a player’s ships and resources. The result is less computational work for CCP Games’ servers, and for its users’ devices, which need not render a virtual world that is constantly changing form, just the few objects changing inside of it.

Furthermore, very little happens in *EVE Online* on a daily, quarterly, or even yearly basis. This is because the goal in *EVE Online*, to the extent one exists, is for various factions of players to conquer planets, systems, and galaxies. This is achieved primarily through the establishment of corporations, formation of alliances, and strategic positioning of fleets. Indeed, much of *EVE Online* actually takes place in the “real world,” via third-party messaging applications and emails, and not even on CCP’s servers. Users have spent years planning attacks, going undercover with enemy guilds in order to later betray them, and creating enormous personal networks that trade resources and construct new ships. While large-scale battles do happen, they’re remarkably rare—and involve the destruction of assets in the virtual world (e.g., ships) rather than of the virtual world itself. The former is far easier for a processor to manage than the latter because it is about removing objects in the world, not altering the world. The nature of space-based combat also means that action is limited in variety and relatively simple in mechanics. Ordering a ship to mine resources from a planet, or send a succession of blasts from and to a fixed position, is far less complex than a pair of individually animated avatars dancing, jumping, and shooting each other.

Because *EVE Online* is set in the vastness of space, most users are far away from one another—enabling CCP Games’ servers to effectively treat them as being in separate virtual worlds until necessary, just like *Warcraft*. And while players do sometimes want to converge on the same location—such as a battle site—the mechanics of *EVE Online* spread out this behavior and dissuade it, too. Depending on the ship and intended travel distance, it can take tens of seconds to several minutes for a given ship to warp to another system—and getting to its final destination might require several systems warps. The time involved in such flights has a direct and indirect benefit for CCP Games. First, it reduces the risk of too many ships arriving at any given moment and instead distributes these arrivals over a few minutes or more. Second, it discourages users from relocating a large number of their ships—or moving in the first place—as the user might not be able to return fast enough should an attack occur after they leave. “Warps” also deplete a ship’s capacitor, thereby producing a resource-related cost to relocation. To aid instances in which there are too many user activities (e.g., ship relocations) or instructions (e.g., to continue to fire on an opponent’s ship), *EVE Online*’s engine will deploy “time-dilation,” slowing the game’s passage of time from one in-game second being equivalent to one real-world second to as little as one-to-ten, which enables the game’s server to catch up and properly synchronize all inputs and outputs. While *EVE*’s time-dilation math is fictional, the concept broadly reflects the theory that spacetime dilates in response to the density of heavy and/or high-velocity objects.

*EVE*’s scale, reliance on real-world decisions, and focus on infrastructure, inventories, and locations, rather than virtual outfits or gunfights, makes it a better representation of what the “real world” Metaverse is likely to be like than games such as *Fortnite* or *Roblox*—and easier to operate than these titles, too. Even so, *EVE Online* inevitably encounters problems. At one point in the 2000s, a group of players realized that a specific star system, Yulai, sat near many high-traffic planets inside a major star cluster, making it an enticing spot to establish a new trading hub.^([14](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr14)) They were right. Not long after setting up shop, many buyers began to flock to the area, which attracted additional sellers, then more buyers, and so on. Ultimately, the number of transactions that were occurring inside this hub caused the CCP Games’ servers to start to buckle, leading the publisher to alter the *EVE Online* universe so that the destination would be less convenient to visit.

The lessons from “the Yulai Problem” helped CCP Games design, expand, and overhaul its maps in the years that followed. But in the real world, trade hubs can’t be moved, nor can travel distances be altered. And no matter how the universe of *EVE Online* is distributed, CCP cannot prevent another inevitable computing challenge: the sudden outbreak of battles so strategically important that thousands of users suddenly converge to save their faction or defeat another. In January 2021, the largest battle in *EVE*’s history occurred. It was more than twice the size of the prior record and the culmination of a nearly seven-month escalation between the Imperium Faction and a coalition of enemies called PAPI. Or at least, it should have been. The only real losers were CCP Games’ servers, which could not keep up with 12,000 players appearing in a single system, and any of those players who were hoping for a decisive victory.^([15](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr15)) Roughly half of the players were unable to ever enter the system, while many of those who did were placed in a sort of purgatory—if they logged in to the game, they’d likely be destroyed before having a chance to enter any coherent commands, while leaving meant that their server spot might be taken up by an enemy that would destroy their allies. There was an eventual winner—Imperium—but this was mostly by default, as the defender naturally wins in a battle that never actually takes place.

For the Metaverse to serve as a platform for human socializing, as well as a computing layer for the real world, it must be able to support large numbers of users and IoT devices without compromising essential technical functions. Furthermore, participants must be individually represented within the Metaverse’s many simulations and able to affect it, too. If these requirements were rendered merely optional, the Metaverse would be technically easier—there would be fewer users to synchronize, fewer simultaneous events and inputs to process, and a reduced need for real-time bandwidth and delivery, and users would be able to share a rendered image instead of needing to generate their own custom view. However, such a limitation would make the Metaverse just a virtual diorama or a larger-scale version of the reality series *Big Brother*.

### **Getting to the Full-Spec Metaverse**

In “Pygmalion’s Spectacles,” Professor Ludwig’s sales pitch invokes the teachings of George Berkeley, an 18th-century subjective idealist who is best known for the saying “To be is to be perceived.” Today, Berkeley’s ideas are more commonly expressed through a thought experiment: “If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound?” The question is commonly attributed to the philosopher but is at best a liberal reinterpretation of his writings. Regardless, Berkeley’s arguments and thought exercises have endured in pop culture for centuries because they are fun and hinge on important and ever-evolving technicalities and concepts.

According to an immaterialist such as Berkeley, the tree—standing, falling, or fallen—exists if someone (or God) perceives it. Others claim that what’s meant by “sound” is just vibrations that propagate through matter. As these vibrations exist irrespective of an observer, the tree does, in fact, make a sound whether or not someone is around to hear it. Another perspective alleges that “sound,” specifically, is a sensation experienced by a brain when these vibrations interact with nerve endings. If there are no nerves to interact with vibrating particles, there can be no sound.

One hundred four years after Berkeley’s death, the Frenchman Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville devised the phonautograph, the first device capable of recording sound waves as they propagated through a medium such as air or wood. From this point on, one could argue that many sounds were now heard by artificial observers, making the distinction between vibrations and sound sensations irrelevant. Nevertheless, 21st-century quantum mechanics largely agrees that without an observer, existence is at best a conjecture that cannot be proved or disproved—thus all that can be said is that the tree might exist—though Albert Einstein, who was instrumental in founding the field of quantum mechanics, took issue with this view.

Although 21st-century examples of *Fortnite* concerts and *EVE Online* battles are helpful to explain the technological requirements of the Metaverse, it’s Berkeley’s 18th-century tree that best reveals the difficulty of creating a virtual plane of existence for all of humanity. As William Gibson explained in *Neuromancer*, the Metaverse (or as he called it, the cyberspace matrix) does not really exist. Instead, it is a “consensual hallucination” that’s “experienced daily by billions.… A graphic representation of data abstracted from the banks of every computer in the human system.”^([16](#notes_split_004.xhtml#ch4fr16))

Accordingly, every aspect of the Metaverse, from its many trees to their individual leaves, and the forests in which they are situated, must be created by a human agent or a subagent thereof (such as a generative AI program). Every aspect of this data, too, must be set—from the specific coloring of the tree to its texture, the way it moves in the wind, what is required to chop it down, the sound it makes when falling, and so on. And for a user to experience this data, they must have systems capable of understanding and representing it. For the data to be part of a shared human experience, it must also be shared with billions of other people, each of whom can correctly interpret and affect it, while sharing their own data back.

Circa 1880 Engraving of Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville’s Phonautograph

![De Martinville’s phonautograph directed sound vibrations down a cone to a firm stylus that would then record these vibrations on blackened parchment. ¶ Universal History Archive / Getty Images](OEBPS/images/pg122.jpg)

De Martinville’s phonautograph directed sound vibrations down a cone to a firm stylus that would then record these vibrations on blackened parchment. ¶ Universal History Archive / Getty Images

In 2024, billions of people can observe a hyperrealistic virtual tree fall in a hyperrealistic forest. But if many users want to observe such an event, they must be separated into individual groups that each watches a different copy of that tree fall and hears the sound of that tree falling. Alternatively, the complexity of that tree may need to be reduced—its rough bark smoothed out into a textureless and uniform brown and its fall reduced to a generic thud. And those who do observe the same tree might see and hear it at slightly different times, thereby determining who responds to it first and last, and requiring some system to decide whose responses should be considered “true” or “false.” Some users might be able to hear the tree fall in spatial sound and see it in a high-resolution, high-frame-rate immersive headset, while another cohort might be treated to flattened sound and a lower-frame-rate, 2D display. And no matter how many see the tree fall, the Metaverse might forget this same fact and reestablish the tree minutes later as though it had never been felled. Or it might remember the tree as having fallen, but differently than its observers. And some systems within the Metaverse might not even recognize the tree as being a tree, let alone be able to use it, or understand who does and doesn’t own it.

The Metaverse will become “the Metaverse” only if it can support a large number of users experiencing the same event, at the same time, and in the same place, without making substantial concessions in user functionality, world interactivity, persistence, and rendering quality, and without fragmenting participants into different and occasionally conflicting instances. This does not require billions of people to share in any single experience at the same time, nor the ability to infinitely affect every particle of it—just as all real-world locations can have capacity limits, dress codes, and prohibited behavior. Yet it’s clear that the shortfalls of current technology are significant.

To close the gap between the present day and the long-awaited Metaverse-shaped future, numerous technologies are required. Some of these technologies exist today, but require substantial enhancements or investments. Some must be created. In other cases, new business models and coding practices are required.

The rest of this book is dedicated to these requirements, the potential solutions to them, and the ways they affect one another.
