## [Chapter 5 NETWORKING VERSUS THE SPEED OF LIGHT](#contents.xhtml#ch_5)

Discourse on the Metaverse typically focuses on the video games that are the most popular, yet the most technically impressive exemplar is a title that, over its lifetime, will likely count fewer players than *Roblox*, *Minecraft*, and *Fortnite* reach in an average day. In fact, the title’s aim is not socializing or the ability to traverse fictional realms or build virtual wonders. Instead, it’s designed to precisely reproduce an experience many deem unpleasant, dull, or terrifying: airplane travel.

### **Bandwidth**

The first *Flight Simulator* was released by Sublogic in 1979 for the Apple II computer, and though renders were limited to fewer than 200 colored lines atop a uniform black background, the title nevertheless amassed a cult following. In 1981—two decades before the debut of Microsoft’s Xbox video game console—Alan Boyd, the 32nd-ever employee at Microsoft and its head of acquisitions, approached Sublogic hoping to license the franchise and produce a new entry that would enable Microsoft to differentiate the still-to-come 16-bit Windows PCs from 8-bit computers such as the Apple II.^([1](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr1))

By 2006, Microsoft had released ten total entries in the rechristened *Microsoft Flight Simulator* (*MSFS*) line, and in 2012 *The Guinness Book of World Records* dubbed *MSFS* the longest-running video game franchise in history, beating *Space Invaders* and *Oregon Trail*, which were a year and a half older but had become dormant, and *Pac-Man* and *Donkey Kong*/*Super Mario*, which launched in 1980 and 1981.^([2](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr2)) Despite this heritage, it took until the 12th entry, which was released in August 2020, for *MSFS* to soar into the public consciousness. The *New York Times* wrote that the 2020 *MSFS* provided “a new way of understanding the digital world,” offering a view “that is more real than the one we can see outside \[and\] a picture that illuminates our understanding of reality.”^([3](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr3)) A number of publications, including *Time* magazine and Polygon, named *MSFS* one of the best games of 2020.

In theory, *MSFS* is what many people see it as: a game. Within seconds of opening the application, they’ll be reminded that Microsoft’s Xbox Game Studios developed and published it. However, the goal of *MSFS* is not to win, kill, shoot, defeat, beat, or score on another player or an AI-based competitor. The goal is to fly a virtual plane—a process that involves much of the same work as flying a real one. Players will communicate with air traffic control and their copilots, wait to be cleared for takeoff, set their altimeter and flaps, check for fuel reserves and mixtures, release their brake, slowly push the throttle, and so on, all before following their selected or designated flight path while managing conflicting routes and accommodating the flight paths of other virtual planes.

Every entry in the *MSFS* series has offered that sort of functionality, but the 2020 edition is extraordinary—the most realistic and expansive consumer-grade simulation in history. Its map is over 500 million square kilometers—just like the “real” planet earth—and includes two trillion uniquely rendered trees (not two trillion copy-and-pasted trees, or two trillion trees made up of a few dozen varieties), 1.5 billion buildings, and reproductions of nearly every road, mountain, city, and airport across the world.^([4](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr4)) Everything looks like “the real thing” because *MSFS*’s virtual world is based on high-quality scans and images of the “real thing” that are then transformed into 3D models using Microsoft’s Azure Stack.

*MSFS*’s reproductions and renders aren’t perfect, but they are still stunning. “Players” can fly past their own house and spot their mailbox or the tire swing in the front yard. When the “game” conjures a sunset that’s reflected across a bay and then refracted yet again by the plane’s wings, it can be difficult to distinguish between a screenshot from *MSFS* and a real-world photograph.

*MSFS*’s life-size and lifelike “virtual world” is made up of nearly 2.5 petabytes of data—roughly a thousand times larger than *Fortnite* and equivalent to more than 2.6 million gigabytes.^([5](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr5)) There is no way for a consumer device (or most enterprise devices) to store this amount of data. Most consoles and PCs top out at 1,000 gigabytes, while the largest consumer-grade Network Attached Storage (NAS) drive is 20,000 gigabytes and retails for close to $750. Even the physical space required to store 2.5 petabytes is impractical.

But even if a consumer could afford such a hard drive and enough space to house it, *MSFS* is a live service. It updates to reflect real-world weather (including accurate wind speed and direction, temperature, humidity, rain, and light), air traffic, and other geographic changes. This allows a player to fly into real-world hurricanes or to trail real-life commercial airliners on their exact flight path while they’re in the air in the real world. This means that users cannot “prebuy” or “pre-download” all of *MSFS*—much of it doesn’t yet exist!

*MSFS* works by storing a relatively small portion of the game on a consumer’s device—roughly 150 GB. This portion is enough to run the game offline, as it contains the game’s core code, visual information for numerous planes and cities, and generic textures and assets to populate a map the size of the earth. The trade-off of offline play is that users see mostly procedurally generated environments and objects, with landmarks such as Manhattan broadly familiar but populated with generic, mostly duplicated buildings that bear only an occasional and sometimes accidental resemblance to their real-world counterparts. Some preprogrammed flight paths exist, but they cannot mimic actual live routes, nor can one player see another player’s plane.

It’s when players go online that *MSFS* becomes a true wonder, with Microsoft’s servers streaming new maps, textures, weather data, flight paths, and whatever other information a user might need. In a sense, players experience the *MSFS* world exactly as a real-world pilot might. When they fly over or around a mountain, new information streams into their retinas via light particles, revealing and then clarifying what’s there for the first time. Before then, a pilot knows only that, logically, something must be around the corner.

Many gamers assume this is what happens in all online multiplayer video games. But the truth is that most online games try to send as much information as possible to the user in advance of them playing, and as little as possible when they’re actively playing. This explains why playing a game, even a relatively small one such as *Super Mario Bros.*, requires purchasing cartridges or discs that contain multi-gigabyte game files, or waiting tens of minutes or even a couple of hours downloading and installing these game files. From time to time, a player might be told to download and install a multi-gigabyte update before they can play again. These files are so large because they contain nearly the entire game—namely, its code, game logic, and all the assets and textures required for the in-game environment (every type of tree, every avatar, every boss battle, every weapon, and so on).

For the typical online game, what actually comes from online multiplayer servers? Not much. *Fortnite*’s PC and console game files are roughly 30 GB in size, but online play involves only 20–50 MB (or 0.02–0.05 GB) in downloaded data per hour. This information tells the player’s device what to do with the data it already has. If a user is playing an online game of *Mario Kart*, Nintendo’s servers will tell the user’s Nintendo Switch which avatars their opponents are using and therefore must be loaded by the device. During the match, the user’s continuous connection to the server then enables a near constant stream of data on exactly where these opponents are (“positional data”), what they’re doing (sending a red shell), communications (e.g., a teammate’s audio), and various other information, including how many players are still in the contest.

That online games remain “mostly offline” comes as a surprise even to avid gamers. After all, most music and video is now streamed—people don’t pre-download songs or TV shows anymore, let alone buy physical CDs to store them—and video gaming is supposedly a more technically sophisticated and forward-looking media category. Yet it is precisely because games are so complicated that those who make them choose to marginalize the internet. Connections are not reliable, bandwidth is not reliable, latency is not reliable. As discussed in [Chapter 4](#chapter4.xhtml), most online experiences can survive this unreliability, but games cannot. As a result, developers chose to rely as little on the internet as possible.

A mostly offline approach to online games works well, but it imposes limitations. The fact that a player’s device can tell individual users which assets, textures, and models should be rendered means that every asset, texture, and model must be known and stored in advance by the same device. By sending rendering data on an as-needed basis, games can have a much greater diversity of virtual objects because they need not be preloaded to a consumer-grade hard drive. *MSFS* aspires for every town not just to differ from every other but to exist as it does in real life. And it doesn’t want to store 100 types of clouds and then tell a device which cloud to render and with what coloring; rather, it wants to dictate exactly what that cloud should look like.

When a player sees their friend in *Fortnite* today, they can interact using only a limited set of preloaded animations (or “emotes”), such as a wave or a moonwalk. Many users imagine a future where their live facial and body movements are re-created in a virtual world. To greet a friend, they won’t pick Wave 17 of the 20 waves preloaded onto their device but will wave uniquely articulated fingers in a unique way that has never happened precisely that way before. Users also hope to bring their myriad virtual items and avatars across the myriad virtual worlds connected to the Metaverse. As *MSFS*’s file size suggests, it’s simply not possible to send so much data to the user in advance. Doing so requires not only impractically large hard drives but also a virtual world that knows in advance anything that might be created or performed.

The need to “pre-send” an otherwise living virtual world has other implications. Every time Epic Games alters *Fortnite*’s virtual world—say, to add new destinations, vehicles, or non-playable characters—users have to download and install an update. The more Epic adds, the longer this takes and the longer a user must wait. The more frequently a world is updated, the more delays a user will experience.

The batch-based update process also means that virtual worlds cannot truly be “alive.” Instead, a central server is choosing to send a specific version of a virtual world out to all users, a world that will endure until the next update replaces it. Each edition is not necessarily fixed—an update might have programmed changes, such as a New Year’s Eve event or snowfall which increases daily—but it is pre-scripted. Finally, there are limitations to where users can go. During Travis Scott’s ten-minute event on *Fortnite*, some 30 million players were instantly transported from the game’s core map to the depths of a never-before-seen ocean, then to a never-before-seen planet, and then deep into outer space. Many people may imagine that the Metaverse operates in similar fashion—that users can easily jump from virtual world to virtual world without first enduring long loading times. But to put on the concert, Epic had to send users each of these mini-worlds in full, days to hours before the event, via a standard *Fortnite* patch (users who had not installed the update were denied entry to the event). Then, during each set piece, every player’s device was loading the next set piece in the background. It was notable that each of Scott’s concert destinations was smaller and more limited than the one before it, with the last being a largely “on rails” experience in which users simply flew forward in largely nondescript space. Think of this as the difference between freely exploring a mall versus traversing one via a moving walkway.

The Travis Scott concert worked so well because Epic Games, in addition to being one of the most creative game developers in the world, designed the experience in a manner that hid its technical limitations. Concerts are also inherently structured events—participants don’t expect to be able to do anything they can imagine but, instead, expect to be mostly guided through a predetermined set list that begins and ends at a fixed time. The decentralized and boundless Metaverse doesn’t have such conveniences.

Some might conclude from the popularity of *Roblox* and the immensity of *MSFS* that modern internet infrastructure can now handle Metaverse-style live data streaming. In truth, the model, too, is possible only in a highly constrained fashion and for specific use cases. *Roblox*, for example, doesn’t need to cloud-stream much data because most of its in-game items are based on “prefabs.” The game is mostly just telling a user’s device how to tweak, recolor, or rearrange previously downloaded items—just as all Lego builds are composed of fewer than 3,800 unique pieces (and 10 of these pieces constitute 20% of all pieces shipped to customers).^([6](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr6)) *Roblox*’s graphical fidelity is also relatively modest and therefore its texture and environmental file sizes are relatively small, too. Overall, *Roblox*’s data usage is much greater than that of *Fortnite*—roughly 100–300 MB per hour, rather than 30–50 MB—but still manageable. At its target settings, *MSFS* demands nearly 25 times as much hourly bandwidth as *Fortnite* and 5 times as much as *Roblox*. This is because it’s not sending data on how to reconfigure or recolor a preloaded house but instead sending a user’s device the exact dimensions, density, and coloration of a multi-kilometer cloud or a nearly exact replica of the Gulf of Mexico’s shoreline. Yet even this need is simplified in ways that won’t work for the Metaverse.

While *MSFS* requires lots of data, it need not arrive particularly quickly. As with real-world pilots, *MSFS* pilots cannot suddenly teleport from New York State to New Zealand, nor see downtown Albany from 30,000 feet above Manhattan, nor descend from the firmament to the tarmac in seconds. This provides the player’s device with lots of time to download the necessary data. In fact, the *MSFS* client can easily predict where the player is headed and preemptively download the related data. And even if *MSFS* doesn’t receive all of the data it requested on time, the consequences are modest: some of Manhattan’s buildings will temporarily be procedurally generated, rather than resemble the real thing, with the realistic details filled in as the user gets closer to the city.

*MSFS* is a remarkable creative experience, technical achievement, and case study on why so many came to view the Metaverse as a practical opportunity in 2020 and 2021—not just an inevitable part of some distant future. Nevertheless, the 2020 *MSFS* is still far from “the Metaverse.” Overall, the title has more in common with a diorama than Neal Stephenson’s bustling Street. Only a handful of *MSFS*’s 1.5 billion buildings can be entered, and none appear operational (let alone do anything). And though AI-operated vehicles can be seen on its countless roads, no traffic jams ever occur, nor does the AI adhere to any realistic patterns, such as rush-hour traffic or 3:30 pickups at the local school. Indeed, if a user lands their plane on the local freeway, nearby cars will not only drive as though there was no such emergency landing, they pass through the plane altogether. There are no baseball or football matches playing on the millions of fields a virtual pilot might see while flying (least of all ones the pilot could join). Altogether, a user can engage with no more than 49 other players—and no one can modify *MSFS*’s virtual world (creating a new map is out of the question).

There is nothing wrong or inherently disappointing about *MSFS*’s limitations. The title’s goal is to let users traverse a surface-level model of the earth, not engage in an earth-like ecosystem. But if users want to use a platform capable of the latter functionality, they will need to be able to download far more data per hour than even the fullest version of *MSFS* demands today—and they will need it on a timelier basis, too. A computer might be able to guess what a Manhattan skyscraper’s windows look like—and a user might be able to wait for the real thing—but the Metaverse is more than just an empty model of the known world. And this means tackling the least understood element of internet connectivity today: latency.

### **Latency**

Bandwidth and latency are often conflated, and the mistake is understandable: both impact how much data can be sent or received per unit of time. The classic way to differentiate the two concepts is by likening an internet connection to a highway. “Bandwidth” is the number of lanes on the highway, and “latency” is the speed limit. If a highway has more lanes, it can carry more cars and trucks without congestion. But if the highway’s speed limit is low—perhaps due to too many curves or because it’s laid in gravel rather than pavement—then the flow of traffic is slow even if there’s spare capacity. Similarly, a high speed limit with only one lane results in constant congestion—the speed limit becomes an aspiration, not a reality.

The challenge with real-time-rendered virtual worlds is that users aren’t sending a single car from one destination to another. Instead, they’re sending a never-ending fleet of cars tethered together both to and from that destination (as [Chapter 4](#chapter4.xhtml) detailed, a “continuous connection” is needed). It’s also not possible to send these cars in advance because their contents (i.e., data) are created only milliseconds before they hit the road. Furthermore, these cars must drive at their fastest possible speed because if they arrive late, the rest of the fleet behind them will carry the wrong packages, too, as will many of the other cars on the road. And should any portion of the fleet ever be diverted to a relief highway or road, it might be necessary to restart the entire fleet’s trip—even if this new route is equally fast.

As “speed” is an abstract concept, it’s helpful to specify how the latency requirements of the Metaverse differ from those of the internet today. In 2024, most internet usage involves a single device pulling static copies of information from a single server, such as a consumer’s iPhone downloading an email or loading a webpage. As the user is not engaged in a simulation or any live experience, a 500-millisecond (or half-second) or longer delay has no consequence other than mild frustration—and tolerance is surprisingly pretty high. Most users don’t notice a 150–200 ms delay between a single button press, such as that of a Netflix pause-or-play button, and the relevant application’s response to that input. Moreover, latency is typically the least valued networking attribute; when watching Netflix, a user would likely prefer higher-resolution video (“bandwidth”) and uninterrupted playback (“reliability”) to an 80 ms–faster start (“latency”). Even when users are participating in a shared experience, latency requirements are typically low. It rarely matters whether an iMessage or WhatsApp message arrives within 50 ms rather than 500 ms—and such a margin is inconsequential in contrast to the speed in which the recipient reads it. Latency in a video call is unquestionably annoying but also straightforward to manage; participants just learn to wait a bit after the speaker stops speaking. Even a second (1,000 ms) is workable.

But the human tolerance for latency in interactive experiences is incredibly low. When controlling a virtual character, a user’s brain must feel as though this avatar is a direct extension of the user’s inputs, rather than merely the accurate execution of them. This is the difference between waving a flag and pressing a button that waves a flag. As these inputs are happening in a continuous fashion, unlike a one-off press of a play-or-pause button, delays are even more noticeable to users, as is variability in response times.

Recall that many modern 3D simulations aspire for at least 60 rendered frames per second, equivalent to at least one frame every 16 ms. The inevitable outcome is that even a seemingly modest 100 ms delay can lead to a dozen consecutive frames that do not reflect what a user has already done and what their brain expects to see. This problem is exacerbated by the fact that more real-time-rendered virtual worlds are multiuser. As such, variations in latency among users mean that certain users (or devices, or networks) are effectively ahead of or behind one another, which results in some users being able to respond to information that others haven’t even received. To put what is still an abstract conversation about speeds and milliseconds into perspective, avid gamers typically notice that latency affects their play at 48 ms, while some can correctly note delays after only 5 ms.^([7](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr7)) Crucially, these determinations do not correlate with skill, just total playtime (i.e., experience). And on average, even novice players will realize that latency, rather than their video game skills, are to blame for their poor play by 100–110 ms.^([8](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr8)) At 150 ms, games that involve quick responses are simply unplayable. In contrast, the average person does not even notice when the audio and video of a movie or TV show are out of sync unless the audio is 45 ms early or 125 ms late (170 ms total variance). Acceptability thresholds, as they’re generally called, are even wider, at 90 ms early and 185 ms late (275 ms).

The Metaverse isn’t a fast-moving pixel-precise game like *Fortnite* or *Call of Duty*, but its requirements are nevertheless quite high. The more realistic an avatar—such as the hyperreal “personas” created by the Apple Vision Pro’s face scan—the more sensitive humans are to the movement, detail, and timing of a smile or eye movement. To this end, few movie watchers are put off by the mouth movements of a cartoonish Pixar character, but many are creeped out by a photoreal CGI human whose lips don’t move exactly right (animators famously call this the “uncanny valley”).

As a category, VR and AR devices are particularly intolerant of latency. In contrast to “2D” displays, such as those of a PC, television, or smartphone, which use keystrokes, touchscreen taps, and mouse movements for inputs, HMDs often rely on a user’s head, eye, and body movements. These latter methods often activate a user’s inner ear, which in turn makes them more susceptible to disconnects between what they are doing (turning left or right, squatting, waving, and so on) and what their eyes can see. The result can be nauseating in a literal sense—less so for experiences where both the user and their virtual avatar remain in a fixed position, as in the case of a meeting, watching streaming video, and some stand-in-place fitness experiences, but brutally so when the user is making steps forward, backward, and side to side and/or their avatar is leaping, climbing, running, and so on. For similar reasons, VR and AR headsets aim not for 30 to 60 or even 90 frames per second but 120–240 fps, which aids visual clarity but also increases the number of “old frames” seen by a user if latency increases.^([9](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr9)) AR device experiences, even those on a smartphone, face another challenge—their renders sit atop the “real world,” which “renders” at the speed of light (an object 100 meters away therefore arrives in 0.0003 ms, or 0.0000003 seconds). A device that is constantly loading information after a viewer has looked elsewhere is useless, and one that is partly lagging is likely to be more frustrating than helpful.

Separate from the issue of what’s tolerable is how latency affects usage. Subspace—a real-time bandwidth start-up whose executive team consists of the former senior vice president of infrastructure and security at *League of Legends* maker Riot Games, the former head of software at SpaceX, and the former head of video infrastructure at Google—says that video game players typically increase or decrease their weekly play time by 6% for every 10 ms decrease or increase in latency. This correlation holds beyond the point at which even “expert” gamers consciously notice latency levels, too.

Fortunately, not all Metaverse applications need ultra-low latency. Digital twins, such as those that oversee an airport terminal or factory floor, have higher acceptability thresholds because they simulate slower-moving and more predictable agents and objects. A relatively tiny portion of their simulations involves synchronization with distant users, devices, or networks. And while industrial AR devices still face high frame-rate requirements, their usage is typically concentrated to a few areas and they can therefore preload more of the data that might be needed, rather than query a distant server for real-time support. That said, the role of latency should not be underestimated. The more powerful a digital twin, the more powerful the computational power that’s required (as discussed in the following chapter). Most companies outsource their compute needs to cloud computing companies such as Amazon’s AWS, whose data centers might be thousands of kilometers away, and charge heavily for real-time bandwidth delivery due to its scarcity. And while industrial simulations often move slower than their fictional counterparts, latency-related inaccuracies compound over a higher volume of interactions, decisions, and AI recommendations.

With a greater understanding of latency requirements, it’s possible to reassess the current state of delivery time. The median time for data to be sent between the 25 largest cities in the United States is roughly 18 ms,^([10](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr10)) which meets nearly all requirements for ultra-low latency experiences but doesn’t tell the full story of delivery times. For example, the specific city pairing matters greatly. Dallas to Houston averages only 2.5 ms one way, while New York City to Los Angeles takes 30 ms, and Orlando to Seattle typically exceeds 35. In addition, these sums reflect only city-to-city or data-center-to-data-center transit time, and therefore excludes the time required for a device outside these locations to send in their data or to receive it. This “last mile” is typically the slowest and least reliable part of delivery. Unfortunately, many buildings or neighborhoods still rely on low-capacity (i.e., low-bandwidth) coaxial copper cable and can easily congest. Households and devices that rely on cellular networks for data face 20 or even 40 ms in added latency compared to wired fiber optics. And while Wi-Fi typically covers only the last few feet of delivery, Wi-Fi routers add 1–2 ms—a small margin, but one that not all users can afford.

Moreover, all connections suffer from “jitter,” variances in delivery time relative to the median. While most jitter is tightly distributed around the connection’s median latency, it can spike latency severalfold due to a congestion at a local internet node, or an event as trivial as a neighbor or family member turning on Netflix or receiving a FaceTime call. Though temporary, such a jump can sever a network connection or otherwise ruin a shared experience.

International delivery is even more difficult. Median delivery times from data centers in the US Northeast to those in Northeast Asia are as long as 170 to 200 ms, and it takes up to 350 or 700 ms for a packet to go from a user in one locale to a user in the other, with jitter also more common, long-lasting, and severe.

Given the many latency-related obstacles faced by internet users some 40 years after the formalization of TCP/IP, it might come as a surprise that there are hundreds of millions of people who frequent online virtual worlds. Yet this is possible only due to numerous tricks and solutions that, unfortunately, don’t work well in the Metaverse. Case in point: Most high-fidelity multiplayer gaming is “match made” around server regions. By limiting the player roster to those who live in the northeastern United States, or Western Europe, or Southeast Asia, game publishers can minimize latency within each region. And because gaming is a leisure activity and typically played with one to three friends, this clustering works well enough. Multiplayer games also use “netcode” solutions that correct for synchronization issues and conflicts. Delay-based netcode will tell a player’s device to artificially delay its rendering of its owner’s inputs until the most latent player’s inputs arrive. This will irk players with muscle memory attuned to low latency, but it works. Rollback netcode is more sophisticated. If an opponent’s inputs are delayed, a player’s device will proceed based on what it expects to happen. If it turns out the opponent did something different, the device will try to unwind in-process animations and then replay them “correctly.”

Although the above tools are effective, they scale poorly. Netcode works well for titles in which player inputs are fairly predictable, such as driving simulations, or those with relatively few players to synchronize, as is the case in most fighting games. It is exponentially harder to correctly predict and coherently synchronize the behaviors of dozens of players, especially when they are participating in a sandbox-style virtual world with cloud-streamed environmental and asset data. And large though the gaming industry might seem on a revenue basis, it remains highly constrained in reach. Even in the United States, which has only 4% of the world’s population and 6% of its land by surface area, yet 26% of its internet networks, Subspace estimates that barely three-quarters of broadband homes can reliably play high-fidelity games such as *Fortnite* or *Call of Duty*.^([11](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr11)) In contrast, the Middle East has 5% of the world’s population, 5% of its land, but only 3% of its networks, and fewer than one in four homes can reliably play the aforementioned titles.^([12](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr12)) It’s even harder to play in India, which has 18% of the world’s population, 2% of its land, and 3.5% of its networks, with only one in ten broadband homes meeting high-fidelity gaming requirements.^([13](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr13))

### **The Battle between** ***H. sapiens*** **and** ***c***

Outlandish though it may seem, the fight to minimize network latency is, at its core, a fight against the speed of light. Consider, as an example, the quest to send just a single byte from a data center in downtown New York City to one in downtown Tokyo or Mumbai as rapidly as possible. At a distance of 11,000–12,500 kilometers, a light photon could hypothetically complete such a trip in between 36 and 42 ms. The physics of the universe, in other words, has only a roughly 6–12 ms margin over the physics of the human brain. In practice, this millisecond benchmark is impossible to attain.

One impediment is silica glass. Many assume that data sent via fiber-optic cables travels at the speed of light. This is technically true, but all glass fibers, unlike the vacuum of space, reflect light. For one thing, the path of a given beam of light is not straight even if the cable itself is perfectly straight. Instead, a beam of light travels in more of a tight zigzag as it bounces between the inside edges of a fiber-optic cable core. The result is a more than 45% elongation of a route, which produces a minimum possible latency of 52–61 ms. Although such a delay already tests the patience of avid gamers, this figure is hypothetical. In 2021, Amazon’s AWS, Microsoft’s Azure, and Google’s Cloud Platform averaged more than 110 ms when sending a packet one way from their northeastern American data centers to their Asia-Pacific data centers, which route to Mumbai and Tokyo. Travel inside the United States faces a comparable increase. Although beams of light could travel from New York City to San Francisco in 14 ms and through fiber optics in 20 ms, average transit times are over 30 ms. There are several causes for these increases.

While the phrase “internet backbone” brings to mind a largely planned-out and partly federated network of cables, the internet is really a loose federation of private networks with individual aims and little concern for collective efficiency. Furthermore, internet cables are rarely laid out as the crow flies. Instead, they must navigate environmental concerns, existing public and private infrastructure (cities, parks, freeways), governmental permits and ordinances, and the costs of given routes (a longer route may require only earthen trenches or may piggyback on an in-construction highway, while the shortest might require blasting rock). In general, the more direct the intended path of a cable, the more likely it is to be politically, socially, financially, or environmentally challenged. And in most cases, there’s not much of a business case for a specific network to be laid so that it is a few milliseconds faster. As a hypothetical, imagine a private broadband operator seeking to connect two cities or regions that are roughly 300 kilometers apart. The most direct path would allow data packets to arrive in 1.3 ms, but laying this cable might require digging through a river or under a school. An alternative route might follow local roads and be laid during an existing roadway repair process. This latter option might save effort and money, but add 100 kilometers and, with it, another 0.4 ms. These milliseconds add up when a user needs to reach a person or server many thousands of miles and many dozens of networks away, but the internet users directly connected by this hypothetical cable won’t pay for the 0.4 ms in savings, and most of the latency challenge comes from the aggregation of the networks in use, not that one segment.

Many countries and even major international cities lack a direct connection. New York City has a direct undersea cable to France but not to Portugal. Traffic from the United States can go directly to Tokyo, but reaching India requires jumping from one undersea cable to another on the Asian or Australian continent, a process that adds thousands of kilometers to the trip. To shorten this path, a dedicated line would need to be dug across at least Thailand, if not also Vietnam, Laos, and Myanmar. And again, such a connection would solve only for shore-to-shore transmission. In 2020, the US government effectively outlawed the construction of cables that directly connected the United States to Hong Kong or mainland China, prompting a still-under-construction cable funded by Facebook and Google to redirect to the Philippines and Taiwan.^([14](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr14)) The following year, the World Bank abandoned a cable project that would have connected three Pacific Island nations, after the United States protested its construction by a Chinese supplier.^([15](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr15))

US Internet Backbone

![A 2023 map of active terrestrial internet networks in the United States. ¶ Infrapedia](OEBPS/images/pg140.jpg)

A 2023 map of active terrestrial internet networks in the United States. ¶ Infrapedia

The layout of the internet’s many networks is exacerbated by the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), one of the core application layer protocols of TCP/IP. When a given device wants to send data to another unaffiliated device or server, at least one intermediary network is required, but within a large country, it’s common for data to travel across five to seven networks. International delivery might span one to two dozen network “hops” or more, depending on how remote and far away the two devices or servers are. These pathways are not fixed, either. Two emails sent from the same device in New York to the same device in Los Angeles might start on the same Wi-Fi network and Verizon FiOS wireline network and terminate on the same AT&T wireless network, but in the meantime, one email might travel through the midwestern United States and head south along the Pacific Coast, while the other might first head south to the Carolinas before traveling across the Southwest. The BGP dictates these pathways by helping every single network leg choose which network will pass a given packet of data. Accordingly, an American’s daily internet usage might involve hundreds or even thousands of the country’s more than 30,000 networks.^([16](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr16))

Global Submarine Internet Cable Backbone

![A 2022 map of the nearly 500 submarine cables and 1,250 landing stations that enable the global internet. ¶ TeleGeography](OEBPS/images/pg141.jpg)

A 2022 map of the nearly 500 submarine cables and 1,250 landing stations that enable the global internet. ¶ TeleGeography

Although BGP successfully routes traffic across more than 110,000 networks globally, it does not know what data is being sent (e.g., an email versus video call), whether it’s an initiation or response (e.g., a user sending a request for the *New York Times* homepage, or the *New York Times* website sending that data back), its urgency (the relevance of 10, 50, or 200 ms), the impact of congestion (whether a key connection might be severed), and so on. Instead, the internet’s “air traffic controller” applies a standardized methodology for routing data, which essentially weighs the shortest path, the fastest path, and the cheapest path, with a general preference for cost.

BGP’s ruleset reflects the internet’s original asynchronous network design. Its goal is to ensure that all data is transmitted successfully and inexpensively. But as a result, many routes are far longer than necessary—and inconsistently so. Although a *Fortnite* player might be located only 500 kilometers from a local server and have a shortest possible network path of 650 kilometers, their data might take an 800-kilometer path while their neighbor ends up traveling 50% farther. Moreover, one of these connections might end up severed, or suffer from recurring bouts of 150 ms latency, all to prioritize traffic that doesn’t need to be delivered in real time, such as an email.

### **Not FTL, but Hopefully Fast Enough**

The many factors listed above explain why a data packet that could travel from New York City to San Francisco, Tokyo, or Mumbai in 14, 36, or 42 ms is instead limited to a minimum of 20, 52, or 61 ms and actually averages 30, 110, or 130 ms. Improving these times will be expensive, difficult, and slow. But there is reason for optimism.

Internet access continues to improve on an annual basis, with average bandwidth increasing, latency falling, and prices (in real terms) declining. The emergence of what many accountancies, consultancies, and investment banks expect will be a multitrillion-dollar Metaverse economy, alongside additional growth in the digital economy, will lead to even greater investments.

In the average year, close to $3 billion is spent laying new submarine cables, many of which reach populations that had previously lacked high-speed internet.^([17](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr17)) The average fiber pairing per cable has grown from 4 to 14 over that time, too, substantially increasing capacity.^([18](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr18))

Compared to wireline infrastructure, it’s comparatively easy to upgrade wireless towers and stations. 5G networks are primarily billed as offering wireless users “ultra-low latency,” with the potential of 1 ms and a more realistic 10 ms expected compared to the 10–20 ms average of today’s 4G networks. This is not a complete solution, as it reflects only the latency from a user’s device to a tower, after which the fixed-line internet backbone takes over. However, it is a substantial leap for mobile devices as well as rural homes without access to in-the-ground broadband.

Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite internet company, promises to provide high-bandwidth, low-latency internet service across the United States and eventually the rest of the world. In contrast to prior satellite internet companies, such as Viasat or EchoStar/Hughes Network Systems, Starlink satellites are an average of 550 kilometers above the earth, rather than 35,700 kilometers,^([19](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr19)) which reduces the theoretical transit time required for a customer to send their data to a satellite and for that satellite to send the data back to earth from roughly 250 ms to 4 ms. As Starlink’s lower-earth-orbit satellites are less than a tenth of the weight of their geosynchronous competitors, the company’s launch costs are substantially lower, which enables more of these satellites to be sent into orbit, which then reduces the distances between a customer and the nearest available satellite.

Though an unprecedented technical achievement, satellite internet doesn’t achieve ultra-low latency, especially at great distances. Though Starlink aspires to 10–20 ms one-way latency (20–40 ms round trip), at the start of 2023, it averages more than 30 ms (60 ms+) when sending data to and from a US server or device—more than double the industry average.^([20](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr20)) In Puerto Rico, latency averaged about 60 ms (120 ms) when sending to and from local computers, four and a half times the local average, while the Philippines was 80 ms (160 ms), seven times the average.^([21](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr21)) Starlink’s actual latency far exceeds its theoretical minimum for several reasons. For example, a given packet of data might need to daisy-chain across several Starlink satellites before being sent down to earth, after which it must still travel through terrestrial networks to reach its destination—and then repeat the process coming back. In some cases, Starlink even exacerbates the speed-of-light problem compared to purely terrestrial alternatives. New York to Philadelphia is around 150 kilometers in a straight line and potentially 200 kilometers by cable, but over 1,200 kilometers when traveling to a low-orbit satellite and back down.^([\*](#chapter5.xhtml#footnote-032)) Compared to fiber-optic cables, Starlink also faces severe capacity constraints. Residential fiber-optic cables can support up to 100 gigabytes per second in bandwidth, while submarine cables can reach into the single-digit terabytes per second. Starlink satellites max out at 20 Gbps, which allows them to support a maximum of 2,000 simultaneous users and experience speed degradation as usage grows. Between Q1 2021 and Q3 2023, average download speeds for US Starlink customers fell from roughly 90 Mbps to 65 Mbps, due to increases in users and usage, with one-way latency growing from 20 ms to 30.^([22](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr22)) Due to lower average population density, Canadian customers experienced no material decline over that period.

As SpaceX founder Elon Musk acknowledges, Starlink is focused on “the hardest-to-serve customers,” people whom telecommunications companies “otherwise have trouble reaching.”^([23](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr23)) With this in mind, satellite delivery should be seen as enabling more people to meet the minimum latency specifications for the Metaverse, rather than offering improvements for those who already meet it. Still, the impact of the technology continues to grow, as do its minimum service levels. In 2018 Musk estimated that Starlink would require $10 billion in investment until achieving sustainable profitability.^([24](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr24)) By mid-2021, Musk’s estimate had grown to more than $30 billion^([25](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr25)) as the company ratcheted up its global ambitions. At the end of 2023, Starlink’s network spanned an estimated 5,600 satellites—over 60% of all active satellites^([26](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr26))—and planned to launch another 6,500 by 2025, with the hopes of eventually operating more than 42,000.^([27](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr27)) In 2019, Amazon announced Kuiper Systems, which has similar aims to Starlink and leverages Amazon founder Jeff Bezos’s aerospace company, Blue Origin. Amazon expects to launch over 3,000 satellites by 2030,^([28](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr28)) with an investment budget of more than $10 billion.^([29](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr29)) SpaceX’s and Amazon’s satellites may relay traffic to each other, just as independent fiber networks do today. But even if these rival constellations remain fully separate, growth in their fleets will increase the number of customers that can be supported and the average bandwidth they’re afforded, while also reducing latency by shortening the average distance between satellites, and from satellites to industrial receiver stations on earth.

Prior to Starlink’s commercial launch in 2020, Facebook, Google, and various start-ups aspired to build internet networks using solar-powered drones or high-altitude balloons in the stratosphere. The benefits of such equipment would include significantly shorter distances to customers compared to lower-earth-orbit satellites and far lower launch costs. Beginning in 2016, Facebook’s Aquila project deployed a series of drones roughly 140 feet wide and weighing 900 pounds that flew at altitudes between 18,000 and 27,000 kilometers (93% closer to the ground than Starlink’s satellites) and were intended to operate continuously for 90 days. Facebook hoped that drones might one day provide internet to four billion people, most of whom lacked acceptable alternatives. Beginning in 2011, Google’s Project Loon launched 50-foot-wide and 40-foot-tall superpressure helium balloons to altitudes between 18 and 25 kilometers, which operated for an average of 100 days before needing to return to earth. In 2018, Facebook halted development on Aquila, while Google shut Loon down in 2021, citing various technical obstacles, rival priorities, and the deployment of 4G networks across the developing world. Despite the failure of these projects, there is still hope that stratospheric internet will prove viable in the decades to come. To this point, Starlink’s satellites not only boasted considerable advances over the satellite models of the 2000s and early 2010s, but the company also realized the very vision once touted by the Bill Gates–backed Teledesic. Between 1994 and 2002, Teledesic had raised over $1 billion as part of its $9 billion plan (equivalent to $19 billion in 2024 dollars) to launch 850 satellites into orbit roughly 700 kilometers above the earth.^([30](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr30)) By 1997, the company’s plans were shrunk to 288 satellites at 1,400 kilometers, and in 2002, Teledesic suspended operations.^([31](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr31))

In theory, improving the Border Gateway Protocol is the cheapest and fastest way to improve delivery times. The Internet Engineering Task Force does not dictate standards development or mandate the adoption of any updates. Instead, it helps organize working groups who put forward various proposals. And while these proposals sometimes receive tacit or explicit approval from IETF leaders or sponsors, their adoption—and thus ability to become standards—requires the voluntary embrace of the many companies that constitute “the internet.” In the case of BGP, this would involve hundreds of computing-device and modem/router manufacturers, over 110,000 network operators, millions of application developers, and so on. Not all of these groups would need to adopt a change for there to be benefits—better routing on two of seven network hops between a user and a server would nevertheless save precious milliseconds—but a critical mass of adoptees is required to have any meaningful effect. And although the benefits of a real-time protocol or packet classification is obvious, the specific solution is less clear. Remember, BGP has multiple criteria in its rank-order preference. Should BGP prioritize real-time traffic that has the greatest distance to travel or the lowest plausible tolerance? Should real-time traffic be moved to the “front of the line” or be boosted by some fixed percentage (and if so, how much)? Should real-time traffic be boosted irrespective of network congestion, thereby significantly worsening the experience for non-real-time traffic? And because the internet is decentralized and largely ungoverned, what system might avoid applications and/or networks coding their traffic as real-time irrespective of its latency needs? Such coding would aid delivery reliability and speed, which benefits most developers and users, even if it’s not required—but it would also take up scarce capacity needed by traffic that did need real-time delivery.

A potential solution for real-time bandwidth standards and protocols may stem from the growing ownership of key backbone infrastructure by big-tech companies. In 2012, data sent to and from Amazon, Facebook, Google, and Microsoft constituted less than 10% of traffic transmitted on submarine cables. A decade later, these four companies were more than two-thirds of total traffic, with companies such as Nvidia, Netflix, and Apple taking up much of the rest. In response to bandwidth fees as well as the desire to improve connectivity across the developing world through non-stratospheric means, these companies began to acquire and purchase the future capacity of existing submarine cables, and co-finance or fully fund the laying of new ones. By the end of 2024, Facebook is expected to have the greatest share of global submarine infrastructure among tech giants, having increased from 0% in 2015 to partial, complete, or de facto (i.e., capacity-based) ownership of 13%—a portion representing more than 170,000 kilometers of cables and connecting nearly 33 countries across 47 connections, while reaching 36% of the global population, mostly in Africa and Southeast Asia.^([32](#notes_split_005.xhtml#ch5fr32))

Facebook’s Submarine Cable Infrastructure

![A map of the submarine cables owned, co-owned, partly financed, or capacity-owned by Facebook since 2016, highlighted by the year thesecables went live (or in the case of Facebook acquired a full or partial stake in an already operational cable, highlighted by the year of the transaction). ¶ Fair Internet Report](OEBPS/images/pg147.jpg)

A map of the submarine cables owned, co-owned, partly financed, or capacity-owned by Facebook since 2016, highlighted by the year thesecables went live (or in the case of Facebook acquired a full or partial stake in an already operational cable, highlighted by the year of the transaction). ¶ Fair Internet Report

The most immediate impact of infrastructure investments by Facebook and its peers will be a reduction in global latency to connected countries, and improved bandwidth should be another benefit. On the other hand, the reach of these companies—especially when combined, and in the context of their broader share of internet traffic—gives them an outsized ability to promote, steer, or deploy potential supplementations to BGP, or to private alternatives.
