Purchasing individual components, each one individually packaged, marked up, and retailed, is expensive. Video game consoles are also subsidized, typically by $100–$200, as their manufacturers pursue a razor-and-blades model in which their hardware is sold below cost and profits are instead attained by taking a cut of all subsequent software purchases made by the hardware owner (e.g., a player), and by selling related services, such as online multiplayer. In contrast, no graphics card or monitor manufacturer gets a cut of a player’s Robux or V-Bucks, and few even offer paid gaming services.

Compared to everyday devices, a video game console has computing power so great that in 2000, Japan even placed export limitations on its own beloved giant, Sony, and its signature PlayStation 2 console. The government feared that the PS2 could be used for terrorism on a global scale, namely for missile guidance.^([22](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr22)) The following year, in touting the importance of the consumer electronics industry, US Secretary of Commerce Don Evans declared that “yesterday’s supercomputer is today’s PlayStation.”^([23](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr23)) Evans’s pronouncement was powerful—even though it was arguably backward: today’s PlayStation is often tomorrow’s supercomputer. In 2010, the US Air Force Research Laboratory built the 33rd-largest supercomputer in the world using 1,760 Sony PlayStation 3s. The project’s director estimated that the “Condor Cluster” was 5% to 10% the cost of equivalent systems and required only 10% of the energy,^([24](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr24)) with the cluster used for activities such as radar enhancement, pattern recognition, satellite imagery processing, and artificial intelligence research.^([25](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr25))

Though powerful, consoles are limited. Consider the PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X, both top-of-the-line video game consoles released in 2020. These devices are each nearly ten pounds and larger than a shoebox—much bulkier in comparison to other consumer electronics devices, but this is not usually a problem, given that these devices are generally placed inside a media shelving console and never moved. In truth, it’s an advantage! Precisely because these devices are so large, unsightly, and stationary, Sony and Microsoft have the leeway to place large and loud fans inside their consoles, which keep the consoles cool as they perform their intensive calculations. The fans are aided by large intake and exhaust vents. Sony and Microsoft can also keep component costs down as they don’t need to prioritize their size the way a smartphone manufacturer always must. And while Sony’s and Microsoft’s consoles are heavy, unlike most consumer devices, they never need a battery. Instead, they receive constant power from the electrical grid. This reduces both the size of the device and the heat it generates, which in turn means that the fan can be smaller, too, and also means they can run indefinitely, rather than just a few hours. Consoles typically support two forms of connectivity, Wi-Fi and Ethernet, but have no need for mobile network support—another chipset that takes up space, increases the device’s build costs, and drains battery power.

Video game consoles also don’t need to bring their own display; they hook into a television. This shifts cost to another purchase—no one thinks of a PlayStation as costing “$500 plus a TV”—while also enabling users to choose their own quality (e.g., 1K vs. 4K definition, LED vs. OLED), which accords similar flexibility to their budgets. Most TVs are also six to ten feet from the viewer, which means that a viewer with 20/20 vision can’t even see detail above 1080p unless the TV is larger than 45 inches (if at six feet) or 75 inches (at ten feet). These televisions also work in optimal or at least relatively stable environments—in a darkly lit living room, rather than in an office, let alone on the street, where lighting is uncontrollable and variable. Lastly, TV screens typically draw their own power from an electrical grid, just as a console does.

Video game consoles also off-load a portion of their work to other devices, such as a stand-alone controller for input or a separately purchased headset for audio (the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X don’t include support for Bluetooth audio, so headset purchases include Bluetooth dongles to add the functionality). Video game consoles don’t need to know or figure out very much. They don’t need to track the user’s motion (and especially not their eyes), or scan and process the environment the user is playing in. And video game consoles are leisure devices. It’s not important that they simulate physics precisely, generate “photoreal” renders, or support commercial “work.” And when a console runs an application, it’s often just running that single application, plus a few other supporting processes (e.g., audio chat), whereas PCs and smartphones are constantly running many concurrent applications.

The power- and hardware-related advantages of consoles must be kept in mind when evaluating the capabilities and supposed inadequacies of VR, AR, and MR headsets. It’s common to hear the critique that the experiences produced by these devices look worse than those produced by the consoles that were manufactured in the late 2000s and that could be purchased for only a few hundred dollars then and tens of dollars now.

When it comes to visually rendering a virtual environment, VR/AR/MR devices will always fall short of a contemporaneous video game console. Always. This is because the “work” performed by these devices is far, far harder while the constraints are far, far greater.

### **Bulking Up and Slimming Down**

Any extended reality (XR^([†](#chapter9.xhtml#footnote-018))) device that aspires to regular use or long session times needs to be lightweight. There is broad consensus that the *tolerable* range for an HMD is about 300–700 grams (0.66–1.54 lbs.), depending on purpose (consumer vs. enterprise) and ideal session length (a user is more likely to use a device for several hours if it weighs 300, not 700, grams). Such a device must therefore weigh roughly a tenth the weight of a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. AR glasses must be even lighter. While no one would reasonably insist that these devices must weigh the 15–40 grams of the average “dumb” glasses worn today, they still must be under about 150 grams if they’re going to be worn all day.

Not only do HMDs need to be far lighter than consoles, but they require considerably more components. These include batteries (which are particularly heavy relative to their size), displays, speakers and microphones, a multitude of internally and externally facing cameras (many experts currently believe roughly 12 total cameras are needed) that can track the user’s eyes, face, fingers, and local environment, as well as a variety of sensors (gyroscope, accelerometer, infrared, heat, ultrawide band, and so on), bifocal lenses, and, in the case of AR/MR devices intended for mobile use, wireless networking chips.

As is always the case, when these components are in use, they generate heat. As such, additional components such as thermal tunnels, fans, and heat sinks are required. But unlike consoles, which sit some feet from the user’s body, this heat is but millimeters away from a user’s head and eyes. For this reason, an HMD’s “heat budget” is strikingly narrow.

Fitting these many components into a single lightweight device is hard. It must also be done in an affordable, aesthetically pleasing, and comfortable fashion. This last aspect is where the distribution of weight matters. For many people, a 300-to-700-gram HMD is still too heavy—even for an hour. What’s more, roughly 85% of that weight is front-loaded (i.e., resting on the wearer’s nasal bridge and pulled to their forehead). Though traditional glasses are typically front-loaded, there’s a material difference between placing no more than 30 grams on a user’s nasal bridge and no more than 10 on their ears, and 630 grams on their forehead and another 70 across the rest of their head.

The tension between an HMD’s form factor and its functionality is made by its core feature: the display. When viewing a TV, computer monitor, tablet, or smartphone display, a user can look directly at the display with no intermediary required (though films or glass typically sit on top of LEDs for protective reasons). In contrast, VR and passthrough AR and MR screens require intermediary lenses that bend light toward the user’s eyes from only one to two inches away. This requirement forces a larger device. If a user wants to wear glasses while using an HMD, additional space and supporting material are necessary. New problems emerge, too. Another lens typically produces incremental blurriness, visual artifacts, and reflections—and the degree to which this occurs would also vary based on the quality (i.e., cost) and thickness (i.e., prescription) of the user’s glasses. For similar reasons, HMDs that support glasses cannot place their eye-tracking cameras in front of the user’s eyes. Instead, these cameras must be placed farther outside the HMD’s lenses and at an angle that leads to less accurate tracking unless more cameras are added to compensate.

The use of contact lenses is a partial solution to the above problem, but roughly 10% of those who require corrective lenses cannot use contacts, and another portion dislike them. Moreover, the heat generated by an HMD often leads to dry eyes and, in turn, eyestrain, an experience exacerbated by the use of contacts. The alternative is to apply a prescription to the lenses inside an HMD, which, alas, adds additional cost to the device. And if the device is to support multiple users, it must also enable these users to easily swap lenses, which adds bulk, weight, and complication. Many HMD makers are investing in R&D intended to address users’ visual impairments through software. In this case, a user would input their optical prescription into the device’s operating system, after which rendered images would be “distorted” and/or sharpened such that, to that user, the image was perfectly aligned and clear. Such a solution does not work well for optical AR/MR as the user would still need correction to see the real world behind the lenses, but even with VR and passthrough AR/MR, other challenges remain. The level of correction that an HMD can provide—and thus its ability to minimize eye strain, headaches, and blurriness—is partly contingent upon the resolution and frame rate of its screen and the application running on it. Furthermore, the degree and nature of the correction that’s needed for a given user is not consistent across a rendered frame: individual objects need bespoke corrections based on their simulated depth inside an image, placement relative to the center of the screen, and where the user’s eye is focused—all of these variables might change every dozen or so milliseconds. Not only is such work computationally intensive and unreliable, even the slightest of errors and delays can quickly nauseate the user. In many cases, the user’s nearly instantaneous ocular reflexes, such as those which aid focus and control light, will conflict with software-based rendering adjustments, too (more on this later).

Those who don’t need custom lenses do still require fine-tuning, unfortunately. The distance between human eyes (known as interpupillary distance, or IPD) ranges from roughly 51mm apart to 77mm (95% of people have an IPD between 56 and 70 mm).^([26](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr26)) This variance is why binoculars have hinges that bring its eyepieces closer or farther apart; without it, the devices would be unusable for some and produce distorted images for many. A poor match between a user’s IPD and that supported or set by an HMD typically results in more severe cybersickness.^([27](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr27)) Most HMDs need their own internal “fit” sliders for this same reason—another requirement not faced by other devices. Some HMDs, such as the Apple Vision Pro, automatically adjust to the user’s IPD through facial scanning and eye tracking.

The display requirements for an HMD are also much higher than those for a console, or any other computing device, for that matter. The portable Nintendo Switch, which weighs 300 grams, affords only 720p resolution when unplugged and 1080p when plugged in (which adds another 500 grams in docking and charging equipment). The Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5, which are stationary, constantly powered, and more than six times as heavy as the Switch, support a maximum of 4K. In contrast, XR devices aspire for at least 8K (optimally 16K) pixels.

This requirement has a few drivers. First, the clarity of a given resolution is affected by the distance from which it is viewed, the size of the individual pixels, and the distances between these pixels, as hinted earlier in this chapter. Apple’s trademarked Retina display is a good example of this phenomenon. iPhones are typically viewed from only 10 inches (25 cm) away. As such, Retina display begins at 326 pixels per inch (128 per cm), and each pixel is at most 78 µm in height and width. In the case of laptops, which are typically viewed from 20 inches (51 cm) away, Apple’s Retina displays begin at 218 pixels per inch (a third fewer), and pixels can be as large as 120 µm in height and width (+54%). From only 1 to 2 inches away, however, these retinal displays, along with the seemingly crisp displays of a 4K TV, appear blurry and individual pixels are not only visible, they’re also framed by the unilluminated (i.e., black) gaps between them. The result can cause eyestrain and nausea—especially for those whose vision is imperfect, but not so imperfect as to bother wearing corrective contact lenses or glasses.

The terms “8K” and “16K” are a bit of a simplification, too—intended to make it easier for the average person to understand the needs of an HMD by likening it to a television. Though most people prefer their television to be as large as possible, they don’t intend for it to cover their entire field of view. Indeed, studies suggest only 30–40 degrees of a user’s average 210-degree horizontal field of view^([28](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr28)) is optimal for TV viewing (which means 17°–23° of their 130° vertical field of view,^([29](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr29)) given the average height-width ratio of a TV).^([30](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr30))

A greater field of view (FOV) results in users constantly moving their head—as human vision is sharpest at the center—and viewing parts of a TV’s picture at a heavy angle, which distorts visuals in varying ways. HMDs, conversely, try to maximize their coverage to aid immersion and/or augment more of the surrounding world while minimizing the distracting and useless black border that surrounds the screen. Head movements are also a key input, rather than a hindrance, and as the screen moves with the user, visuals do not suffer as a result either. To expand FOV, an HMD needs to add more pixels (i.e., increase the resolution) or stretch out a current display by enlarging pixels and/or the gap between them, which worsens image clarity. More pixels mean more heat generated and more battery drained.

Optical AR/MR displays face two final requirements. Most laptops support between 300 and 600 nits of brightness, with enterprise-level laptops typically peaking at 1,000 to support field use. Higher-end TVs run between 1,000 and 1,500 nits due to their distance from users and frequent usage in brightly lit living rooms. Top-of-the-line smartphones, conversely, offer as many as 2,000 nits so that they might be seen during bright daylight. Outdoor billboards run between 3,500 and 7,000 nits to ensure visibility on sunny days and from great distances. The advantage of these device form factors is that they block off the light sources directly behind them, then replace that light with their own. As such, they need only be bright enough to survive the light crossing between the screen and the user’s eyes as well as the light around the screen that causes a user’s pupil to contract to reduce the amount of light the eye receives. Optical displays, meanwhile, let light pass through their screen and hit the user’s eye directly. As such, they must add more and brighter light for any render to be visible. In a darkroom, 50 nits is sufficient. When staring at a white wall in the sun, upwards of 10,000 nits are needed, while white paper in the sun can be 20,000 nits (which is why vehicular heads-up displays typically run at 15,000 nits or more).^([31](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr31)) This is incredibly power intensive. One alternative to this model is for the entire lens to be dimmed, thereby reducing all light hitting the user’s eyes, though this still requires brightly illuminated pixels, works less well when the local environment is brighter, and reduces the user’s ability to move or pay attention to what’s around them. Because passthrough AR/MR reproduces the world outside the headset from inside the headset, while preventing the user from seeing the world directly, only a few hundred nits are required.

Lastly, there is the “work” that these devices must do, which far exceeds that asked of a console. One baseline requirement of HMDs is to preemptively warn the user of key boundaries and dangers around them—including hard-to-parse reflective or transparent surfaces. This means that the device must understand the environment around it, not just see it. AR and MR devices must go further. They’re expected to understand not just the placement and shape of objects but also what they are, what they’re doing, what they’re likely to do, their relevance to the task at hand, and potentially detailed attributes such as their materials and composition. An HMD must also track the user’s hands, eyebrows, lips, and other body parts both precisely and quickly and reproduce them in real time inside a virtual environment. Often, these devices are asked to support video-calling—that is, displaying “real-world” video inside a simulated environment—or to reproduce the screen of a “real-world” device, such as a PC or iPhone, inside the virtual environment. Consoles, of course, are asked to do none of this. Instead, these devices can focus their relatively abundant computing power on “graphics.”

Then there are the graphical requirements of HMDs themselves. Due to their higher resolution, HMDs must render at least 11 and as many as 22 times as many pixels per second as the Nintendo Switch and up to 4 times as many as modern PlayStations and Xboxes. Yet the number of pixels is only half of the equation. The other half is how frequently they are updated. Most video games target 60 frames per second (technically, a 60 Hz display). Some titles will support 120 fps or more, though this typically means reducing the resolution in exchange. So *Fortnite* supports 4K in 60 fps, but if a player wants 120 fps (which helps with competitive play), the resolution drops to 1440p. On the Nintendo Switch, a relatively low-powered device, *Fortnite* maxes out at 30 fps. Games with particularly complex simulations are sometimes capped at 30 fps even on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S|X.

To avoid nausea, there is broad consensus that an XR headset must refresh at 120 fps, if not more.^([32](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr32)) This minimum threshold primarily stems from the movement of a user’s head and body as an input, which both activates the user’s inner ear (where balance is regulated) and makes the lag between action and response perceptible. But by increasing frames per second from 60 to 120 or 240, the total number of pixels that must be rendered by an HMD versus modern video game consoles grows by another two to four times—a massive burden on scarce battery life and computing power. The need to produce frames every 8 or even 4 milliseconds also reveals again the impracticality of cloud-based rendering, at least under today’s networking standards; even 20 ms of latency—a level that isn’t even discernible to six out of seven expert gamers—would result in three to five outdated frames.

Passthrough experiences face an additional computational challenge: the need to create the video that is passed through. Though it’s common for an HMD user to assume they are just staring through their device’s front-facing cameras, these video feeds must first be algorithmically assembled, adjusted, and corrected to account for the fact that these cameras are set tens of millimeters in front of the user’s eyes (a placement the brain struggles to appreciate) and often below or to the side, too (an even stranger placement that also results in light entering an artificial lens at an unfamiliar angle). The device must also work to remove visual artifacts and distortions caused by dirt or dust in front of a lens, “lens flare” from bright light directly in front of the camera, and sudden changes in brightness. And all of this must happen within milliseconds—ideally 20, if not fewer—otherwise users are likely to experience nausea and occasionally miss the real-world items they are trying to grab because their device is showing them frames that reflect where their eyes were, not where the brain knows they should now be.

### **The Hardest Technology Challenge of Our Time**

With a better understanding of what it takes to build a mass-market HMD, a few summarizing points can be made. First, HMDs face more technical trade-offs than almost any other kind of computing—there’s a weight budget and a heat budget, a minimum viable battery life and device price, the compute needed for pixels and that required to run software, and so on. In 2021, Mark Zuckerberg wrote that “the hardest technology challenge of our time may be fitting a supercomputer into the frame of normal-looking glasses.”^([33](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr33)) At the time, Zuckerberg’s forecast for widespread adoption of AR was already years behind schedule—and he would subsequently delay the release of the company’s first AR device at least three more. Second, the complexity and constraints facing these devices explain why the (exaggerated) criticism that, say, the graphics of the 2020 Quest 2 look like those of a 2007 Nintendo Wii, is actually a compliment—it’s a bit like saying that an adult ran 100 meters as fast as a 12-year-old, even though the adult was wearing a 50-pound backpack and solving math problems at the same time. Overall, “graphics” is a terribly unhelpful term in the first place because it refers to visuals rather than the simulation they reflect, let alone the other demands on a CPU’s or GPU’s finite power or the need to preserve battery life. Similarly, the aforementioned trade-offs mean that progress in these devices is not always obvious to users. A 10% reduction in weight or heat, a 10% improvement in battery life, a 10% improvement in eye tracking are all significant, yet hard for the average person to appreciate unless they use the device regularly and for extended periods of time.

The third takeaway is that extraordinary investments are likely required to simultaneously address the many competing requirements of an HMD. Since 2014, Facebook has spent tens of billions on HMD R&D, and though not all these investments are reflected in current devices (some R&D never pans out, and some succeeds on a technical basis but at too high a cost), the company’s Quest VR and passthrough MR line remain far from target specifications and its AR glasses have yet to ship. Indeed, producing a mass-market HMD might require altogether new innovations, rather than just improvements in existing technologies, such as battery life or pixel density—the fourth takeaway. According to Facebook’s CTO, Andrew Bosworth, and CK Kalinowski, who heads up Facebook’s AR glasses hardware, between four^([34](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr34)) and six^([35](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr35)) “new technology introductions” need “to be solved before we can even think about shipping,” including neural interfaces. Apple’s total investment in HMDs is not known, but in the seven and a half years from the time Vision Pro’s team was assembled^([36](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr36)) to the device’s 2023 unveiling, the company invested nearly $135 billion in R&D.^([37](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr37)) Tim Cook has also said the Vision Pro is the “most advanced personal electronics device ever,”^([38](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr38)) with Mike Rockwell, Apple’s head of AR/VR, boasting that over 5,000 patents were awarded during its development^([39](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr39)) (equivalent to 30% of all patents received by the company from 2016 through 2022).^([40](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr40)) In an interview with *GQ*, Cook explained why the device had taken so long to come to market and implicitly acknowledged its enormous cost, saying, “I’m not interested in putting together pieces of somebody else’s stuff. Because we want to control the primary technology. Because we know that’s how you innovate.”^([41](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr41)) This approach stands in contrast to the first several iPhones, which were almost entirely made up of components designed by independent suppliers and used by other smartphone makers. The first iPhone’s CPU came from Samsung, its GPU from Imagination Technologies, various image sensors from Micron Technologies, the touchscreen’s glass from Corning, and so on. Apple’s innovations were primarily in how these components were brought together, paired with remarkable ingenuity in the interface used to engage with them.

A fifth and final takeaway is evident in the HMD use cases that have seen the greatest adoption so far and those that have seen the least. General-purpose VR, AR, and MR HMDs such as Google Glass and companies such as Lenovo or HTC have been largely ignored by consumers and businesses. And while Facebook often advertises how a Quest headset might be used in offices and job sites, the device is primarily used to play video games—and here, “fun” is more important than technical sophistication, and passthrough MR is rarely used. Surgeons, meanwhile, can use far more powerful, heavier, heat-generating devices, as most components can be placed under an operating table or inside a nearby rack, with only a lightweight display and cameras worn on the face. Military users, too, can put an expanded battery, larger fan, and processor in their backpacks. These enterprise/industrial devices can also be more expensive as they are more likely to be shared, not individually owned, devices, and they support far more critical activities than an hour of spare time.

Even so, progress is observable. The original Oculus Rift, released in 2016, had a 90 fps 1K display with an 87-degree horizontal and 88-degree vertical field of view, weighed roughly 500 grams, had no cameras (making it VR-only and incapable of hand and eye tracking), required the user to plug into a PC in order to use its computing power and receive power, and cost $600.^([42](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr42)) The 2023 Quest 3 (which followed the 2019 Quest, 2020 Quest 2, 2022 Quest Pro) has a 120 fps 4K display with a 97-degree horizontal and 93-degree vertical field of view, weighs the same as the Oculus Rift, has four outward cameras (enabling color passthrough and hand tracking), does not require the use of a PC (battery life is two to three hours), and costs $500 (a 17% decrease compared to the Rift, despite 28% compounded inflation since 2016).^([43](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr43)) The facial profile of the Quest 3 was more than a third smaller than that of the Rift. Although the Quest 3’s passthrough mode is capable of boundary protection—identifying whether the user is straying too far from their specified position—it isn’t capable of mixed-reality experiences, such as placing a virtual TV on a real-world wall or understanding the world around it. The Quest 3 also faces severe concurrent user constraints, as evidenced by the battle royale genre. Whereas high-end consoles and gaming PCs can support 150 or more CCUs in nearly photoreal 5–8 km² maps (e.g., *Call of Duty: Warzone*), mid-range consoles and gaming PCs and higher-end mobile phones and tablets run up to 100 CCUs on relatively high-fidelity 2–3 km² maps (*Fortnite*), and lower-end smartphones are limited to 50 CCUs with low-end graphics on 2–3 km² maps, the Quest 2 and Quest 3 appear capped at about 24 CCUs (the Facebook-owned *Population: One*) even when the visuals look akin to a game running on a 2006 PlayStation 3 and the map is but 1 km².

As the Vision Pro is Apple’s first HMD, it’s not possible to compare it to earlier models. Nevertheless, it demonstrates the partial closure of the gap between the devices that are currently possible and the combined specifications needed for mainstream adoption and frequent use.

Facebook’s 2022 Quest Pro

![The first edition of Facebook’s Quest Pro mixed-reality headset was released in 2022. Pictured here is an internal test unit that was built with a transparent shell that reveals its components and construction. ¶ Meta Platforms](OEBPS/images/pg236.jpg)

The first edition of Facebook’s Quest Pro mixed-reality headset was released in 2022. Pictured here is an internal test unit that was built with a transparent shell that reveals its components and construction. ¶ Meta Platforms

The Vision Pro’s resolution meets the lower band of target specifications, running 8K combined (i.e., each eye has a display that is over 4K),^([‡](#chapter9.xhtml#footnote-017)) though the frame rate is limited to 100 fps overall, with most interactive experiences capped at 90 fps.^([44](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr44)) The device achieves passthrough reproduction in 12 ms, which compares to a typical performance range of about 38–50 for both the Quest Pro and Quest 3,^([45](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr45)) but still results in a 1–2 frames lag for the user—enough that “the illusion of true pass-through is broken” whenever the user moves their body or head, according to Apple expert John Gruber.^([46](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr46)) With an approximately 97-degree horizontal and 74-degree vertical field of view, the Apple Vision Pro falls short of contemporary devices, such Facebook’s Quest 2, Quest 3, and Quest Pro devices (97–110 degrees horizontal and 93–96 degrees vertical).^([47](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr47)) Some reviewers likened the Vision Pro’s relatively limited FOV to looking through binoculars with “fairly large black borders.”^([48](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr48)) Due to minor distortions, “vignetting,” and “color fringing” at the borders, The Verge also reported, “the usable field of view feel\[s\] even smaller.”^([49](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr49))

The Vision Pro’s 12 total cameras and two depth sensors support rich color passthrough, facial, eye, and hand tracking, and reliable boundary and obstacle detection. As with its display, most reviewers consider the Vision Pro’s sensors far more capable and reliable than those available on any other device available for consumers to purchase. However, passthrough cameras struggle to capture the full color of the world around them—and the display supports just under half of the colors the average human eye can see. The cameras also produce blurriness or inaccurate passthrough video tinting when capturing environments in low, high, or inconsistent light.^([50](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr50)) According to The Verge*,* Vision Pro’s OS “feels also designed for an eye tracking system that’s just slightly more precise than it actually is.”^([51](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr51)) The device’s external cameras and computer vision can accurately map the dimensions of a room and anchor virtual objects (e.g., a virtual screen against a living room wall), though it is unable to understand most of what it sees (i.e., identify an object or place it in context), let alone what it does or how the user might interact with it—core requirements for many industrial passthrough MR use cases, as well as for optical MR glasses.

The consumer costs of the Vision Pro’s advances are also evident and considerable. As discussed earlier in this chapter, the entry-level version of the device costs US$3,500 (in many countries, the sales tax on the device will exceed the price of a Quest device).^([§](#chapter9.xhtml#footnote-016)) Users who require corrective lenses will need to spend another $99–$149, and if the device is intended for multiple users, Apple recommends each user purchase their own $199 “Light Seal,” which comes in 28 different sizes and shapes, and “gently conforms to your face and helps deliver a precise fit while blocking out stray light.”^([52](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr52)) The user may also need a different version of the four “Light Seal Cushions,” which cost $29 each.^([53](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr53))

Depending on the head strap used, the Vision Pro also weighs between 600 and 650 grams, equivalent to 3.7 iPhone 15s and just 60 grams less than the largest and heaviest iPad Pro, the 12.9" sixth-generation iPad Pro, released in 2022. In contrast, Facebook’s Quest 3 is 515 grams, while the Quest Pro, Facebook’s highest-end HMD at the time of the Vision Pro’s debut, is 722 grams. And while Facebook’s headsets have an integrated battery, the Vision Pro requires the wearer to physically connect to a separate, pacemaker-like battery that is roughly as thick as two iPhones and weighs twice as much as well (or 350 grams) or stay plugged into an electrical outlet. Though the Quest Pro headset is 100 grams (0.22 lbs.) heavier than the Vision Pro headset, many reviewers have reported that the Quest Pro feels lighter (or at least more comfortable). This perception stems from Facebook’s decision to place the Quest Pro’s battery inside the back of the device’s headband. As such, the Quest Pro is more balanced than the Vision Pro, with its weight more centered on the wearer’s spine, rather than pulling their head downward.

Apple’s decision to use an external, rather than integrated, power source for the Vision Pro was reportedly controversial within the company,^([54](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr54)) but it was no doubt required to power the device’s brightly illuminated high-resolution screens and robust processors and sensors, and to avoid overheating the user’s face. Even though the Vision Pro’s battery is 39.5 watt hours versus the Quest 3’s 18.88 and Quest Pro’s 20.58, the Vision Pro supports up to 2 hours of general use and 2.5 hours of video playback—less than Facebook’s HMDs.^([55](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr55)) After the Vision Pro was unveiled, Zuckerberg told employees in a company-wide meeting, “From what I’ve seen initially, I’d say the good news is that there’s no kind of magical solutions that they have to any of the constraints on laws of physics that our teams haven’t already explored and thought of.”^([56](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr56))

As one might expect, mainstream optical AR devices are even further from release in 2024. Snap’s Spectacles 4, released in 2021, cost only $500, weighed 134 grams, and resembled boxy, somewhat stylish sunglasses. The device also augmented less than 10% of the wearer’s FOV and on a barely 0.5K display that supported 30–120 fps depending on simulation complexity, could not scan, much less understand, what it saw, lacked both eye and hand tracking, and had a battery that lasted no more than 30 minutes.^([57](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr57)) Microsoft’s 2019 HoloLens 2 cost $3,500 and weighed over 550 grams (making it a headset, not glasses), but augmented only 20% of a wearer’s FOV on a 2K display at a max of 60 fps and had limited environmental scanning functionality, though it was capable of both eye and hand tracking.^([58](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr58))

Apple’s May 2008 Patent Filing, “Head Mounted Display”

### **The Future of HMDs**

In 2022, Tim Sweeney, who in 2016 imagined that Oakley-sized supercomputers would be possible by 2023, told The Verge, “Well, I think that augmented reality is the platform of the future. But it’s very clear from the efforts of Magic Leap and others that we need not just new technology but, to some extent, new science in order to build an augmented reality platform that’s a substitute for smartphones. And it’s not clear to me whether that’s coming in 10 years or in 30 years. I hope we’ll see it in my lifetime, but I’m actually not sure about that.”^([67](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr67)) This uncertainty is reflected in the go-to-market strategies and products of big tech.

Amazon, Apple, Facebook, Google, and Microsoft have all entered the market at different times (2014 for Google Glass, 2024 for Vision Pro), with different starting products (optical AR for Google, VR for Facebook, audio-only glasses for Amazon, optical MR for Microsoft, passthrough MR for Apple), different prices (from $250 for the Echo Frames to $3,500 for the Vision Pro), and prioritization of different customers (Facebook targets everyone; Microsoft, enterprise users; Apple, high-end households and designers).

There are also fundamental differences in what each company believes to be the “minimum viable product” in a given category. With the Vision Pro, Apple opted to add an externally facing multicolor display that would show a reproduction of the user’s face and eyes (“EyeSight”). This decision substantially increases the device’s costs, battery usage, heat generation, and computational needs, while also forcing front-facing cameras to the side rather than center front of the device, which makes accurate passthrough video harder to produce and even more demanding on computing resources.^([¶](#chapter9.xhtml#footnote-015)) Apple insists that the feature is needed to avoid social alienation and for the device to be embraced in semipublic environments such as the office. Facebook obviously does not share this view. Apple also believes that an externally tethered battery pack is an acceptable trade-off for more power, despite the aesthetic implications and potential challenges and even dangers that come with wires, whereas Facebook again disagrees (Apple’s longtime chief design officer, Sir Jony Ive, who led or co-led the design of the Apple Newton, the iPod, the iPhone, the iPad, and the Apple Watch, apparently agrees with Facebook on this issue).^([#](#chapter9.xhtml#footnote-014)) With its first HMD, Apple also decided to add a small external wheel (not unlike the “crown” on an Apple Watch) that enables users to instantly shift to (or phase in to) passthrough mode even when they are inside a purely VR-based experience. Such a component has never appeared on a Facebook device, which instead activates passthrough mode based on hand gestures or button presses, but Apple believes it essential to users’ feeling comfortable in their headset.

The Vision Pro boasts 12 cameras that varyingly support face, eye, and hand tracking, while the Quest Pro has 5 total cameras for face, eye, and hand tracking, and the Quest 3 has only 4 cameras, all dedicated to hand tracking. The Vision Pro’s larger and higher-quality fleet of cameras reflects Apple’s belief that HMDs should not require handheld controllers for non-specialized use cases (such as graphic design, data entry, etc.). In fact, Apple does not even produce such controllers, whereas Facebook’s HMDs ship with and require the use of Quest controllers. But as a result, the Vision Pro must be capable of precise and reliable eye- and hand-based inputs. The Vision Pro’s external cameras can also be used to scan a user’s face to help generate a photorealistic 3D avatar (or “persona,” in Apple’s terms). In contrast, Facebook’s avatars are created through an avatar maker and offer a more cartoonish aesthetic, rather than aspiring to realism.

Apple has even departed from its customary approach to product rollout, too, as the release of the Vision Pro will be the first time Apple has ever debuted a “Pro” model before offering a standard edition. The first Plus or Pro model iPhone launched seven years after the first standard-issue iPhone and a year after Apple introduced a low-end model. The iPad Pro came five years after the first iPad and three after the low-cost iPad Mini, while the Apple Watch Ultra was seven years after the first and two after the Apple Watch SE. The AirPod Pros came two years after the AirPods, with the AirPods Max debuting after three. Apple’s inverted approach to the Vision HMD doubtless reflects its belief that, in 2024, releasing a more affordable model would require so many concessions that the device would not be worth selling. Facebook, which continues to sell its 2020 Quest 2 for $300, clearly disagrees.

The disagreements regarding the “best” way to build an HMD computing platform is an echo of the early stages of the mobile era. Early leaders, such as Microsoft, with its Windows Mobile OS and the supporting manufacturing ecosystem, and Research in Motion’s BlackBerry, believed that the winning smartphone must have a battery that lasted for days, rather than one that supported only a few hours of use; that wireless data usage should be minimal, not used in abundance; that a smartphone would be the average person’s secondary computer, not their primary computer; that a physical keyboard was essential and a touchscreen optional at best; that the market would be led by business customers, not ordinary consumers; that the price had to be $200 or less, not $500 or more; that the device needed to be able to survive frequent drops (and especially not crack on its first), and so on. Apple took the other side of all of these bets. And while Apple was originally opposed to third-party apps on the iPhone,^([68](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr68)) the company reversed course within a year and, the year after that, released its famous “There’s an App for That” campaign to help sell the device. Apple’s legacy competitors, such as BlackBerry, had long supported apps but never imagined there might be thousands, let alone millions, of app developers for its device, and prioritized device security so greatly that developers needed notarized documents just to receive the application-development kit.

Apple’s unusual bets continued into its interface choices. Take the original iPhone’s most iconic design element—its home button. Although Jobs showed little interest in physical keyboards, he nevertheless decided to place a large home button on the front of the iPhone—taking up space that might otherwise have been used for a larger screen, a longer-lasting battery, or a more powerful processor. Jobs saw it as an essential part of introducing consumers to both touchscreens and pocket-sized computing. Not unlike closing a flip phone, a user knew that no matter what was happening on their iPhone’s touchscreen, pressing the home button would always take them back to the main screen.

In 2011, four years after it released the first iPhone, Apple added a new feature to its operating system: multitasking. Before this point, users could operate only a few predetermined applications at the same time. It was possible to listen to music through the iPod app while reading the *New York Times* app, but if the user then opened up their Facebook app, the *Times* app would close. If the user wanted to return to a given article in the *Times* app, they’d have to reopen the app, then navigate back to the article and scroll back down to where they left off. Doing so would mean exiting the Facebook app, too. Multitasking now allowed users to effectively “pause” an app while switching to another, all of which was managed by the home button. If a user clicked the home button, the app would be paused, and they’d return to the home screen. If they double-clicked, the app would still be paused, and the user would then be able to swipe through a tray of all paused apps.

The first few iPhones could have supported multitasking. After all, other smartphones with similar CPUs supported the feature. Taking the long view, Apple believed that it needed to ease users into the mobile computing era, and this meant focusing not just on which technology was possible but on when users were ready for it. To this end, it wasn’t until 2017, with the release of the tenth iPhone, that Apple felt comfortable removing a physical home button and requiring users to “swipe up” from the bottom of the screen instead.

There are no “best practices” in any newly established device category. In fact, many of the choices considered obvious today were once controversial—not just the iPhone’s touchscreen. Indeed, some early Android builds and apps used Apple’s pinch-to-zoom concept but believed it was backward—if a user is bringing their fingers closer together, shouldn’t whatever they’re looking at come closer, not move further out? It’s almost impossible to imagine this logic today, but that’s partly because billions of people have undergone 15 years of training in the opposite logic.

What might the future of HMDs have in store? A particular area of focus is minimizing the incidence of eyestrain. Increases in resolution and frame rate will help address this issue, as will reductions in heat. A more intractable issue relates to the very nature of HMDs. Human eyes “verge” as they look at objects nearer or farther away—that is, they move in opposite directions inward (looking at the tip of one’s nose) or outward (the horizon line). These movements automatically trigger the “accommodation reflex,” in which a person’s lens shape and pupil accommodate in order to establish focus (which also places non-focal objects and environments out of focus). When wearing an HMD, users often experience “vergence-accommodation conflict” (VAC) as their eyes converge and diverge to look at parts of a virtual world that are of varying distance but always in focus, which strains the accommodation reflex and leads to blurriness. The impact of VAC increases the longer an HMD is in continuous use. VAC is far less common when playing a video game on a monitor or TV screen, as the distance between the user and their display provides reference distances that stabilize the accommodation reflex and both the background and foreground of the virtual world are relatively closer to each other and therefore require less vergence.

To better address HMD VAC, Facebook unveiled a prototype in 2023, the Butterscotch Varifocal, which tracks a user’s eyes to determine where on a screen they’re looking, then uses mechanical actuators to move the screen forward or back. This movement, complemented by software that blurs the parts of a rendered scene proportionate to their distance from the user’s focal plane, reportedly reduces VAC-related weariness.^([69](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr69)) As is always the case, these additions have costs. Most obviously, the Butterscotch Varifocal’s actuators and rails add bulk and weight to the device, and increase battery usage. The HMD must also support rich eye tracking, which requires not just more cameras but cameras that are placed behind the device’s lenses (not on the periphery), which means many users will need to order prescription lenses.

Another emergent solution used by Facebook’s Quest Pro and Apple’s Vision Pro is “foveated rendering,” which takes advantage of the fact that human eyesight is sharpest at the center and blurriest at the periphery. By tracking the user’s eye, it’s possible for a headset to concentrate its computing power where the user is looking and reduce fidelity elsewhere. An 8K–16K display is still needed, as the user’s eyes might be directed at any point on the screen, but 90% of the screen might be rendered in only 2K–4K at any given time, saving battery and computing power. This functionality also requires eye tracking and is therefore not supported on Facebook’s non-Pro HMDs, such as the Quest 3.

In 2023, Facebook unveiled another prototype, Flamera, that was designed to improve passthrough video quality and reduce the frequency of distortions by using “bug eyes” that split incoming light beams into 106 apertures before they reached the device’s two light sensors. According to the company, this segmentation approach reduced visual artifacts and produced a more accurate passthrough video feed.^([70](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr70))

### **Beyond Headsets**

Alongside the many investments in immersive headsets are countless other efforts to produce new Metaverse-focused hardware that will complement primary computing devices, rather than substitute for them, as some imagine AR and VR devices might one day.

Most commonly, gamers imagine wearing smart gloves and even bodysuits that can provide physical or “haptic” feedback to simulate what’s happening to their avatar in a virtual world. Many such devices exist today, but they’re so costly and functionally limited that they are typically used for industrial purposes. Specifically, these wearables use a network of motors and electroactive actuators that inflate tiny air pockets which apply pressure on their owner’s skin or limit their ability to move.

Haptic vibration technology has advanced considerably since Nintendo introduced the Rumble Pak for the Nintendo 64 in 1997. A PlayStation 5 controller’s triggers can be programmed with context-specific resistance—a shotgun, sniper rifle, and crossbow will all feel different to “pull.” The crossbow might even fight back, with the user struggling to hold it down and sensing the vibrations of a virtual bowstring.

Another class of haptic interface devices emit ultrasonic sound (that is, mechanical energy waves beyond the audible range for humans) from a grid of microelectromechanical systems (MEMS), producing what a user might describe as a “force field” in the air in front of them. The force field produced by these devices, which looks a bit like a short, perforated tin box, is typically less than six or eight inches tall and wide, but its nuance tends to surprise. Test subjects claim to be able to sense everything from a plush teddy bear to a bowling ball and the shape of a sandcastle as it crumbles, aided in part by the fact that fingertips contain more nerve endings than almost any other part of the body. Crucially, MEMS devices can also detect the user’s interaction, enabling its sound-based teddy bears to respond to the user’s air-based touch, or the castle to crumble if it’s touched.

Gloves and bodysuits can also be used to capture a user’s motion data, rather than just relay feedback, thereby allowing the wearer’s body and gestures to be reproduced in a virtual environment in real time. This information can also be captured using tracking cameras. The problem is, such cameras require unobstructed views and relative proximity to the user, and they are prone to struggle if required to track more than a single user in rich detail. Many users—families, for instance—will want multiple tracking cameras in their “Metaverse rooms” and might add a few smart wearables to their wrists or ankles.

Such bands may seem clumsy—how could a bracelet or anklet substitute for a high-definition camera watching every finger?—but the current technology is in fact impressive. The sensors in an Apple Watch, remarkably, can distinguish between a user clenching or releasing their fist, or pinching one finger versus two fingers to their thumb, and the watch owner can use these movements to interact with the Apple Watch (and potentially other devices) without ever needing to touch or even look at them. In addition, people wearing the device can use the clenching motion to place a cursor on the watch face, then use the orientation of their hand to move it. The software involved, Apple’s AssistiveTouch, works using mostly standard sensors, including an electric heart monitor, a gyroscope, and an accelerometer. Other approaches promise even greater capabilities. Facebook’s most expensive acquisition since Oculus VR in 2014 was CTRL-labs, a neural interface start-up that produces armbands that record electrical activity from skeletal muscles (a technique called electromyography). Although the CTRL-labs devices are worn more than six inches away from the wrist and even farther away from the fingers, the CTRL-labs software enables minute gestures to be reproduced inside virtual worlds; individual fingers can be raised to count, point, or gesture to “come hither,” and pinches involving different combinations of fingers can accomplish various microtasks. Importantly, electromyographic signals on the CTRL-labs devices can go beyond reproducing human appendages. A famous CTRL-labs demo involves a user—in this case, an employee—mapping their fingers to a crab-like robot and then walking it forward, back, and side to side by flexing their fist and moving their fingers.^([71](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr71))

Facebook’s CTRL-labs Electromyography Bracelet

![On the right-hand side of this 2021 demo, it’s possible to see the stream of electromyographic signals that are captured by the CTRL-labs device and then used to precisely reproduce the position and actions of the wearer’s hands and fingers. In contrast to traditional motion-capture techniques, there is no need for a tracking camera or motion sensors. Meta Platforms](OEBPS/images/pg249.jpg)

On the right-hand side of this 2021 demo, it’s possible to see the stream of electromyographic signals that are captured by the CTRL-labs device and then used to precisely reproduce the position and actions of the wearer’s hands and fingers. In contrast to traditional motion-capture techniques, there is no need for a tracking camera or motion sensors. Meta Platforms

Facebook is also planning its own line of smartwatches. But unlike Apple, Facebook doesn’t see the device as secondary to, or dependent upon, a smartphone. Instead, Facebook’s watch is intended to have its own wireless data plan and include two cameras, both of which are detachable and intended to be integrated into third-party items, such as a backpack or a hat. Meanwhile, Google’s fifth-largest acquisition ever was the smart wearables company Fitbit in early 2021.

Wearables will shrink in size and increase in performance, and as their technologies improve, they will be integrated into everyday clothes. These developments will help users enhance their interactions with the Metaverse and enable them to interact with it in more places. Carrying a controller everywhere is not practical, and if the primary goal of AR is to make technology disappear into an everyday pair of glasses, then pulling out a thumb-stick or a smartphone to use it would defeat the purpose.

Although patent applications are an unreliable predictor of the future, a pair of December 2022 filings published by the US Patent and Trademark Office showed that Apple was working on a wearable smart ring capable of “self-mixing interferometry.” The field of interferometry uses interference of intersecting light rays to detect changes in the state of an object or environment. Apple imagined a ring with inward-facing sensors (and potentially a light emitter) that could be used to sense the wearer’s “physiological condition” by “\[detecting\] and/or \[monitoring\] … heart rates, blood oxygen saturation, blood pressure, sleep cycles, body temperatures” and/or “detect force and/or touch inputs, whether static or motions, speed, direction, force, displacement or other parameters of gestures.”^([72](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr72)) The second filing imagines such a ring being used to help “variously sense the presence of objects, distances to objects or proximities of objects, movements of objects (e.g., whether objects are moving, or the speed, acceleration, or direction of movement of objects) and so on” for AR, VR, and MR applications.^([73](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr73))

A Patent for a Potential Apple Smart Ring

![Sketches from one of Apple’s 2022 Self-Mixing Interferometry Ring patent applications. ¶ US Patent and Trademark Office, Apple](OEBPS/images/pg251.jpg)

Sketches from one of Apple’s 2022 Self-Mixing Interferometry Ring patent applications. ¶ US Patent and Trademark Office, Apple

Some believe that the future of computing isn’t a pair of AR glasses or a watch but something much smaller. In 2014, only a year after its ill-fated Google Glass launch, Google announced its first Google Contact Lens project, which was intended to help diabetics monitor their glucose levels. Specifically, this “device” was made up of two soft lenses, with a wireless chip, a wireless antenna that’s thinner than a strand of human hair, and a glucose sensor placed in between. A pinhole between the underlying lens and the wearer’s eyes enabled tear fluid to reach the sensor, which measured blood sugar levels. The wireless antenna drew power from the wearer’s smartphone, which was intended to support at least one reading per second. Google also planned to add a small LED light that could warn users of spikes or drops in blood sugar levels in real time.^([74](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr74))

Google discontinued its diabetes smart lens program four years after it was launched, but the company claimed that the cancellation stemmed from “insufficient consistency in our measurements of the correlation between tear glucose and blood glucose concentration,”^([75](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr75)) which had been widely noted by researchers in the medical community. Regardless, patent filings show that the major Western, Southeast Asian, and other Eastern technology companies continue to invest in smart lens technology.

Fanciful though such technologies might seem in a world in which internet connections remain unstable and computing power scarce, they nevertheless feel within reach compared to so-called brain-to-computer interfaces (BCIs), which have been in development since the 1970s and continue to attract greater investment. Many purported BCI solutions are noninvasive—think of Professor X’s helmet in *X-Men*, or perhaps a grid of wired sensors hidden underneath the wearer’s hair. Other BCIs are partially invasive or fully invasive, depending on how close the electrodes are placed to brain tissue.

In 2015, Elon Musk founded Neuralink, of which he remains CEO, and announced that the company was working on a “sewing machine–like” device that could implant sensors that are four to six micrometers thick (roughly 0.000039 inches, or one-tenth the width of human hair) in the human brain.^([76](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr76)) In April 2021, the company released a video in which a monkey played the game *Pong* using a wireless Neuralink implant. Only three months later, Facebook announced that it was no longer investing in its own BCI program. In prior years, it had funded several projects inside and outside the company, including a test at the University of California, San Francisco, that involved wearing a helmet that shot light particles through the skull, then measured blood oxygenation levels in groups of brain cells. A blog post on the subject explained that “while measuring oxygenation may never allow us to decode imagined sentences, being able to recognize even a handful of imagined commands, like ‘home,’ ‘select,’ and ‘delete,’ would provide entirely new ways of interacting with today’s VR systems—and tomorrow’s AR glasses.”^([77](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr77)) Another Facebook BCI test involved a physical mesh of electrodes placed on top of the user’s skull, which enabled the subject to write at a speed of roughly 15 words per minute purely through thought (the average person types 39 words per minute, two and a half times faster). Facebook reported that “while we still believe in the long-term potential of head-mounted optical \[brain-computer interface\] technologies, we’ve decided to focus our immediate efforts on a different neural interface approach that has a nearer-term path to market for AR/VR,”^([78](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr78)) and that “a head-mounted optical silent speech device is still a very long way out. Possibly longer than we would have foreseen.”^([79](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr79))

The “differential neural interface approach” that Facebook referenced is likely CTRL-labs, which offers several comparative benefits including lower costs, easier upgrades, replacements and repairs, less operational risk, and, well, clearer ethics than BCI devices (especially those which are surgically implanted on a permanent basis). Still, BCI is expected to offer functionality that no other device type or sensors could reliably provide and which could transform not just interaction with virtual worlds, but the quality of human existence. For this reason, the most likely adopters of neural implants—at least early on—are those with severe physical disabilities. In May 2023, Neuralink received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration to perform its first (live) human trial and by the end of the year, the company was recruiting surgical candidates with “quadriplegia due to cervical spinal cord injury or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).”^([80](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr80)) On January 29, 2024, Musk announced that a robot had implanted Neuralink’s BCI technology into the portion of a patient’s brain that controlled the “intention to move,” and that a day later, the patient was “recovering well” and “initial results show promising neuron spike detection.”^([81](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr81)) Three weeks later, Musk reported that “progress is good, and the patient seems to have made a full recovery, with no ill effects that we are aware of. Patient is able to move a mouse around the screen by just thinking.”^([82](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr82)) In March, 2024, the patient, identified as 29-year-old Noland Arbaugh, began to speak publicly about his experience as a “cyborg” and “neuralnaut,” as well as his newfound capabilities.^([83](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr83)) “It makes—this is going to sound really kind of crazy—but it makes being paralyzed really not that bad,” Arbaugh reported in Neuralink townhall that was released by the company. “Anything that makes me more independent I’m all for and this is probably going to make people like me the most independent that they might ever be until it all gets cured—and I think that’s a very real possibility.”^([84](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr84)) Neuralink and Arbaugh also shared several videos show his ability to successfully play turn-based strategy games such as *Civilization VI* and even-fast moving competitive multiplayer titles such as *Mario Kart*, using only his thoughts.^([85](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr85))

Alongside the new devices that will be used to interact with the Metaverse are those that will help generate it. Leica Geosystems, a descendent of the storied camera manufacturer, now sells $30,000–$60,000 photogrammetric 3D cameras (and camera-equipped drones) that can capture hundreds of thousands and even millions of “laser scan set points per second” that are designed to capture the entire interiors of buildings such as malls and family homes, or office parks, with greater clarity and detail than the average person would ever see if they were physically on-site.^([86](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr86)) The satellite-imaging company Planet Labs, mentioned in [Chapter 7](#chapter7.xhtml), performs scans of nearly the entire earth daily across eight spectral bands, enabling not just high-resolution imagery but details including heat, biomass, and haze. To produce this imagery, it operates the third-largest private fleet of satellites of any company in the world, with over 200, many of which weigh less than 5 kilograms and are smaller than 10 × 10 × 30 centimeters.^([87](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr87)) Every photo from these satellites covers 20–25 square kilometers and is made up of 47 megapixels, with each pixel representing 3 × 3 meters. Roughly 1.5 GB of data is sent from each of these satellites per second and from an average distance of 1,000 kilometers. Will Marshall, the CEO and co-founder of Planet Labs, believes that the cost per performance of these satellites has improved a thousandfold since 2011.^([88](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr88)) Such scanning devices make it easier and cheaper for companies to produce high-quality “mirror worlds” or “digital twins” of physical spaces—and to use scans of the real world to produce higher-quality and less expensive fantasy worlds.

Also important are depth-sensing cameras that can track the precise movement of individual customers, equipment, and objects in real time and produce them inside a digital twin (more on this in [Chapter 12](#chapter12.xhtml)). Without such device, a digital twin is largely “fixed” in time or otherwise limited to information generated through location sensors (e.g., pressure sensors, UWB transmitters, NFC chips). Technologies such as Google’s Starline, as detailed in [Chapter 3](#chapter3.xhtml), also allow remote workers to be simultaneously “present” in the store (potentially from an offshore “Metaverse call center”), jumping across different screens to help the customer.

A final technology, which has seen limited deployment outside of immersive art installations thus far but also seems poised for popularity later this decade, is XR projectors. These devices are intended to transform any surface or collection of surfaces into fully rendered touchscreens—irrespective of how uneven or partially obstructed the surface might be, or its originally intended purpose. To do so, these projectors use various depth sensors to understand the dimensions of the surface they are projecting onto, and then use an onboard computer processor to alter the pixels that are being cast onto that surface so that the combined projection appears cohesive and undistorted. Depth sensors are also used to determine what parts of the projection the user is pointing to or touching, and to convert these gestures into inputs (traditional touch displays have onboard sensors to literally feel the user’s movements). As users often obscure part of a projection while attempting to use it, a network of XR projectors is typically needed to operate larger displays.

There are many potential applications and uses for XR projectors, spanning games, productivity, education, and engineering. For example, they can turn an entire wall into a chess board or iPad homescreen, or a kitchen table into a keyboard and trackpad, can transform a blank plastic (though potentially mechanized) mannequin into a fully clothed, animated, and seemingly sense-capable character, or highlight the real-time operations, weather, and topography of a physical 3D model of a city (as per Strategic Development Partners’ Water Street development). In November 2023, Reuters reported that Amazon was preparing a major push into the XR projector field, having bought projection mapping hardware start-up Lightform two years earlier, with Lightform’s co-founder and CEO, Brett Jones, becoming a head of product in Amazon’s devices group.^([89](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr89)) According to a job posting made by Jones earlier in the year, his group was looking for design technologists with “experience designing 3D spatial interactions for AR/VR or games using tools like Unity, Unreal Engine, etc.”^([90](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr90))

In January 2024, Disney publicly unveiled its HoloTile technology, which the gaming website Kotaku described as a computer-powered “omnidirectional treadmill-like floor” made up of a “layer of small, circular roller \[tiles\] that can shift and rotate as people walk on them.”^([91](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr91)) The purpose of HoloTiles is to enable users to “run, walk, and even dance” while remaining in the same position (give or take an inch or two), thereby offering users the ability to more fully immerse their bodies inside a virtual environment without needing to be physically present inside an enormous (and likely padded) room.^([92](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr92)) According to Disney, HoloTile can be used by multiple people at the same time and can be programmed to directly move the user (thus prompting a response) or alter the level of resistance (e.g., simulating thick muck or slick floors).^([93](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr93))

### **Long Live the Smartphone**

It’s fun to imagine all the brilliant new devices that soon enough will allow humanity to “jack into the Metaverse.” But, at least through the end of the 2020s, it’s likely that most devices for the Metaverse era will be updated versions of the same devices used in 2024 (and 2014). Most experts, including Unity Technologies CEO John Riccitiello, estimate that by 2030, there will be fewer than 250 million VR and AR headsets in use.^([94](#notes_split_009.xhtml#ch9fr94)) Of course, betting on such long-term prognostications is dangerous. The first iPhone was released in 2007, eight years after the first BlackBerry smartphone and at a point when smartphone penetration was less than 5% in the United States. Eight years later, the iPhone had sold more than 800 million units and driven US penetration to nearly 80%. Few in 2007 believed that by 2020, two-thirds of everyone on earth would have a smartphone.

AR and VR devices face not just significant technical, financial, and experiential obstacles but also the need to squeeze in. Behind the rapid growth of smartphones was a simple pair of facts: the personal computer was one of the most significant inventions in human history, and more than 30 years after it was invented, fewer than one in six people worldwide owned one. And those lucky few who did? Well, their computers were large and all but immovable. AR and VR devices will not be a person’s first computing device, nor even their first portable one. They are fighting to be a person’s third, fourth, fifth—and for a long time yet will probably be one of their least powerful, too.

While AR and VR may come to replace most of the devices in use today, that time is unlikely to be soon. Even if the combined number of VR and AR headsets (two very different device types) in use by 2030 tops one billion, four times the aforementioned forecast, they would still reach fewer than one in six smartphone users. And that’s okay. There are, in 2024, hundreds of millions of people spending hours each day inside real-time-rendered virtual worlds through smartphones and tablets. These devices are also rapidly improving—and not just in their computational power. Modern smartphones are packed with infrared sensors and lidar scanners, ultra-wideband and near-field communication chips, larger screens, more cameras, higher resolutions despite faster frame rates, and longer-lasting batteries.

Some believe that the future role of the smartphone includes serving as a user’s “edge computer” or “edge server,” providing connectivity and computation to the world around us. Versions of this model already exist: most of the Apple Watches sold today lack a cellular network chip and instead connect to their owner’s iPhone via Bluetooth. The approach has limitations: the Apple Watch cannot make a phone call when taken too far away from its tethered iPhone, nor play music to a wearer’s AirPods, download new apps, retrieve messages not already stored on the watch, and so on. But in exchange, the device is much cheaper, lighter, and less battery intensive—all because the user’s iPhone, a far more powerful device and one with greater cost per performance, is doing most of the work.

Given the shortage, cost, and importance of compute, it makes sense to focus on a single device’s capabilities, rather than invest in scores of others, especially when those devices have greater physical, thermal, and cost limitations. A computer worn on the wrist or face simply cannot contend with one in the pocket, just as that one cannot contend with one stored on a desk or under a TV stand. This logic applies to more than just compute. If Facebook wants users to wear a CTRL-labs band on each limb, why load each one with its own cellular and Wi-Fi network chips, if cheaper, less energy-intensive, and smaller Bluetooth chips are available that can send data to a nearby smartphone? Personal data may be the most important consideration. Though there are risks to concentrating information on a single device, such an approach may be preferred to a model where it’s shared across a wide network of devices, not all of which a user considers equally trustworthy. For these reasons, it’s likely that the first optical AR/MR glasses to go mainstream—whatever decade they materialize—will be possible only because they run on a device that long, long preceded it.

### **Hardware as the Gateway**

The many devices required and expected to support the Metaverse can be grouped into three categories. The first consists of “primary computing devices,” which for most consumers are smartphones but might someday be an immersive HMD. The next category is “secondary” or “supporting” computing devices, such as a PC or PlayStation or, for the foreseeable future, HMDs. Secondary devices may or may not rely on a primary device or be complemented by one, but they will be used less frequently than a main device and for more specific purposes. Last are tertiary devices, such as a smartwatch or tracking camera, which enrich or extend a Metaverse experience but will rarely operate it directly.

Improvements in each category will increase engagement and revenues in the Metaverse—and offer manufacturers an opportunity to generate a new business line. However, the massive investment in these devices—many of which are years from mainstream viability—has broader motivations.

The Metaverse is a mostly intangible experience: a persistent network of virtual worlds, data, and supporting systems. At the same time, physical devices are the gateway to accessing and creating the Metaverse. Without them there is no forest to be known, heard, smelled, touched, or seen. This fact provides the device manufacturers and operators with significant soft and hard power. The manufacturers and operators will determine what GPUs and CPUs are used, the wireless chipsets and standards deployed, the sensors included, and so on. Critical though these intermediary technologies are to a given experience, they rarely interface directly with a developer or end user. Instead, they’re accessed through an operating system, which manages how, when, and why the capabilities are used by a developer, what sorts of experiences they’re allowed to offer a user, and whether and to what extent a commission must be paid to the maker of said device. In other words, hardware is not just about what the Metaverse might offer and when; it is a fight to influence how it works and, ideally, to take a cut of as much of the resulting economic activity as possible. The more essential the device—and the more devices that connect to it—the greater the control afforded to the company that makes it.

[¶](#chapter9.xhtml#footnote-015-backlink) According to John Gruber, “EyeSight is not an ‘Oh my god, I can see your eyes!’ feature, but instead more of an ‘Oh, yes, now that you ask, I guess I can sort of see your eyes’ feature. Apple seemingly went to great lengths (and significant expense) to create the EyeSight feature, but so far I’ve found it to be of highly dubious utility, if only because it’s so subtle. It’s like wearing tinted goggles meant to obscure you, not clear goggles meant to show your eyes clearly” (John Gruber, “The Vision Pro,” Daring Fireball, January 30, 2024).
    
6.  [#](#chapter9.xhtml#footnote-014-backlink) At one point, Apple considered designing “stationary hubs” that could be used to wirelessly provide the Vision Pro with more computing power, but eventually opted for a wearable external battery pack and a less powerful processor contained exclusively inside the HMD (Mark Gurman, “Apple’s Secretive AR and VR Headset Plans Altered by Internal Differences,” Bloomberg, June 19, 2020).
    

## [Chapter 10 PAYMENT RAILS, PLATFORM PREFERENCES, AND PUBLIC POLICIES](#contents.xhtml#ch_10)

Most Metaverse fiction provides little detail of the economies of its synthetic realities, or the physical world in which these fantastical worlds exist. This is a reasonable choice. Though writers such as Neal Stephenson and William Gibson hope to provoke their readers, their primary ambition is to entertain, not educate. And with rare exception, their novels are also set in a version of the 20th- or 21st-century earth that has suffered some sort of economic collapse—making the odd fictional lesson of dubious applicability to a would-be “real Metaverse.” But if the “real Metaverse” is ever to generate the trillions in annual revenue that so many expect, its economic underpinnings are of crucial importance. They will define the nature of competition and the cost of doing business, and sometimes pick winners, shape business models, and decide what’s “fair” and which disruptions are even possible.

Many of these underpinnings are legal or regulatory. Others are by convention or culture. Some of the most powerful are known as “payment rails”—a technology that, like the internet, is composed of a complex series of systems and standards that are deployed across a wide and decentralized network, are largely automated, and support trillions of dollars in economic activity each week. These ecosystems are difficult to build and even harder to displace, but unlike the internet, they are typically privately owned. Visa, MasterCard, and Alipay are each among the 50 most valuable public companies in the world, with most of their peers being the likes of Google, Apple, Facebook, Amazon, and Microsoft, as well as financial conglomerates such as JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America, which hold trillions in deposits and manage the transfer of trillions more in financial instruments each day.

Unsurprisingly, there is already a fight to become the dominant “payment rail” in the Metaverse. What’s more, this fight is arguably the central battleground for the Metaverse and potentially its greatest impediment, too. To understand this dynamic, one needs to first understand how various payment rails operate today, their role in the modern gaming industry, their influence over the payment rails of the mobile computing era, and the ways mobile payment rails can and often are used to control emergent technologies and stifle competition ([Chapter 11](#chapter11.xhtml) will then discuss these points in the context of blockchains and cryptocurrencies).

### **The Major Payment Rails Today**

Over the past century, the number of distinct payment rails has grown because of new communication technologies, the increase in the number of transactions made per person per day, and the fact that most purchases are not in physical cash. From 2009 to 2022, cash’s share of US transactions fell from over 45%^([1](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr1)) to 18%.^([2](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr2))

The most common payment rails in the United States are Fedwire (formerly known as the Federal Reserve Wire Network), CHIPS (Clearing House Interbank Payment System), ACH (Automated Clearing House), credit cards, PayPal, and peer-to-peer payment services like Venmo. These rails have different requirements, merits, and demerits, having to do with the fees that are charged, network size, speed, reliability, and flexibility.

Start with the classic payment rail: wires.
