Users who wanted to buy or sell cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin or ether could do so using trading applications such as Robinhood, Interactive Brokers, Coinbase, MetaMask, etc. In addition, users could use these apps to review their own NFT collection, browse NFTs owned by other users, search for NFTs, and view NFTs available for sale. The activities not available to users were buying and selling these NFTs.

What makes this distinction especially strange is the fact that there is no technical distinction between these two purchases—the only difference is that bitcoin is a “fungible” crypto-based token, in that every bitcoin is substitutable with another, while buying an NFT piece of artwork is a non-fungible token, in that it isn’t substitutable with any other token. Things get more confusing if the right to this non-fungible token is fractionalized into fungible tokens (think of selling shares to a piece of artwork, rather than the artwork itself). These “shares” can be bought and sold via an iPhone app. In fact, a user could even buy all outstanding shares, therefore owning the NFT outright.

In October 2022, Apple formally revised its policies to allow NFT sales in iOS apps, but many catches applied. Most notably, NFTs could not be used to “unlock” functionality, as would be the case with NFTs used inside games, or to access content, such as a streaming video service.^([48](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr48)) Apple would also be owed 30% of the fee from the transaction, which would paid in a traditional currency rather than a cryptocurrency (Apple’s typical store rules, such as the prohibition on telling users of alternative payment methods, continued to apply). No major marketplaces or applications accepted Apple’s proposal, citing several issues. A key matter was that marketplaces could not practically determine (and therefore prevent) NFTs which had, or might soon have, unlocking capabilities. It was also impossible to imagine any user would choose to purchase or sell a multi-thousand-dollar NFT, let alone a multimillion-dollar one, through an app that added thousands or millions in added fees, rather than do so via browser. And even if both options were available, it was obviously problematic for a “marketplace” to simultaneously offer two very different prices—not only would this produce confusion, but it would lead to angry customers demanding a partial refund after buying through the “wrong channel.” Worse still, a 30% fee would eventually devour the entirety of an NFT’s value if it traded hands enough times. As a hypothetical, imagine an NFT that sells for $100 in ether, netting Apple $30 and the seller $70. If the buyer then wanted to sell the NFT, it would need to sell for $143 (+45%!) to break even on the $100 purchase, as Apple would collect another $43 (or $73 total on an NFT worth $143). If the buyer could not resell the NFT for more than $50 (which might be due to declining demand and/or erosion in the underlying cryptocurrency), they would net only $35, while Apple would collect $15 (cumulatively $45 on an NFT worth $50). Lastly, such a transaction would require the buyer, seller, or marketplace to pay Apple in cash. Web3 advocates disliked this requirement as it would likely require selling off some of their cryptocurrency as a result (which would create downward pricing pressure on the ecosystem), and told Apple the “real-world” identity of the NFT’s owner.

In December of 2022, Apple reportedly proposed a new App Store rule whereby select (i.e., not all) marketplaces (not games) would be allowed to support blockchain-based in-app payments for select NFTs (those that did not have unlocking functionality), and Apple would take a 30% cut of the associated “gas fee,” rather than the value of the NFT.^([49](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr49)) Though this fee would be far more modest in dollar terms, marketplaces again refused Apple’s rules and, as such, declined to update their apps to support in-app purchasing or trading. To these marketplaces, Apple’s willingness to take a comparatively lower fee solved only one of the aforementioned problems with its IAP solution—and created several others. For example, gas fees can run from tens of cents to tens of dollars or more based on network congestion, making Apple’s fee both highly variable and uncorrelated to the services being rendered. Apple’s fee would also have to apply to NFTs that were gifted to users or simply transferred between a user’s own wallet, as there was no way for Apple to distinguish between transactions.

Although the major platforms sometimes suggest that their refusal to support or distribute blockchains stems from a concern about user safety, government regulations, or energy use, such claims don’t hold up to scrutiny. Sony’s music label has invested in NFT start-ups, and created its own NFTs, while Microsoft’s Azure offers blockchain certifications and its corporate venture arm has made numerous start-up investments. Apple CEO Tim Cook has admitted that he owns cryptocurrencies and has been interested in the field for a “while.”^([50](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr50)) Instead, it’s obvious that these platforms refuse blockchain games because they simply do not work with their revenue models. Allowing *Call of Duty: Mobile* to connect to a cryptocurrency wallet would be akin to a user connecting the game directly to their bank account, rather than paying through Apple’s App Store or Sony’s PlayStation Store.

The impact of these many bans and limitations has been profound. Web3-focused games could run natively only on the PC, were limited to the browser on iOS, and were not available on the Microsoft Xbox, Nintendo Switch, or Sony PlayStation. It’s for this reason that nearly all of the hit blockchain games of 2020 and 2021 were focused on collecting (virtual sports cards, digital artwork, and so on) or otherwise limited to simple 2D graphics and turn-based play (consider *Axie Infinity*, a sort of reimagining of the 1990s hit *Pokémon*). Furthermore, there have been no high-profile “AAA blockchain games,” despite industry leaders such as Electronic Arts, Konami, Nexon, Roblox, Sega, Square Enix, Ubisoft, and more having once announced plans to launch such a title or blockchain-related capabilities. To this end, claims that “gamers beat NFTs”^([51](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr51)) are misleading. Even if gamers don’t want blockchain games, they haven’t been given much of an opportunity to play them.

### **Digital First Requires the Physical First**

At the core of the virtual payment rails problem is a conflict. The very idea of the Metaverse supposes that the “next platform” is not based on hardware, or even on an operating system. Instead, it is a persistent network of virtual simulations that exist irrespective of, and in fact are agnostic regarding, a given device or system. The difference is that between a *New York Times* app that runs on a single user’s iPhone and an iPhone used to access a living *New York Times* universe. There is evidence of this transition today. The most popular virtual worlds, such as those of *Fortnite*, *Roblox*, and *Minecraft*, are designed to run on as many devices and operating systems as possible, and are only lightly optimized for any specific one.

Of course, no one can access the Metaverse without hardware. And every hardware player is fighting to be a (if not *the*) payment gateway to this multitrillion-dollar opportunity. To win this fight, the market leaders forcibly bundle their hardware and operating systems with first-party services, third-party software distribution, payment rails, browser engines, identities, and entitlement management solutions. The combined force of this bundle enables a platform to limit to development of threatening business models, technologies, or competitors, while also protecting lucrative payment-processing fees, as WebGL, cloud gaming, NFC, browser engines, blockchains, and so on demonstrate.

There are always justifications for an individual policy, but they’re impossible for the market to validate when there are only two smartphone platforms and their respective stacks are so extensively bundled. Even regulatory efforts to introduce more competition to individual service offerings tend to be stymied by platform power. In August 2021, a bill passed in South Korea banning app store operators from requiring their own payment systems, arguing such a requirement was monopolistic and harmed both consumers and developers. Three months later, and before the law changes were set to come into effect, Google announced that apps which chose to use an alternative payment service would have to pay a new fee for using their app store. Its price? Four percent less than the old fee—almost exactly the cost of its old fee, less the fees charged by Visa, MasterCard, or PayPal. As such, any developer who chose to use another payment rail would end up with savings of less than 1%—a margin so small that changing payment systems would be senseless, and no price cut to consumers would be possible.

In December 2021, Dutch regulators ordered Apple to let dating apps use third-party payment services (the category-specific requirements stemmed from the fact that category leader Match Group had filed a complaint with the Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets). In response, Apple updated its store policies in the Netherlands, allowing developers to issue (and therefore maintain) a Dutch-only version of their app which supported alternative payments. The catch was that this new version would not be able to support Apple’s IAP, so developers would need to choose between offering two different apps in the marketplace and offering a single SKU supporting one of the two payment options. More annoying still, the versions that supported an alternative payment model would not be able to offer that inside the app, as Amazon does with its e-commerce app or developers might support through an integrated PayPal or Visa button. Instead, users would need to click a link that would send them into a web browser, then log in, then place and complete their order. And before the user’s web browser launched, the app would need to display a disclaimer that it would not “support the App Store’s private and secure payment systems.”^([52](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr52)) Various regulators, executives, and analysts argued the phrasing chosen by Apple was designed to “scare” users.^([53](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr53)) Moreover, Apple required developers to send a monthly audited report detailing every single transaction placed under this payment alternative, rather than the total or even summary figures, a policy some viewed as both unnecessary and deliberately burdensome.^([54](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr54)) Naturally, this flow would be complemented by a new transaction fee of 27%, thereby ensuring the developer saved no money and could not afford to offer consumers lower prices, all in exchange for new compliance burdens. Dutch regulators were quick to declare that Apple’s revised plans did not satisfy its demands.^([55](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr55)) In June 2022, Apple partially relented. The required warnings were toned down, and developers were able to offer a single app that included payment pathways in addition to the ability to advertise the prices of the browser-based alternative. All other limitations and requirements remained.

In September 2023, Google settled a lawsuit brought by all 50 US state attorneys general, plus those of the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico, which alleged Google had illegally used monopoly power to benefit its own apps and increase the price of Android applications.^([56](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr56)) In its settlement, Google agreed to pay $700 million (equivalent to about three weeks of Google Play profits), most of which would be paid to Android users, as well as a series of changes to its Android OS that would make it easier for users to download and pay for apps outside the Google Play Store and permit developers to tell these users about alternative download and payment options—even when these users are inside an app distributed by Google Play.^([57](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr57)) However, developers that used so-called “user choice billing” in the United States would nevertheless owe Google a 26% commission on all eligible transactions.^([58](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr58))

In September 2021, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers delivered her ruling in *Epic Games v. Apple*, in which Epic had argued Apple illegally monopolized its controls over the distribution of and payment systems used by iOS apps. Judge Rogers sided with Apple in nine of ten counts, but found that Apple violated “anti-steering policies” and could no longer prohibit developers from telling their users about alternative payment options inside their iOS apps, or providing in-app links to those alternatives.^([59](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr59)) Though Rogers gave Apple 90 days to comply with her order, Apple promptly filed an appeal with the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which subsequently provided a stay on Rogers’s ruling relating to in-app links to alternative payment mechanisms, pending a full ruling from the Ninth Circuit.^([60](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr60)) In April 2023, the Ninth Circuit found in favor of Rogers’s original ruling, but extended its stay so that Apple could appeal to the Supreme Court (Epic had also appealed the nine counts in which Rogers ruled in favor of Apple).^([61](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr61)) In August 2023, the Supreme Court rejected Epic’s request to remove the stay, and in January 2024, the court declined to hear either company’s appeal, thus ending the stay.^([62](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr62)) That same day, Apple announced a new App Store payment model that largely mirrored that which the company had deployed in the Netherlands, but was even more expansive in its controls and less practical for developers.

In the case that a user clicked an in-app link to a payment option other than Apple’s own, Apple would take 27% (again, its typical 30% less 3% of payment processing fees).^([63](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr63)) As a result, even those apps which did not have to offer Apple’s IAP solution, and chose not to do so, such as Netflix, would now owe Apple a fee if they used a link inside their app (no fee would be owed if the app just told the user they could pay online). In addition, Apple would be entitled to its 27% if the user paid within seven days of originally clicking the link, rather than just at the time they originally clicked it.^([64](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr64)) Apple also introduced an interstitial page that would appear after a user clicked a link to an alternative payment option, but before it loaded, which warned, in a large font size, “You’re about to go to an external website. Apple is not responsible for the privacy or security of purchases made on the web,” with smaller text warning that Apple would not provide refund requests and could not verify any “pricing or promotions offered by the developer.”^([65](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr65)) Though such a warning was accurate, it was widely criticized as a “scare tactic,” with many critics noting that these same points were true when a user made purchases through most apps, such as those in the rideshare, e-commerce, food, gambling, and banking businesses.^([66](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr66)) Instead, Apple seemed to only want to warn users about the potential privacy or security risks involved with making a transaction that, were it not for Epic’s lawsuit and Judge Rogers’s ruling, would have been placed through Apple’s own payment system.

Less than two weeks after Apple revised its US App Store policies, the company unveiled revisions to its policies in the European Union in response to the EU’s Digital Markets Act. Though the DMA was originally passed in 2022, affected companies had until March of 2024 to comply with some provisions. One such example was the requirement for companies such as Apple and Google to allow users to install app stores that competed with their own proprietary stores, and to support alternative payment methods for all applications distributed by their proprietary stores. In January 2024, Apple unveiled its “new capabilities and terms for apps in the EU,” which would go into effect in May of that year and exclusively cover apps that were distributed in the EU and only when they were distributed in the EU (i.e., an application such as Spotify, which is owned by a Swedish company, would be eligible for these terms inside the EU, but not in the United States, South Korea, Argentina, etc.).^([67](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr67))

Under these new terms, developers would be allowed to distribute their apps inside the App Store, exclusively through unaffiliated third-party app stores, or both.^([68](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr68)) Whenever these apps were installed by a user through Apple’s App Store, Apple would take a 17% commission in place of its prior 30% commission.^([69](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr69)) Apps distributed through Apple’s App Store would also have the choice of offering Apple’s in-app billing services, or those of a third-party payment provider, or both. In the case where a developer chose to offer Apple’s IAP, Apple would also charge another 3% to eligible transactions to cover payment processing, for 20% total.^([70](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr70)) Apple would not take any commission from an app distributed through a third-party app store, but apps distributed through these stores *or* through the App Store under its modified commissions model would also encounter a new charge called the “Core Technology Fee.”^([71](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr71)) This fee would be equal to €0.50 for every user’s first installation or an existing user’s first update in a 12-month period, with fees waived for the first one million qualifying installs/updates.^([72](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr72)) Alternatively, a developer could choose to continue to operate under the pre-DMA business terms of 30% (inclusive of transaction fees) and no Core Technology Fee and inclusive of transaction fees; however, this would require the developer to stick to all of Apple’s other App Store policies too, which meant the developer could not distribute their app on other stores or educate the consumer about alternative payment options inside that app.^([73](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr73))

While Apple estimated “99% of developers would reduce or maintain the fees they owe to Apple” and “<1% of developers would pay a Core Technology Fee on their EU apps,”^([74](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr74)) Apple’s plans were widely criticized as “egregious” and “punitive … will burn its political and developer goodwill” by top technology journalists,^([75](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr75)) a “heads I win, tails you lose” strategy by mobile app experts,^([76](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr76)) “Malicious Compliance^([#](#chapter10.xhtml#footnote-008)) … forcing developers to choose between App Store exclusivity and the store terms, which will be illegal under DMA, or accept a new also-illegal anticompetitive scheme” according to Tim Sweeney,^([77](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr77)) and “masquerading as compliance with the law … a complete and total farce,” according to Spotify, which had been a key advocate for DMA-like regulations in the EU and around the world.^([78](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr78))

David Heinemeier Hansson, a Danish programmer who created the Ruby on Rails web-development framework and Hey, a digital calendar and email application, wrote that “once you start peeling the onion \[of Apple’s new policies\], you realize it’s stuffed with poison pills so toxic you can scarcely believe Apple’s chutzpah.… Might be the most blatant extortion attempt ever committed to public policy by any technology company ever.… Explicitly designed to ensure that no second-party app store ever takes off.”^([79](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr79)) Nikita Bier, a serial entrepreneur who sold his start-ups to Facebook and Discord, highlighted that an app that chose Apple’s new IAP program and was installed 10 million times in a year, while also generating $10 million in in-app revenue that year, would owe Apple $6.2 million (62%), with only $3.8 million left to cover sales tax (typically 21%, or $2 million of this $3.8 million) and all operating expenses.^([80](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr80)) “If you make less than $0.57 per user—which is most apps—you will end up negative and you will owe Apple money,” Bier added.^([81](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr81)) Hansson also highlighted that in the EU, Instagram, a free app with roughly 250 million monthly users, would need to pay $135 million to Apple annually if it chose to adopt Apple’s new terms, rather than $0—even if no part of the app changed. Facebook would also need to pay this fee for each of its EU apps, such as WhatsApp, Facebook, Meta Quest, and so on.^([82](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr82)) Companies that planned to launch their stores by placing their popular apps inside said store would end up having to pay the fee twice. Epic, as an example, would have to pay one fee when a user installed the Epic Games Store on iOS, and then again when the user downloaded *Fortnite*.

Apple’s nonfinancial terms were also considered obstructive and unnecessary. “While Apple is also under an obligation to allow ‘sideloading’ (i.e., the ability to download apps directly from a website, as software can be downloaded from websites on PCs),” Damien Geradin of the European competition and digital-regulation law firm Geradin Partners wrote in a blog post, “\[Apple\] interprets this obligation in an extremely narrow way: ‘sideloading refers to downloading iOS apps outside of an official app marketplace—and in the EU, users will have the option to download alternative marketplaces that offer apps for download.’ ”^([83](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr83)) And if a developer chose to make their app available outside the App Store, users would need to delete the version of the app they had already downloaded before they could install that new version—a confusing, unclear, and unfamiliar requirement that would likely lead to customer loss and annoyance and impede competition.^([84](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr84))

Third-party app stores also had to be “mainly app stores,” blocking apps such as Instagram and Snapchat from selling games or digital products inside their apps as Tencent’s WeChat does in China.^([85](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr85)) And while a third-party app store could focus on a single category of apps, such as games or photos, it must “be open to submissions from any developer in that same category” and could not define that category such that only their own apps qualified.^([86](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr86)) Even when apps skipped Apple’s App Store entirely, developers would still need a developer account issued and managed by Apple, and “all apps and every update must still be submitted to Apple for notarization. After review, Apple will then forward apps to each marketplace where the app is distributed \[not the developer\].”^([87](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr87)) Apple’s review would involve both automated checks and human reviews, and though non–App Store apps would no longer be subject to Apple’s content restrictions (enabling pornographic and pirated-content apps, among others, on iOS), Apple would still enforce technical controls regarding background processes, permissions, APIs, and other design choices.^([88](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr88))

As part of its new DMA policies, Apple also disabled support of web apps for EU users—though the company only acknowledged this policy change after public outcry.^([89](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr89)) As a result, users would no longer be able to add a “progressive web app” (PWA) to their device. Instead, users would only be able to install an icon that looked like an app but was a just a bookmark that would open up the PWA’s webpage inside a web browser. Though the difference might seem trivial, the technical implications are significant. For example, PWAs would no longer have access to the iPhone’s “long-term storage,” be able to send notifications to the user, or run their own window in multitasking (i.e., they would be limited to a tab inside the browser app), and would face greater limitations in leveraging the iPhone’s full capabilities and components.^([90](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr90)) In response to backlash, Apple argued its new PWA constraints were needed to preserve system security given the company’s reduced oversight over app distribution. Notably, Apple had previously claimed that the fact users could use web apps rather than native apps managed by Apple’s App Store was proof that the App Store did face competition and Apple did not have unjust control of software distribution on its platforms.^([91](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr91)) Some developers and industry observers speculated that Apple’s crippling of PWAs was prompted not by security concerns, but a DMA decree that required Apple to permit third-party browser engines on iOS.^([92](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr92)) Since 2012, Apple had technically permitted third-party browsers on iOS (e.g., Chrome, Firefox), however these browsers could not use their own engines (Blink, Gekco), only Apple’s own WebKit, which had limited support for PWAs. Accordingly, critics alleged, Apple was now crippling web apps at the operating system level to prevent PWAs from becoming “legit, untaxed \[i.e. non-commission paying\] competitors to native apps.”^([93](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr93)) This theory was seemingly confirmed by Apple’s response to PWA-related backlash. Barely two weeks after the company confirmed reports it was disabling PWAs in the EU, Apple announced it would continue to support them—but only if the PWAs ran on WebKit.^([94](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr94))

Lastly, Apple also chose to permit third-party app stores only on the iPhone—applications for the iPad, Apple Watch, Apple TV, and Apple Vision Pro would continue to be exclusively distributed by Apple’s App Store, though these apps would now be able to accept alternative forms of payment and/or skip Apple’s IAP (in which case Apple’s revised commissions and Core Technology Fee would apply).^([95](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr95)) As a result, developers would be unable to offer consumers a consistent way to install their applications across Apple devices, would have to continue using Apple’s App Store in order to reach consumers across all Apple devices, and if they did publish across multiple Apple devices they were effectively still constrained by Apple’s App Store policies, including its content guidelines. By restricting alternative distribution to the iPhone, Apple appeared to have rejected a key DMA order. In a September 5, 2023, decision the EU Commission wrote: “With respect to Apple’s online intermediation service App Store, Apple argued that there are five device-specific versions of the app store (i.e., iOS App Store, iPad OS App Store, etc.,) which individually constitute distinct online intermediation services.… This is because, according to Apple, app stores serve different purposes from both an end user as well as a business user perspective depending on the device. According to Apple, only the iOS version of the App Store offered for the iPhone meets the thresholds for designation. The Commission designates Apple’s software application store App Store, which is currently offered on different Apple devices running on iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and tvOS (together the ‘App Store’), as a single \[Core Platform Service\]. This is because, based on the evidence in the file, the App Store is used for the same common purpose from both an end user and a business user perspective across all devices on which it is available, namely to intermediate the distribution of apps.”^([96](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr96)) Seventeen days before Apple debuted its new EU rules, the company filed an appeal contending the commission’s September 5, 2023, decision was based on “material factual errors.”^([97](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr97))

A day after Apple unveiled its changes, Thierry Breton, commissioner for internal market of the European Union, was asked about allegations that Apple’s policies were insufficient and may, in fact, violate the DMA. He responded, “The DMA will open the gates of the internet to competition so that digital markets are fair and open. Change is already happening. As from 7 March we will assess companies’ proposals, with the feedback of third parties.… If the proposed solutions are not good enough, we will not hesitate to take strong action.”^([98](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr98)) And the EU was certainly empowered to take “strong action,” having been authorized by the EU Parliament to fine non-compliant companies “up to 10% of the company’s total worldwide annual turnover” and “up to 20% in the event of repeated infringements.”^([99](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr99)) And sure enough, less than a month after the DMA came into full effect, the EU Commission announced Apple was under investigation for non-compliance “relating to Apple’s new fee structure for alternative app stores … Apple’s new fee structure and other terms and conditions for alternative app stores and distribution of apps from the web (sideloading) may be defeating the purpose of its obligations under Article 6(4) of the DMA.” The Commission also opened non-compliance investigations into Google, including but not limited to its app store controls for Android, Amazon, and Facebook.^([100](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr100)) On April 29, 2024, the European Commission affirmed that iPad OS, like iPhone’s iOS, would need to comply fully with the Digital Markets Act, and provided Apple with six months to meet these obligations.^([101](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr101)) Yet few markets boast the political and governmental strength of the EU, nor could the EU control the actions of companies such as Apple outside its territories. As such, most of the world remained subject to Apple’s original App Store rules and the company’s efforts to maintain its controls and fees irrespective of legislative or judicial attempts otherwise.

Though far from the most riveting aspect of Metaverse theory, the centrality and influence of hardware over payments helps to explain why Facebook, in particular, is so committed to building its own AR and VR devices, and why it is investing in fanciful projects such as brain-to-machine interfaces and smartwatches with their own wireless chips and cameras. As the only member of the big-tech giants without a leading device and/or operating system, Facebook is uniquely familiar with how operating solely on the platforms of its largest competitors is an impediment. Its cloud gaming service has effectively been blocked on every major mobile and console platform. And whenever Facebook sells something to one of its users, it collects as much net revenue as it sends to its own foes. The company’s integrated virtual world platform, *Horizon Worlds*, meanwhile, is fundamentally constrained by the fact that it can never offer a developer a greater cut of revenues than iOS or Android. The most painful example may be Apple’s “App Tracking Transparency” (ATT) changes, which were implemented in 2021, 14 years after the first iPhone. In a simplified sense, ATT required app developers to receive explicit “opt-in” permission from users in order to access key user and device data, while also explaining exactly what data was being collected and why (much of this script was written by Apple, and the company’s App Store team would have approval rights over all alterations). Apple argued the changes were in the interest of users, 75% to 80% of whom were believed to have rejected the prompt by December 2021.^([102](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr102)) Others saw the move as a deliberate effort to stymie the company’s advertising-focused competitors, build up Apple’s own advertising business, and, by reducing the efficacy of advertising, prompt more developers to focus their business model on in-app payments, where Apple collected a 15%–30% fee. In February 2022, Mark Zuckerberg said Apple’s policy change would reduce Facebook’s 2022 revenues by roughly $10 billion, or 8%—equivalent to nearly 80% of the company’s spend on the Metaverse that same year.^([103](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr103)) In August 2022, Snap CEO Evan Spiegel announced that his company would be laying off one in five employees, including the entirety of its AR/VR hardware division, in response to a worsening economy and Apple’s ATT implementation.^([104](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr104)) By the end of 2022, Facebook’s stock had fallen by two-thirds, prompting high-profile investors to call on Zuckerberg to reduce his Metaverse investments by at least as much,^([105](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr105)) while Snap was down 80%, compared to the NASDAQ (down by a third at that point) and Apple (a quarter). Five months later, Apple unveiled the Vision Pro—an announcement many pundits viewed as Machiavellian. How better to enter an existing category than by impairing the profits of the long-standing market leader?

 

### **New Payment Rails**

Having covered the ways in which payment rails determine the “cost of doing business” in the digital era, and how they’re used to control it, it’s important to review how they can also transform an economy. Here, China provides a useful case study.

When Tencent’s WeChat launched in 2011, China was primarily a cash society. But within the span of a few years, the messaging app hurled the country into the digital payments and services era. This was a consequence of many of WeChat’s unique—and in the West, effectively impossible—opportunities and choices. Anyone on WeChat could connect directly to their bank account rather than require an intermediary credit card or digital payments network, which is prohibited by the major gaming consoles and smartphone app stores. Without intermediaries, and because Tencent wanted to build up its social messaging network, WeChat offered tiny transaction fees: 0%–0.1% for peer-to-peer transfers and less than 1% for merchant payments, with no fees for real-time delivery or payment confirmations. And because this payment capability was built upon common standards (QR codes) and built into a messaging app, it was easy for everyone with a smartphone to adopt and use. WeChat’s success also helped Tencent build up the domestic video gaming industry, too, which would have otherwise been limited by the lack of credit cards across the country.

In the West, these systems would normally be at the mercy of the hardware gatekeepers. In China, by contrast, Tencent grew so powerful and so rapidly that even Apple was forced to allow WeChat to operate its own app store within its app, and directly process in-app payments—even though the iPhone launched in China two years before WeChat’s debut. In 2022, WeChat processed the equivalent of “several” hundred billion in US dollars, with an average value of only a few dollars each.^([106](#notes_split_010.xhtml#ch10fr106)) For the Metaverse to emerge, it’s likely that developers and creators in the West will need to find their own ways around hardware gatekeepers—a need that partly explains why so many see the Metaverse and the blockchain as two inextricably linked parts of the internet’s future.

## [Chapter 11 THE CASES FOR AND AGAINST A BLOCKCHAIN-BASED METAVERSE](#contents.xhtml#ch_11)

The Metaverse is frequently conflated with “blockchain” and its related use cases, such as cryptocurrencies and NFTs, and with its overarching ethos, known as Web3. Yet the two concepts are, in a technical sense, distinct. In fact, there’s little consensus regarding whether they overlap at all—or should. Some executives, entrepreneurs, analysts, and investors consider blockchain an integral component to building the Metaverse. Others see blockchain as an effective (indeed, potentially ideal) solution without being in any sense strictly necessary. A third group views blockchains as a poor solution that may nevertheless become a working standard. Another group believes blockchains have no relevance to the Metaverse at all (and usually no future whatsoever). While more individuals have moved toward the fourth category than the first since the end of the 2020–22 crypto boom, the opposite was true during the 2010s, and it’s always possible that opinions may flip again as blockchain technology evolves. To examine these various and sometimes oscillating perspectives, one must first consider a technology used every day but rarely if ever consciously thought about: the database.

 

### **Who Watches the Databases?**

The modern world runs on billions of databases. These databases track everything from who owns which homes, to the mortgages on these homes, their addresses and tax liabilities, the utilities they consume, and which resources should be dispatched in the event of an emergency. The individuals who live in these homes have their medical histories stored in multiple databases managed by their family doctor, insurance provider, and even the ER they visited years earlier. And when they make a deposit in a bank, their money isn’t placed in a lockbox or tagged in a common vault; it is instead recorded in a database. A database also manages when these individuals are paid by their employer, in what sums, and through which payment rails. At least one database stores every email, photo, and document a user creates or receives.

Most databases are centralized—that is, they are managed by a single, definitive authority. In the United States, the largest retail bank is Chase, which manages over $2.5 trillion in assets, all of which is stored on a series of databases that track not just the current balances of its customer deposits but all of the records of how that balance accumulated. To be sure, Chase has many backups of this record (as users might too), and it really operates a network of different databases, but what matters here is that these digital records are managed and owned by a single party: Chase.

Blockchains are decentralized databases with no owner or operator. Instead, their information is recorded, maintained, and updated by a network of unknown computer “validators” that rarely know (or care) what information and transactions they are validating. Furthermore, the process of “validation” does not directly involve the relevant transaction—such as confirming a $5 coffee purchase at Starbucks. Instead, validators (i.e., computers) spend their time solving solutions to complex cryptographic problems that are automatically generated by the transaction. And while the answer to the problem is established through consensus across this network, each validator is in competition with every other to solve it first and, in doing so, to collect the largest share of the associated transaction fee (known as “gas”), which is typically paid in a blockchain’s native cryptocurrency.

The first blockchain, the Bitcoin blockchain, debuted in January 2009. The goal of this blockchain was expansive: a digital currency that could operate a global payment network capable of processing transactions in near real time 24 hours per day and 365 days a year; was accessible to all and excludable to none; could be used for any possible transaction; relentlessly minimized transaction costs; could resist tampering, corruption, and seizure; would not be affected by central banks that might pay off their debts by printing more money; and had no central authority, lead, or managing organization. For this reason, the sole focus of the Bitcoin blockchain was to operate a database that tracked ownership of a proprietary cryptocurrency, the lowercase *b* bitcoin, which also paid its validators in that same cryptocurrency, which appreciated in value as its usage grew.

Bitcoin’s creator, who is known only by his (presumed) pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto, designed its blockchain to have several interrelated attributes. First, Bitcoin would be a “permissionless” blockchain—anyone could become a network validator or bitcoin owner without needing to be invited or approved, and additionally, no one could be stopped from doing so. Second, Bitcoin’s code would be all but immutable—neither the blockchain itself nor any records/transactions on it could ever be changed unless roughly half of network validators chose to do so. Third, this underlying code would be fully transparent, which also meant that Bitcoin validators and bitcoin owners alike would know the maximum possible supply of bitcoin and when more would be released.

These first three attributes enabled the next two attributes, which in turn strengthened the first three. As more individuals and businesses purchased and used Bitcoin, it became increasingly decentralized. This theoretically stabilized its price swings and increased its utility. Moreover, the volume of bitcoin transactions grew, which increased the value of validating transactions and attracted more validators to the network. This not only drove transaction fees down through validator competition, but it further decentralized the blockchain, thereby ensuring its incorruptibility. Consider: If there were only seven validators, then four of them might collude to falsely “validate” transactions that never took place and, in doing so, rob the users. Alternatively, these four validators might “validate” only transactions that took place at their stores, effectively forcing users to hand over their bitcoin.

By 2023, the number of validators supporting Bitcoin on a daily basis exceeded more than a million,^([1](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr1)) making it functionally impossible for its transactions and codes to be hijacked, and achieving Nakamoto’s final aspiration: trustlessness. With all of Bitcoin’s code transparently available, immutable to change, permissionlessly accessed, and operated by a widely decentralized network, no users, business, or validator need ever wonder whether a fee would be paid, a policy changed, or their business individually halted.

### **A General-Purpose Blockchain**

Not long after Bitcoin emerged, two early users, Vitalik Buterin and Gavin Wood, began developing a new blockchain, Ethereum, which they described as a “decentralised mining network and software development platform rolled into one.”^([2](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr2)) It launched in 2015. Like Bitcoin, Ethereum pays those operating its network through its own cryptocurrency, known as Ether. Buterin and Wood additionally established a programming language (Solidity) that enables any developers to permissionlessly and trustlessly program on top of Ethereum. Most of these products are built around “smart contracts,” which are collections of code and data that reside at a specific address on the Ethereum blockchain.

The simplest implementation of smart contracts are “non-fungible tokens” (NFTs). In this case, a smart contract is written that publishes (or “mints”) data to a blockchain and assigns ownership of this data to an individual address (“wallet”) on the blockchain. This data might be a record that the owner of that wallet had bought a ticket to the county fair—or it could be the deed to a home in that county. Once this NFT is minted, the receiving address has full control over this record and can freely reassign (i.e., sell or transfer) it to any other address on the blockchain. While the underlying code to this NFT “smart contract” can easily be copied, as can the data it relates to (e.g., a ticket receipt or a house deed), the actual NFT and its record can be neither copied nor substituted—hence “non-fungible”—as these are unique and immutable identifiers written to the blockchain. As such, proponents of NFTs believe that they can serve as a worldwide system that irrefutably and automatically validates ownership of both virtual and physical goods and that can be accessed by any application or user in the world.

Smart contracts can also interact with other smart contracts. A smart contract might be written to recognize ownership of an NFT in order to permit some activity, such as signing into a members-only Discord channel or entering a local fair. Many NFTs include code that automatically activates a second smart contract whenever the NFT is sold. The latter smart contract is typically used to send the NFT’s original creator (or some other predesignated address) a portion of the proceeds (a “royalty”), often between 5% and 10%, which enables artists to directly participate in the appreciation of their works—a luxury not typically afforded to painters, photographers, designers, and so on, and which was even harder to collect, audit, and enforce.

During 2021 and 2022, roughly $65 billion was spent on NFTs globally.^([3](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr3)) These purchases were diverse. NBA Top Shots from Dapper Labs turned individual moments from various NBA seasons into collectible, trading-card-like NFTs that ran on Dapper’s own blockchain, Flow. Artists such as Damien Hirst also released paintings and photographs as NFTs (which sometimes included rights to a physical work).^([4](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr4)) Larva Labs, a crypto-focused design studio, released an NFT collection of “Cryptopunks,” which spanned 10,000 algorithmically generated 24-by-24-pixel 2D avatars that many owners used as profile pictures across the internet. Bored Ape, another profile-picture NFT series, provided owners with select IP rights to the underlying artworks and the ability to use their “Ape” to gain access to the affiliate social club, the Bored Ape Yacht Club, in addition to select rights to the artwork. In April 2022, a record $78 million was being paid to NFT creators each week as royalties.

Collections of smart contracts have been used to produce decentralized apps (“dapps”) that can execute complex tasks akin to traditional applications. Examples help bring this concept to life and demonstrate some of the prospective benefits of blockchain-based applications.

Uniswap enables users to exchange hundreds of different tokens with other users, all without the need for contracts, brokers, clearinghouses, delays, or fears of nondelivery, and at a modest fee of 0.3%—far lower than the 1%–3% spread on currency exchanges that traditional banks typically demand. In the five years following its November 2018 debut, Uniswap has managed more than $1.5 trillion in trades, processing as much as $90 billion in its biggest month (November 2021) and $14 billion on its biggest day (March 10, 2022).^([5](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr5)) Despite its enormous operating scale, Uniswap has only a few dozen employees.^([6](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr6))

OpenSea is a marketplace focused on the exchange not of cryptocurrencies or tokens but of NFTs, taking an average of 2.5% on sales. The platform allows users to display their own collection of NFTs, as well as browse those of others, and to search, bid on, and purchase individual NFTs or to make their own NFTs available for sale. OpenSea’s staff, which peaked at roughly 300 in 2022, also provides editorial and curatorial functions (such as featured collections), verification services (confirming the legitimacy of NFTs made available for sale), and blocking the sale of stolen NFTs. In the six years since OpenSea’s December 2017 launch, it has processed over $35 billion in NFT sales, with a peak of roughly $5 billion traded in January 2022.^([7](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr7))

Mirror has used smart contracts and token systems to reimagine the independent journalism and blogging business model. On the platform, authors can finance their research, investigations, and writings by preselling NFT copies of the finished works or issuing tokens that would be needed to access the finished work or would entitle owners to a portion of revenues generated by this work. In other cases, a collective of authors has issued tokens to fundraise for a new magazine that is then made exclusively available to token holders. Some writers use smart contracts to automatically share tips with those who helped or inspired them.

*Axie Infinity* and *Zed Run* have used blockchain to build a “Web3” version of the video game *Pokémon* and virtual racing, respectively. In both cases, these games issue NFT-based creatures that can be collected, bred, traded, trained, battled, rented, or gambled upon, with smart contracts managing profit sharing and genetic inheritances while also operating the in-game odds and combat. As NFTs are minted to the blockchain, not recorded on the private database of their makers, outside developers are able to access and use these creatures, too—and not necessarily to build games. In 2020, the collective known as Yield Guild Games (YGG) was founded primarily to buy “Axies” that would then be lent out to *Axie Infinity* players in exchange for a portion of their winnings and/or rental fees. YGG, in other words, was making money enabling Sky Mavis’s own players to play Sky Mavis’s own game.

In a few cases, dapps and smart contracts have been used to establish and operate large-scale and decentralized infrastructure networks, with these dapps and smart contracts often issuing their own cryptocurrencies on top of the blockchain upon which they operate. One leading example is Otoy, a cloud-based rendering company that in 2020 publicly launched the Ethereum-based RNDR network, protocol, and token. Specifically, RNDR establishes a token-based marketplace where idle computers can make their GPUs available to those in need of additional computing power. All of the negotiation and contracting between parties is handled by RNDR’s protocol in a matter of seconds; neither side has any knowledge of the identity or specifics of the task being performed; and all transactions occur using RNDR cryptocurrency tokens. According to the company, RNDR can perform tasks at a fraction of the cost offered by centralized databases, while also increasing the global supply of available computing resources by several orders of magnitude.^([8](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr8))

Another example is Helium, which the *New York Times* has described as “a decentralized wireless network for ‘internet of things’ devices, powered by cryptocurrency.”^([9](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr9)) Helium sells a $500 hot-spot device that allows the secure rebroadcasting of a home internet connection—at speeds up to 200 times faster than a traditional home Wi-Fi device. This internet service can be used by anyone, from consumers wanting to check Facebook to infrastructure (a parking meter processing credit card transactions) and transportation networks (whose tens of thousands of bikes, scooters, and mopeds often encounter mobile network “dead zones”).^([10](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr10)) Those operating a Helium hot spot are compensated with Helium’s HNT token in proportion to usage. As of the summer of 2023, Helium’s network spanned more than 400,000 active hot spots, up from fewer than 25,000 at the start of 2021, distributed across roughly 50,000 cities in 175 countries.^([11](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr11)) Notably, the company was founded in 2013 but struggled to gain adoption until it pivoted from a traditional (i.e., unpaid) peer-to-peer model to one that offered contributors direct compensation via cryptocurrency. The long-term viability and potential of Helium remains uncertain; most internet service providers (ISPs) prohibit their customers from rebroadcasting their internet connection, and while the ISPs typically have ignored such service violations as long as the connection was not resold and total data usage was low, there is no guarantee that the ISPs will continue to ignore such violations by users of Helium or any analogous system. Regardless, the company, which has pivoted to making deals directly with ISPs, serves as a further reminder of the potential of decentralized payment models.

The tokens issued by a dapp can reward network participants for more than just providing computing and networking resources, as is the case with Bitcoin, Ethereum, RNDR, and Helium. These tokens can also be awarded for contributing personal time, delivering new users (customer acquisition), data entry, IP rights, capital (money), bandwidth, good behavior (community ratings, perhaps), or helping to moderate, and may include governance rights and, of course, are likely to appreciate alongside the underlying project.

To some, such systems offer a potential solution to the harassment and toxicity that is so prevalent on large-scale online social networks. Imagine a model in which Twitter users were awarded valuable Twitter tokens for reporting poor behavior or reviewing previously reported misbehavior, and lost them for violating the rules. Instead of relying on tips or promotional tweets on behalf of advertisers to generate income, superusers and influencers could be awarded tokens for hosting events. By the end of 2021, Kickstarter, Reddit, and Discord had all publicly described plans to shift to blockchain-based token models. Kickstarter and Discord later abandoned these plans due to user backlash, but in July 2022 Reddit announced the launch of its first NFT avatar collection, starring the company’s familiar “Snoo” mascot; users could purchase, sell, or earn through contributions to the community, which could be managed in a Reddit-branded crypto wallet. After a year, 20 million avatars had been minted across four “generations,” with nearly 17 million users purchasing or earning an avatar and close to $40 million in peer-to-peer (“secondary”) sales taking place.^([12](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr12)) Not long after, the company announced it was depreciating all of its non-crypto-based loyalty, points, and reward systems, implying a shift to a mostly blockchain-based framework.^([13](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr13))

Smart contracts serve as the basis for decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs), collectives that use these programs to raise capital, maintain and administer governance processes, complete investments, and issue dividends—all without hiring a lawyer, performing credit checks, establishing a bank account, confirming payments, or tracking membership. The diversity of these DAOs and their achievements have been pretty remarkable.

Many of the most expensive NFTs have been purchased not by individuals but by DAOs made up of countless pseudonymous crypto users who could never have made the purchase on their own. The most notable of these DAOs, ConstitutionDAO, was formed in November 2021 to bid on a physical copy of the US Constitution that would be put up for auction less than a week later, which Sotheby’s estimated would sell for between $15 and $20 million. In the span of three days, over $47 million was raised from 20,000 mostly anonymous contributors. Despite the striking scale of its treasury, ConstitutionDAO ultimately lost the auction, though Bloomberg reported that the auction had “showed the power of the DAO,” which has “the potential to change the way people buy things, build companies, share resources and run non-profits.”^([14](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr14)) Such prognostications take time to be proved or disproved, but a potential example might be the Komorebi Collective, a DAO-based venture capital fund formed in late 2021. The purpose of the DAO is to invest in crypto start-ups with “exceptional female and nonbinary founders”—two profiles that are chronically overlooked by traditional funds. Among Komorebi’s founding 36 members are high-profile “Web 1.0” and “Web 2.0” venture capital giants such as Kleiner Perkins, the design and consulting firm IDEO, and former executives from companies such as Spotify and Twitter, in addition to individuals who don’t typically participate in the financial sector, such as journalists and human rights workers.^([15](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr15))

DAOs have also been used to establish crypto-based social clubs, such as Friends with Benefits, which requires its members to purchase FWB tokens to access the club’s Discord channel and events. Some have argued that by requiring users to buy tokens to gain entry, FWB is simply replicating the centuries-old “membership dues” model of every exclusive club that came before it—with extra juice in the form of “crypto” hype. However, members do not pay annual “dues.” Instead, they need to buy a certain number of FWB tokens to gain entry—and then hold them to remain members. As a result, every member is a part owner of FWB, and can leave at any time by selling their tokens. Because these tokens appreciate as the club becomes more successful or desirable, every member is incentivized to invest time, ideas, and resources into the club. And as the effective entry fee goes up, the practicality of joining the club just to spam goes down. Appreciation also means that the club must work harder to earn its ongoing role in a member’s life, too. If an individual joins a club by buying $1,000 in tokens, they intuitively see enough value in their membership to forgo access at least temporarily to $1,000 of their money (and potentially see its value decline if the club’s popularity declines). If these tokens quadruple in price, the club must be thriving, but it also has to offer enough value to those who joined at $1,000 to keep them from selling and taking a profit—which would create downward pressure on FWB’s token price while publicly broadcasting that members were leaving and membership was generally unstable. Finally, many social DAOs use smart contracts to issue tokens to individual members for their contributions or to those who cannot afford to join the collective but are deemed worthy by its members.

Nouns DAO is another form of membership club, but instead of focusing on cultural events, this DAO manages the intellectual property rights of its eponymous NFTs. Each day, one new Noun—a cute pixelized avatar—is auctioned, with 100% of the net proceeds going into the Nouns DAO treasury, which exists exclusively to enhance the value of Nouns NFTs. The treasury does this by funding proposals authored by and voted on by the owners of the NFTs. In effect, it is a constantly growing investment fund governed by a constantly growing board of governors.

A final example, which unites many of these themes, is CityDAO, which was formed in 2021 by several thousand outdoors enthusiasts (including Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin and entrepreneur Mark Cuban) to purchase a 40-acre plot of land near Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming, which had passed legislation recognizing DAOs as legal entities earlier in the year.^([16](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr16)) CityDAO’s purchase was successful, with the collective’s de facto figurehead telling the *Financial Times* that he hoped Wyoming’s embrace of the DAO structure and CityDAO’s experiment would “become this fundamental link between digital assets, crypto and the physical world.”^([17](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr17)) Two years later, CityDAO has largely lived up to this ambition.

Since its formation, all of CityDAO’s major decisions have been made through vote, including motions to programmatically collect dues from all members to pay land taxes and legal fees, acquire and assign land rights, and even dilute some members’ voting powers. In May 2022 CityDAO held a vote intended to start the transition from a governance model that gave individuals votes for every token they held to a more democratic “one person, one vote” model. The initial proposal, which passed with 88% support under the then-current “one token, one vote” model, involved the issuance of “voting credits” equal to the rounded-down square root of the number of tokens held. Users with 4 to 8 tokens would get two votes; those with 9–15 tokens would get three votes, and so on.^([18](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr18)) Two months later, the DAO approved a $10,000 purchase of a new parcel of land in Colorado which would then be split into smaller parcels with NFTs managing the leases. The goal of this latter purchase, which was completed in early 2023, was to serve as a template for the development of a crypto-native city that would be based on the purchase of a distressed American town, college campus, or remote retreat.^([19](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr19)) Around the same time, the DAO began accepting development plans for its first NFT leases in Colorado, which would be given free to the winning proposal.^([20](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr20)) In August, CityDAO began discussing another proposal to spend up to $1.5 million to purchase a property in Denver, Colorado, that would serve as the group’s “city hall.”^([21](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr21))

### **A Tale of Android Alliances and Crypto Foundations**

Even during times in which enthusiasm for crypto is in short supply and investment dollars even more scarce, blockchains regularly prove capable of new use cases and achieve new cultural, creative, and commercial highs. But to its advocates, blockchain’s core advantage is not in the new structures it enables but in what it prevents and preserves.

Forty years into the digital era, there is an expanding consensus that the natural arc of a platform is to extract ever more value from its users and developers, while also locking these groups in so that they can’t flee to a competitor or launch a plausible alternative.^([22](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr22)) The most significant case study here is not Apple’s iOS, which was never billed as “open,” let alone developer focused, but Google’s Android. Although the Android OS is based on code bought by Google in 2005 for “at least $50 million,” the project is technically open-source and is managed by the nonprofit Open Handset Alliance, a consortium of nearly a hundred device makers, network operators, and chip companies.^([23](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr23)) Any smartphone manufacturer, whether it is a member of OHA or not, is free to use Android in whichever (legal) way they like. In fact, an Android original equipment manufacturer (OEM) could fork Android to make it their own and then prevent others from using their variant. Or they could choose to use Android but take none of Google’s apps or services and instead exclusively integrate their own competing software suite.^([24](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr24)) In practice, though, nearly every Android OEM outside of China, with the exception of Amazon, which forked Android to create its Fire OS, uses Google’s end-to-end version of Android. This means that Google Search is the default search engine; the user’s smartphone account must be a Gmail account; Google’s suite of apps must be preinstalled and natively integrated; and the device must observe Google’s policies on data and security and the company’s various UI/X specifications too.

Android OEMs support Google’s version of Android on an end-to-end basis, because they can’t really do so on a piecemeal basis.^([25](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr25)) If an OEM wants their device to include the Google Play app store or support Google Maps or Google’s YouTube app, they must first support Google Play Services. To receive Google Play Services, the OEM must make Google Search the default search engine and preinstall a laundry list of Google apps and services (which the user is naturally blocked from deleting) and conform to a variety of policy requirements relating to how the Android OS can (and cannot) be visually customized, which end-user data is captured and how it is used, and which services and apps the OEM can themselves preload on their device or offer to the user who buys it. OEMs must also sign agreements not to fork Android or sell devices with a forked version of Android.^([26](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr26)) In exchange for these commitments, Google shares some of its Android revenue with OEMs—they receive a portion of search-related revenues from their respective devices and also a cut of app store profits.^([27](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr27))

Over time, Google has moved many of Android’s core functions, such as background services and libraries, into Google Play Services and also expanded Google Play Services to include health and fitness, payment processing, native advertising, and the like.^([28](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr28)) Many analysts considered Google’s de facto and creeping closure of Android to be a response to Samsung’s increasing success with the operating system. In 2012, the South Korean giant sold more than 40% of Android-powered smartphones (and the majority of high-end ones)—more than seven times as many as the second-largest Android OEMs, ZTE and Huawei.^([29](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr29)) In addition, Samsung had become increasingly aggressive with its alterations to the “stock” version of Android, producing and marketing its own interface (TouchWiz), while also preloading its devices with its own suite of apps, many of which competed with those offered by Google. Samsung even added its own mobile app store. Samsung’s success as an Android manufacturer is inarguably connected to these investments, but its approach was not dissimilar to “forking” in that it threatened to disintermediate Google from its developers and users. And not only did Google clamp down on its OEM policies in response, but it acquired one of Samsung’s biggest competitors, Motorola, which subsequently released co-branded Google-Motorola Android devices that received earlier access to the newest versions of Android than truly independent Android OEMs like Samsung, LG, or HTC, among others.

After 15 years, it’s clear that Android serves a different role than what was originally pitched in 2008. At the time, Google positioned the “open-source OS” as a collective effort to build a shared ecosystem. To OEMs, Android was not just a free alternative to licensing Windows Mobile but an opportunity to participate in mobile app revenues, steward the platform’s overall development, and develop OS-level services without needing to develop and manage the underlying OS itself. For wireless operators, it was an opportunity to participate in application-layer profits and diversify from Apple. Now Google is effectively paying its partners to deploy all of its services, not just Android, while also blocking them from touting competing services or deploying their own. And if they choose to support a rival, substitute their own services, or otherwise become noncompliant, then the OEM’s users—having already bought the OEM’s device—will lose access to all of Google’s apps and service-level integrations such as cloud backup and will also need to reinstall all third-party apps from an app store they’ve never used before and that might lack some of their apps.

The history of Android serves as a warning. Though the emergence of the Metaverse offers the opportunity to disrupt today’s gatekeepers, such as Apple or Google, it’s possible that these kings will simply be replaced by another, be it Roblox, Epic, Facebook, or some as-yet-unknown entity. And the outcome may not be better, either. While Tencent’s WeChat’s 0.6% fee for real-world transactions is a fraction of that paid by consumers across the rest of the world, the company has used its control over digital payments and video games to charge 40%–55% for all in-app downloads and virtual items—a sum that far exceeds that of Apple, whose power Tencent was able to overcome with its own might, as discussed in [Chapter 10](#chapter10.xhtml).

In contrast to most major technology platforms, decentralized blockchains have no central operating entity, let alone a for-profit authority. There is no “Ethereum Corp.” that might suddenly co-opt Ethereum transaction fees or impose new ones, deny an emerging technology or standard for its own benefit, launch a first-party service that competes with the most successful dapps, and so on. What’s more, Ethereum’s trustless and permissionless programming actually encourages developers to “compete” with its core functionality.

As Ethereum became more popular throughout the 2010s, its transaction fees increased and its processing times slowed. This prompted some entrepreneurs to construct competing blockchains, such as Solana and Avalanche, both of which debuted in 2020. Other entrepreneurs instead built “scaling solutions” designed to support Ethereum, such as “Layer 2,” a “mini-blockchain” that sits on top of Ethereum, or “sidechains” that run parallel to it. These solutions process transactions in ways that are typically less secure than Ethereum but are faster and/or cheaper. One approach is to batch transactions, rather than process them individually. While this delays a payment or transfer, it also helps to minimize fees per individual transaction—and not all bills need to be paid on the spot. Another approach is to poll only a portion of eligible validators or operate a network with fewer total validators, both of which increase the risk of a transaction being hijacked but can be appropriate for less valuable transactions such as a $5 coffee (a similar approach is taken by most merchants: small purchases require only a credit card, larger ones require a zip code, and luxury purchases require address and photo ID). In theory, Layer 2s and sidechains are competitive with Layer 1s as they shift developers, validators, and users away from the “main chain.” Yet these would-be alternatives remain compatible with this Layer 1, run many of their operations through this Layer 1, and either keep “pegged” or associated tokens on or (eventually) move these assets to this Layer 1. These scaling solutions also help the Layer 1 use cases where its relatively high cost, slow speeds, and security are impractical, while also helping to reduce its network congestion, which in turn reduces its average transaction fees and time, to the aid of all developers and users on the Layer 1, which then helps the validators which support it. The model of “co-opetition” isn’t new to tech, but it’s rare that it ends well for the smaller party—especially if they run on the larger party’s own platform.

The lack of a single authority, or even group of authorities, also does not prevent a blockchain’s underlying programming from being revised, improved, or otherwise altered. However, updates require support from the community, which must therefore be convinced that any revisions are to their collective benefit. An instructive example of such a change occurred in 2022 and was dubbed “the merge.” Not only was the merge a massive overhaul of Ethereum’s operations, it also was one that involved substantial technical risks and potentially jeopardized the billions invested in “scaling solutions,” yet also offered the opportunity to dramatically improve the blockchain and resolve one of its most widely criticized problems.

At its launch in 2015, Ethereum was based on a proof-of-work (PoW) system akin to that pioneered by Bitcoin in 2009. Specifically, validators would confirm a transaction (and therefore be paid) when they had solved the cryptographic problem that was automatically generated by a proposed transaction. Though this approach is considered secure, it’s also resource-intensive, as vast computing resources were required to solve the problem—which is precisely why Ethereum transactions typically involved high costs, slow processing times, and massive energy use. Moreover, this work was not performed by a single validator but rather many validators, all of which were racing to solve it, even though only one of them would be rewarded in any given situation.

Three years after Bitcoin’s debut and two years before that of Ethereum, an alternative model known as proof-of-stake (PoS) had been deployed by a different blockchain, Peercoin. In this case, the blockchain would pick a single validator based, at least in part, on the number of tokens that validator had “staked” on the problem. Though the model created the opportunity for validators to “confirm” false transactions, other validators would be able to “whistle-blow” by proving the “correct” transaction, which would result in the dishonest validator losing their staked tokens and the auditor collecting them. These incentives and costs naturally scale, too—the larger the transaction, the more likely it is that validators will stake to validate it, and the greater the bounty from successfully disputing it and the more likely a validator is to spoof it.

As Ethereum grew from 2020 through 2022, many developers called on the community to switch from PoW to PoS to reduce fees, improve transaction times, and mitigate energy usage and the related environmental impact. Furthermore, PoS-based blockchains, such as Cardano, which debuted in 2017, and Solana, from 2020, were rapidly attracting users and developers who might otherwise have leveraged Ethereum. Some developers, conversely, feared that a switch would erode Ethereum’s security-related advantages and produce widespread compatibility errors, if not outright data loss. The adoption of PoS also put at risk the value propositions of many scaling solutions, whose tokens were worth billions combined.

Fortunately, the nonprofit Ethereum Foundation had been investigating a potential switch from PoW to PoS even before the blockchain’s launch, with a parallel PoS “test network” (Ethereum 2) launching in December 2020. In April 2022, the foundation approved plans to merge Ethereum 1’s records into Ethereum 2, which would henceforth be renamed Ethereum.^([30](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr30)) In August of that year, the foundation announced the merge would occur the following month, take roughly 15 minutes, and have no impact on token holders, developers, or system capabilities, but would permanently reduce the energy needed to process a transaction by 99.95% and potentially double or triple network throughput, too.^([31](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr31)) The merge was completed successfully and on schedule, with no known errors or losses. Validators and developers were also free to remain on the newly named “EthereumW” (as in Ethereum Proof-of-Work, or EthW for short) and, crucially, the foundation could not shut down EthereumW even if it wanted to! The immutability of EthW meant that it could stop operating only if there were no validators to run its network. And as long as there were developers and users who preferred EthW, validators would be financially incentivized to support the network—especially if most validators shifted to Ethereum 2, but the community largely remained on EthW. Nearly all users, developers, and validators did shift to Ethereum 2, though EthW was still in operation in Q4 2023.

### **Breaking the Cycle**

Blockchain’s collectivist orientation extends down into the application layer, too, where it again stands in contrast to the arc of Web 2.0. When services such as Google Maps, Gmail, Facebook, and Instagram launched in the late 2000s and early 2010s, they were considered revelations for consumers. Not only were they far better than prior solutions—where those existed at all—but they also tended to be free. A decade or so later, the situation feels quite different. In return for “free service,” users provided these services with “free data” that was of considerable value and constitutes the foundation for corporations of unprecedented profit and control. Many users now believe these companies have also harmed the world through the spread of mis- and disinformation, rampant privacy violations, algorithmic manipulation, and the relentless pursuit of profit over happy users. Their products, too, seem to have become more expensive and less useful. Searches made on Google and Amazon are increasingly cluttered with “sponsored results”—and these results are often difficult to distinguish from the genuine article. Despite this, the products of “big tech” rarely face competitive pressure. There are many reasons for this, such as the large and talented staffs wielded by these companies, their influence over consumer hardware (as discussed in [Chapter 10](#chapter10.xhtml)), and the billions in data-center or warehouse costs required to operate a large-scale service in 2024 and attract customers. One of the easiest impediments to understand is the decades of customer data the tech companies have collected and retained.

Amazon’s recommendations are powerful because they are based on years of prior searches and can also leverage a detailed understanding of a user’s prior purchases (which offers clues about what they already own and the price they might pay). Lacking such data, competitors will always have a hard path to stealing away an Amazon customer—even if they did have the equivalent inventory, prices, and delivery networks. It is certainly true that Instagram and Facebook users can download all of their photos in the form of a ZIP file, then upload them to a competing service, but it’s not an easy process and there’s no way to carry over each photo’s likes and comments or reassemble one’s social graph. In the end, a user who feels that Facebook is adversely affecting their mental health has one true alternative: to abandon the service altogether and, with it, the many years of memories and to some degree friendships. As [Chapter 10](#chapter10.xhtml) summarized, Steam’s control over player entitlements, achievements, and social graphs allowed it to beat away competitors offering exclusive games at two-thirds the price and with greater rights to developers and players alike.

Even when applications do support external data sharing via APIs, they are typically shut down whenever the application seeks out the revenues of its one-time developer partners. Facebook long allowed Tinder users to sign up for the dating app using their Facebook account, which would also help populate their Tinder profile. In the abstract, Tinder would prefer that all of its users establish and fill out stand-alone profiles, which would provide the company with greater data independence, more insight into its users, and the ability to establish its own social graph. Weighed against these benefits were several considerations. First, Tinder, unlike Facebook, was not intended to be a lifelong service for its users—but instead one used for days to months at a time, with users typically deleting their account after use. Tinder also wanted to make creating a profile “effortless,” which would help distinguish the service from market leaders such as Match or eHarmony (which required users to answer hundreds of questions about their life, beliefs, and wants) and make sure that those who downloaded the app would try its signature feature: swipe-based matchmaking.^([32](#notes_split_011.xhtml#ch11fr32)) Not only did the use of the Facebook profile API enable Tinder users to instantly sign up, they could also quickly import their Facebook profile photos, which were among the user’s “best” photos and suitable for public view—a far better experience than asking the user to dig through years of cloud storage to find that same shot, or go through the clumsy (and quality-eroding) process of screenshotting their Facebook profile photo and then uploading it to Tinder.
